authors/don.title: ᴅᴏɴ †
authors/don.content:
ᴅᴏɴ †

Self-improvement essayist publishing on Substack. Direct address, building each piece from a named mechanism — a cognitive bias, a neurochemical loop, a Japanese or Stoic philosophy, a figure from myth or history — toward a concrete practice. The recurring argument: potential is lost by default through consumption, excuses and inherited belief, and recovered deliberately through creation, incremental progress, and a curated internal world.

Website: nqdonzo.substack.com
Appears in: Neuroscience, Philosophy, Psychology
Works in this wiki: 30
What they write about
16 recurring subjects across the 30 sources, each with the pieces that carry it.
Attention, consumption and the modern environment
Short-form video read as a variable-ratio reward schedule — the slot-machine comparison is explicit — plus the dopamine-spike to cortisol chain it runs, the attention economy stated as arithmetic (view → engagement → ad revenue), akrasia as the resulting loss of self-control, and the evolutionary-mismatch argument that hardware calibrated for scarcity is being fed abundance. Returns as doomscrolling in the habit lists, as Naval’s “the modern devil is cheap dopamine”, and as notifications stealing momentum.
In: The Consumption Dilemma · Remove These Five Destructive Habits That Are Destroying Your Potential · How to Destroy Your Potential in 90 Days · I’ll Make You Believe You Can Achieve Anything after Reading This · Read this If You Want to Cure Your Procrastination
Execution — starting, finishing, prioritising
Clarity and confidence as outputs of action rather than prerequisites for it (“the cold water won’t get any warmer if you jump late”), analysis paralysis, and procrastination given a cognitive-load account rather than a moral one: the brain’s energy budget, conscious bandwidth, state-dependent memory, the Zeigarnik effect, second-order consequence chains, and the outright denial of multitasking. The allocation half is the Pareto Principle with its provenance — Pareto 1906, Juran’s “vital few and trivial many” — used mainly in reverse, to name busywork.
In: The Execution Dilemma · Read this If You Want to Cure Your Procrastination · You Need a Mindset Shift on Priorities · Five Habits You Need to Implement Immediately
Excuses, inherited belief and identity
The recurring mechanism: an excuse is a neural pathway being myelinated until avoidance fires before conscious thought, and beliefs installed in childhood run as subconscious programs that awareness alone will not remove — evidence over months does. Named endpoints are learned helplessness, victim mentality and identity-based coping (“that’s just how things go for me”); the named antidote is an internal locus of control. Identity is treated as upstream of behaviour rather than downstream.
In: Discard These Excuses Immediately Before You Severely Cap Your Potential · Five Belief Systems You Need to Remove to Become Greater · Remove These Five Destructive Habits That Are Destroying Your Potential · How to Destroy Your Potential in 90 Days · I’ll Make You Believe You Can Achieve Anything after Reading This
Mental models and cognitive biases
Munger’s latticework — big ideas from the big disciplines, the man-with-a-hammer tendency, inversion, circle of competence, the map that is not the territory, the Lollapalooza effect, ignorance removal, second-order thinking — and the five biases marked for removal by the same two-step route: novelty bias and shiny object syndrome, loss aversion (worked through 2008), herd mentality and FOMO, Dunning–Kruger including its expert’s-doubt half, and overconfidence.
In: Why You Should Adopt Many Mental Models For Your Life · Rid Yourself of These Cognitive Biases so You Can Conquer · You Need a Mindset Shift on Priorities · How to Stop Wasting Your Life (and your time)
Compounding and incremental progress
Kaizen lifted out of manufacturing and applied to a person: small continuous steps, floors rather than ceilings, the bamboo’s invisible root years, Lucretius’ water wearing stone, 1% daily compounding to 37.7×, systems over goals, and the author’s own term “escape velocity” for the point where accumulated work converts into visible results. Hormozi’s “volume negates luck” is argued here and then qualified elsewhere — ten thousand kicks are worthless if they are subpar.
In: Kaizen: A Philosophy Every Creative Should Adopt · The Anatomy of Greatness: The Psychology of Being the Best · Five Crucial Lessons from the Human Embodiment of Self-Actualization: Bruce Lee · Nine More Timeless Lessons from Naval to Make You Greater
Greatness and what it costs
Greatness decomposed into traits — strong self-concept routed through ikigai, internal locus of control, intrinsic motivation, high agency, assiduity, delayed gratification tested by the marshmallow study — and then priced: trade-offs stated as non-optional, Kobe’s 3:30 AM, Jordan’s doubled work-rate becoming the team’s baseline, ego as the ceiling via Genghis Khan’s meritocracy. Why most people stop is answered statistically, with regression to the mean, and neurologically, with the path of least resistance myelinating until quitting is the identity. Environment, social circle (no yes-men), solitude as distinct from isolation, and Taleb’s antifragility are named as the inputs you actually control.
In: The Anatomy of Greatness: The Psychology of Being the Best · How You Can Reach Excellence in a World that Demands Lesser · How to Develop an Iron Mindset to Dominate · How to Develop Unwavering Confidence and Self-Belief
Burnout, recovery and the limits of optimisation
The counterweight to the rest of the corpus’s intensity: “are we chasing the vision, or the validation?”, the cortisol feedback loop of goal-attachment, monk mode reported as personal failure and busywork, Naval’s work-like-a-lion against grazing, rest between sets as what permits intensity, what neglected sleep costs through the glymphatic system, the law of diminishing returns against twelve-hour days, and a refusal to sacrifice your twenties for your thirties.
In: Forget “Locking In.” Sometimes You Need to Lock Out. · Five Belief Systems You Need to Remove to Become Greater · Kaizen: A Philosophy Every Creative Should Adopt
Habits, protocols and the neuroscience underneath
Five habits given with mechanisms — fasted morning runs (amygdala down, cortisol down, pain tolerance up), cold showers as a graduated Wim Hof protocol whose real yield is sitting with discomfort, journaling as “releasing internal tension by way of an external channel”, finishing what you start against a RAM-limited mind, and complimenting people, costed out in dopamine, oxytocin, serotonin and reward circuitry — against five to subtract: doomscrolling, broken promises to yourself, people-pleasing, vices, negative self-talk. Neuroplasticity and myelination are the engine in both directions, with ninety days as the point of permanence.
In: Five Habits You Need to Implement Immediately · Remove These Five Destructive Habits That Are Destroying Your Potential · How to Destroy Your Potential in 90 Days
Stoicism, non-attachment and the dichotomy of control
Marcus Aurelius through Meditations — the dichotomy of control, thoughts as the quality of life, the best revenge being not to be like your enemy, embodying rather than debating a philosophy, gratitude on waking — plus the distinction that carries a whole piece: detachment pushes a thought away and rehearses it (the pink elephant), non-attachment releases the claim on an outcome. Also Seneca and Epictetus’ premeditatio malorum, memento mori as a brake rather than a spur, and five Latin phrases read as portable dispositions.
In: How To Curate An Internal World So Unshakeable that Nothing Can Stop You · The Art of Non-Attachment (in Philosophy) · The Beauty of Latin Phrases: Five Powerful Sayings from Conquerors · How to Stop Wasting Your Life (and your time) · Modern Self-Help Books Isn’t Enough: Read History, Fiction, and Mythology
History, myth and the case against modern self-help
The industry sells shovels rather than gold, so read history, fiction and mythology instead — advice that survived harder conditions than ours. The recurring cast: Caesar weeping at Alexander’s statue, Diogenes telling Alexander to get out of his sunlight, Columbus anchoring his own status with an impossible ask, Hannibal crossing the Alps, Napoleon’s speed and then his Russia, Genghis Khan absorbing what he conquered, and Icarus read twice — flight worth dying for, and the pride that spent the altitude.
In: Modern Self-Help Books Isn’t Enough: Read History, Fiction, and Mythology · What You Can Learn from Icarus on Ambition · The Beauty of Latin Phrases: Five Powerful Sayings from Conquerors · The Anatomy of Greatness: The Psychology of Being the Best
Naval Ravikant’s framework
Eighteen lessons across two pieces: long-term games with long-term people, specific knowledge that cannot be taught or automated, desire as the fundamental delusion and happiness as the absence of wanting, the modern struggle as evolutionary mismatch, “save yourself” accountability, impatience with actions and patience with results, life lived in the arena rather than in theory — then inspiration as perishable, hard choices for an easy life, the optimistic contrarian, intelligence measured as getting what you want out of life, work that is play to you and work to others, and happiness as a trainable skill.
In: Nine Timeless Lessons from Naval To Make You Greater · Nine More Timeless Lessons from Naval to Make You Greater
Faith, self-belief and its calibration
Belief acted on before the evidence exists — Topuria’s faith placing the outcome outside himself, stated intention preceding the result, first-principles mastery of each discipline separately, Neville Goddard’s law of assumption qualified so it stays non-mystical, Muhammad Ali before Foreman — and the corpus’s own correction, since the same author later uses Topuria’s loss to Gaethje as the worked example of overconfidence bias. The tension between delusional optimism and staying close to objective reality is one the author names and does not resolve.
In: How to Develop Unwavering Confidence and Self-Belief · I’ll Make You Believe You Can Achieve Anything after Reading This · Rid Yourself of These Cognitive Biases so You Can Conquer · Remove These Five Destructive Habits That Are Destroying Your Potential
Other people — approval, boundaries and the circle
People-pleasing named as the single most destructive habit, boundaries as the highest form of self-respect, Aesop on pleasing all and Lao Tzu on being their prisoner, the ship that does not open holes to let water in. On the other side: an inner circle that tells uncomfortable truths instead of comforting lies, courage redefined for a digital era as indifference to judgment, authenticity traded for approval as the disease of the feed, and complimenting people against a norm that calls it glazing.
In: How to Destroy Your Potential in 90 Days · Remove These Five Destructive Habits That Are Destroying Your Potential · Five Belief Systems You Need to Remove to Become Greater · How You Can Reach Excellence in a World that Demands Lesser · Nine More Timeless Lessons from Naval to Make You Greater · The Consumption Dilemma
Meaning, purpose and finite time
Nietzsche’s why that makes any how bearable, Maslow’s self-actualization reached in Bruce Lee, the good life as a process rather than a state, and the paradox that meaning is generated by contrast — mapped to yin and yang, argued through cheat codes and frictionless goals. The urgency machinery is explicit: a vision and an anti-vision run together (the rat, the cheese, the cat), roughly 75 of each season, 109 billion people already dead, and time as the one commodity no amount of money buys back.
In: The Art of Perseverance · The Paradox of Life · Five Crucial Lessons from the Human Embodiment of Self-Actualization: Bruce Lee · How to Stop Wasting Your Life (and your time) · What You Can Learn from Icarus on Ambition
Neurodegeneration and protecting the brain
The longest piece in the corpus reads Everywhere at the End of Time against the actual pathology of Alzheimer’s — amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles, hippocampal atrophy and ventricular expansion, retrogenesis, sundowning, aphasia decaying the album’s own cover titles, terminal lucidity in the final five minutes — and William Utermohlen’s self-portraits as the same decline in paint. The countermeasures are the point: sleep and glymphatic clearance, movement and BDNF, diet, and cognitive load heavy enough to keep synapses in use.
In: Everywhere at the End of Time: The Scariest Album Ever Created
The Genius Series
A recurring format rather than a subject: one figure studied per instalment — Charlie Munger (I), Naval Ravikant (II), Ilia Topuria (III), Michael Jordan (IV), Marcus Aurelius (V), Bruce Lee (VI) — each read for a transferable system rather than a biography.
In: Why You Should Adopt Many Mental Models For Your Life · Nine Timeless Lessons from Naval To Make You Greater · How to Develop Unwavering Confidence and Self-Belief · How to Develop an Iron Mindset to Dominate · How To Curate An Internal World So Unshakeable that Nothing Can Stop You · Five Crucial Lessons from the Human Embodiment of Self-Actualization: Bruce Lee

authors/ixcarus.title: ixcarus
authors/ixcarus.content:
ixcarus

Self-development writer publishing on Substack. The work blends neuroscience, evolutionary psychology, Jungian depth psychology, health optimization and social dynamics into a single claim: humans are biological machines running largely on autopilot, but the hardware can be reprogrammed.

Website: ixcarus.substack.com
Appears in: Economics, Neuroscience, Philosophy, Psychology, Sociology
Works in this wiki: 179
What they write about
25 recurring subjects across the 179 sources, each with the pieces that carry it.
Dopamine, wanting, and the economy of the baseline
Dopamine is treated throughout as the chemical of anticipation rather than pleasure — four pathways (mesolimbic, mesocortical, nigrostriatal, tuberoinfundibular), reward prediction error firing on the gap between expected and actual outcome, and a peak-versus-baseline economy in which artificial spikes buy height by lowering the floor toward anhedonia. Two inversions recur: “detox” is the wrong verb, because a system that kept ancestors alive for ten thousand years panics and finds worse replacements when starved, so the move is redirection into a need the low-value source was filling; and the wanting itself is not a defect but the engine of ambition, which is why work should be structured as a sequence of hunts where you never quite arrive. The downstream cases are the goal-achievement letdown, self-sabotage as the anticipation peak nearing its end, scarcity and reactance manufacturing desire unrelated to the value of the thing, the gym as a substitute that pays out visible progress while the harder invisible work starves, and delayed gratification framed as the one capability — with 98.2% never finishing what they start. Apathy is the floor of the same system: depleted baseline plus derealisation and dorsal-vagal shutdown, an empty quiet routinely mistaken for peace.
In: The Dopaminergic System: The Complete Neuroscience Breakdown · Your ‘Dopamine Problem’ Is Actually a Superpower · Why Your Dopamine Detox Is Failing · The Neuroscience of Desire (Why Wanting Feels Better Than Having) · Why You Always Want What You Can’t Have · The Four Chemicals That Control Your Happiness (And Why They’re Broken) · The One Ability That Separates Winners From Losers · Why Gym People Stay Poor (The Uncomfortable Truth) · The Psychology of Apathy
The attention economy and the engineered environment
Short-form video is the mechanism he returns to most, always described identically: the payout is the half-second of anticipation before the next clip loads, an eight-second variable-ratio schedule explicitly compared to a slot machine, with the threshold for “stimulating” recalibrating upward until real work and real conversation fall beneath it, and myelination making the damage structural rather than habitual. Around it sit Herbert Simon’s attention scarcity and the 1833 penny press as the origin of the you-are-the-product model, 47 videos watched and 3 remembered, the phone as most people’s primary emotional-regulation tool, screens as “digital cocaine” that leaves real life tasting like decaf, and consumption mistaken for progress — motivational content as “emotional porn” the brain cannot distinguish from succeeding. The prescribed antidote is boredom: receptor upregulation, the default mode network switching on, wall-staring before demanding work, walking without earphones. Two longer pieces move the argument from willpower to environment — algorithms supplying the predictions perception is built from (Plato’s cave, Bentham’s panopticon and Foucault’s internalised guard, Debord’s spectacle, the claim that ~90% of visual-cortex input comes from inside the brain), and trance as the brain’s factory setting, with infinite scroll defined as the deletion of the stopping cue and Costco and casino architecture as its physical-world equivalents. The reversal of the Flynn Effect is the population-scale version of the same claim.
In: What Short-Form Content Is Doing To Your Brain · Why 5 Second Videos Are Worse Than Drugs · The Attention Economy: You Are The Product · You’re Addicted and Don’t Even Know It · The Psychology Behind Phone Addiction · They Don’t Need To Cage You If You Cage Yourself: How Algorithms Are Constructing Your Reality · How You’re Killing Your Potential Without Realizing It · The Illusion Of Progress · Has The World Lost Its Color? · The Psychology of Consumerism: How Capitalism Needs You Miserable · The Neuroscience Of Hypnosis: How To Hijack The Exact Brain State Advertisers Use Against You · The Intelligence Decline Is Real. Here’s How To Go The Other Direction.
The subconscious as installed software
Between the third trimester and age seven the brain runs in theta — hypnotic absorption with no critical filter — so whatever went in during that window is still executing, in five named patterns: emotionally absent parent, conditional love, scarcity, unworthiness, hypervigilance. The subconscious is described not as a library but as a live predictive-processing machine that generates the emotional and physiological state before the event and then interprets reality through it, which is why “the knowing is conscious, the program is subconscious, and until you actually go in and update the program, the program wins.” Updating it takes felt experience rather than information, worked in the alpha/theta window twenty minutes either side of sleep; the crude Pavlovian version is anchoring — Robbins’ pre-speech gesture, Jordan’s free-throw ritual, and the accidental poverty anchors installed by a childhood of “we can’t afford that” — with the five-monkeys experiment standing for conditioning that outlives everyone who remembers the original punishment. The same substrate produces the rest of the cluster: thoughts arrive fully formed (ask for a blue dog and it appears), so you are the observer rather than the thinker, and Ironic Process Theory means suppression only rehearses; intuition is that machinery read back as pattern recognition delivered bodily, with the warning that a trauma response impersonates it; and micro-hesitation names the split second in which conditioning overrides the authentic move.
In: How To Reprogram Your Subconscious Mind (The Framework) · Subconscious Methods To Aid The Reprogramming Of Neural Pathways · The Conscious And Subconscious Mind: Everything You Need To Know · Internal Conflict and the Conscious-Subconscious Divide · Intuition and the Subconscious Mind: A Manual for Becoming Genuinely Intuitive · I Hacked My Brain to 10x My Income · The Forbidden Knowledge About How Your Brain Actually Works · In 1973, Three CEOs Disappeared After Exposing How Microhesitation Controls 90% of Human Behaviour
Neuroplasticity, myelination and the mechanics of habit
Plasticity is insisted on as value-neutral — the brain reinforces whatever is repeated, so bad habits are the ones running on myelinated superhighways — and the pieces here take the mechanism apart layer by layer. Synaptic connection has to exist before myelin can wrap it, which produces a four-phase habit model: reps 1–50 are barely-there construction and the point at which most people quit mistaking building for failure, 50–200 strengthen, myelination begins past 200, automaticity follows; daily repetition is mandatory because untended synaptic change decays in 24–48 hours, and habits are built one at a time because the construction budget is finite. Underneath sits hardware — Eriksson and Gage’s 1998 confirmation of adult neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus, BDNF as “miracle-gro” released by aerobic exercise, cortisol as directly neurotoxic to the hippocampus, and the split that exercise makes new neurons while novel learning is what keeps them alive — and the anterior midcingulate cortex, which grows on resistance and atrophies on comfort, so the disciplined have more structure rather than more will. Two companion pieces draw the conclusion: discipline is a lie because willpower is a depleting pool, and motivation is kindling rather than the log — a specific “dark motivation” carries the early phase until the pathway carries itself. Kaizen supplies the philosophy for all of it, 1.01^365 = 37.78×, alongside kintsugi and wabi-sabi against perfectionism as a fear response and shu-ha-ri as the ladder from following the rule to becoming it.
In: Neuroplasticity: Rewiring Your Brain To Do Hard Things · Synaptic Plasticity: What’s Actually Happening When You Try to Change · Neurogenesis: Your Brain Is Not Finished Building Itself · The Anterior Midcingulate Cortex: Your Brain’s Discipline Center · Why Discipline is a Lie · The Real Reason Discipline Alone Never Works · 5 Japanese Philosophies That Changed My Life
Perception as construction: the filter, the lens and the narrator
Roughly eleven million bits of sensory data arrive each second and forty to fifty reach consciousness, so what you call reality is the residue after the reticular activating system — a brainstem gatekeeper tuned by whatever you have repeatedly signalled as important — has finished filtering. Identity follows from this as “memorised focus,” the person you have been rehearsing, and the sharpest line in the cluster is that most people are building prisons with their focus and calling the prison their circumstances. The filter’s priorities are evolutionary rather than benevolent: six relevance filters running physical threat, social threat, uncertain reward, novelty, emotional intensity and identity relevance, with neutral good news failing to trip any of them — hence a day 95% fine that the brain spends on the 5%, and a nervous system calibrated in childhood chaos that reads peace as danger. Belief then reaches back into the body: Turin’s 1996 saline injections producing 30–50% pain reduction through genuine endogenous opioid release, open-label placebo working even when the patient knows, and nocebo doing the same in reverse. The countermeasures are training rather than positivity — romanticising as deliberate reappraisal with raised medial prefrontal activity, reduced amygdala reactivity and lower cortisol, and the inner narrator handled as construction rather than noise: Broca’s area making inner speech neurologically real, rumination holding cortisol up, Kross’s distanced self-talk converting self-evaluation into coaching, and the rule that “I made a mistake” stays outside the self-concept where “I’m an idiot” does not.
In: Your Brain Deletes 99% of Reality Before You Ever See It · How To Create Your Own Reality: The Reticular Activating System · How Your Brain Decides What Matters · The Placebo Effect: Your Brain Generating Physical Reality From Belief · How To Romanticize Your Life: A Simple Shift In Perception That Changes Everything · The Voice In Your Head Is Sculpting Your Brain
Consciousness, free will and the permanent observer
The hard problem is stated in Chalmers’ terms and left unsolved on purpose: Global Workspace, integrated information and phi, predictive processing, panpsychism and even Penrose–Hameroff’s microtubules explain correlates and never the fact of there being something it is like to be you, and “you” cannot be located anywhere in the tissue — a finding he presents as either the most terrifying or the most liberating available. Free will gets the same treatment through Libet’s readiness potential, with the conscious mind cast as “the PR department for decisions already made” and the eleven-million-bits-to-forty gap doing the rest of the work; thoughts arriving unbidden then supply the practical version — you are the sky and not the clouds, Descartes inverted into “I am, and thoughts happen around me.” The most personal piece in the cluster costs that insight honestly: awareness installs an observer that cannot participate in what it observes and cannot be switched off, partial awareness is the worst place to stop because you see enough to ruin the experience and not enough to transcend it, and the exit is not less awareness but awareness gentle enough to reach “I see the patterns, I contain the same patterns, and we’re all doing this together.” The speculative end of his range sits here too and is treated with the same posture — REM and lucid-dream induction by reality testing, MILD and wake-back-to-bed; the pineal gland, endogenous DMT and calcification; and the Kybalion’s twelve hermetic laws read back through mirror neurons, the RAS, dopamine contrast and Jung’s anima/animus, on the thesis that the ancients had imagination without instruments and the overlap with modern findings is startling.
In: Where Does Consciousness Come From? · Warning: This Post Will Give You an Existential Crisis · Do You Actually Have Free Will? · You Are Not Your Thoughts · The Paradox Of Self Awareness: You Think Too Much, And That’s Your Problem · The Neuroscience of Lucid Dreaming · The Third Eye They Don’t Want You to Know About · The 12 Laws Of The Universe: The Ancient Framework For Reality
Depth psychology: Jung, Freud and the shadow
Jung’s apparatus is laid out whole — the persona that turns pathological when you can no longer find the face beneath it, the ego as narrator rather than director, the shadow that runs behaviour from below and returns as projection (what enrages you in someone else is shadow content), the personal archive and the collective layer with archetypes recurring across cultures that never met, anima and animus projected onto partners to explain otherwise inexplicable attraction, and individuation as the lifelong integration, mapped onto neuroplasticity. Freud is read even-handedly: the cocaine, the Oedipus complex and the male-centrism conceded, the architecture kept — id, superego and ego in a war that never resolves, where the aim is only to stop being a casualty of it unknowingly; defence mechanisms as edits applied before the thought reaches you, with projection distinguished precisely (“mild dislike is just preference but that specific rage is recognition”), rationalisation as the story manufactured after the emotional decision, and repression that still moves the strings; dreams as disguised wishes, backed by imaging showing the reasoning regions powering down while the emotional core runs hotter than waking — “the censor leaving the building while the prisoners run the yard”; and free association’s heuristic that the question you least want to ask holds the answer. The split is put in one line: Jung asked who you are beneath the mask, Freud asked what is hiding under it and why you put it there. The applied pieces follow from the shadow — hatred of someone’s success as a confession about the hater, narcissism as universal design with pathology only at the exploitative end, ego as the driver of every apparently selfless act (humility included, which is why the people certain they have no ego are the most dangerous), and maladaptive daydreaming (Eli Somer, 2002) as the escape where an overdriven default mode network pays real dopamine for an imagined life and quietly prevents the person being imagined.
In: The Most Important Psychology You Will Ever Read: Jungian Psychology · You Are Not The Master Of Your Own Mind: The Psychology of Sigmund Freud · The Psychology of Hate: Hatred Is Not An Opinion About You. It’s A Confession About Them. · Why We’re All Narcissistic (And Why That’s Okay) · Everyone is Selfish (Including You) · Maladaptive Daydreaming: The Art Of Disappearing
Emotion, the nervous system and regulation
The governing fact is that the amygdala fires before you know what happened, so the only thing available for control is what comes after: Jill Bolte Taylor’s ninety-second chemical cascade dissipates on its own unless thought keeps re-triggering it, which makes rumination — not the event — the thing that holds the chemistry open, and 86,400 seconds a day surrendered to ten bad ones the standing illustration. Underneath sits Porges’ polyvagal map: ventral vagal safety where performance lives, sympathetic activation as the road to burnout, dorsal vagal shutdown as learned helplessness, neuroception scanning other nervous systems below awareness, and co-regulation making states contagious — which is why a regulated nervous system reads as magnetic and a dysregulated one repels before a word is spoken. Alongside it: Epicurus on death being nowhere we are, Stoicism’s dichotomy of control, Heraclitus on rebuilding daily, and Socratic examination as the classical form of auditing inherited belief. Mortality is done by arithmetic — roughly 700,000 lifetime hours cut to about 250,000 usable ones after sleep, childhood and old age — with terror management explaining why the brain suppresses the sum, Kant invoked for time as a frame we bring rather than find, sunlight eight minutes old and starlight from things that no longer exist, the twin paradox with its actual evidence base in atomic clocks and particle decay, temporal discounting explaining why the future self is “a character in a story you’re telling yourself,” and the hedonic treadmill closing the other end with lottery winners and people who lost the use of their legs both back near baseline in about eighteen months. The residue is practical: memento mori and mono no aware presented as tools for waking up rather than dread, felt duration as memory density so that a life optimised for routine comfort disappears in retrospect, Camus’ Sisyphus for the peace available inside struggle, and Icarus reread — the source of the pen name — as a prisoner for whom flying too high was the free choice and the labyrinth was the cage.
In: 6 Greek Philosophies That Still Run Circles Around Modern Advice · How A Man With Nothing Became Wealthier Than Emperors · How To Find Peace In Struggle · Unfortunately, The Clock is Ticking · You’re Going To Run Out Of Time Before You Run Out Of Excuses · How to Make Your Life Feel Longer Without Living Longer · Would You Rather Live in a Cage or Die Free
Meaning, belief and freedom
Nihilism is treated as intellectual cowardice rather than a position — the philosophy adopted after the failure, giving inaction a costume — while granting that cosmic indifference is true and arguing it says nothing about whether effort, mastery or connection produce meaning; the existentialist answer is to construct it anyway, and the piece notes that quitting has a philosophy while finishing only has a practice. The essay he says he was afraid to write is the most honest in the corpus, running Sisyphus, terror management theory and Frankl’s insistence that meaning is made rather than found, and ending in engagement with the uncertainty rather than an answer — while noting purpose is physically measurable in cortisol, immune function and lifespan. Belief itself is presented as structural: nobody knows what happens after death and billions organise a life around their answer, secular people hold unprovable beliefs about success and worth as rigidly as any doctrine, beliefs become neural patterns through repetition, and challenging a core one triggers the threat response reserved for physical danger. The fine-tuning piece pushes furthest — odds around one in 10^120, DNA as information, consciousness unlocated in tissue — and the wiki files it as theological philosophy rather than neuroscience; synchronicity gets a similarly personal treatment, held as meditation rather than argument. The constructive half insists purpose is built rather than discovered, since a prediction machine can only learn from actual movement, with a validation test attached — would you still do this if nobody ever knew — and freedom is decomposed into physical, mental, financial and spiritual domains, cages built from perceptual narrowing where the brain stops generating options it has learned are not for you, and real freedom named as responsibility with nobody left to blame.

demo.title: Demo
demo.content:
Demo

A map of human knowledge that grows where you walk.

Symposium reads what named people have written and distils each work into pages. A pipeline computes the links between those pages, the order to read them in, and who gets credit. As you read, it records where you went and grows the map in that direction.
The interactive version needs WebGL and JavaScript. If you are reading this text, your browser has neither switched on, and what follows is the same account in prose.
01 Intake
A work goes in, and its ideas come out as pages. Every page starts from something a named person wrote. The pipeline fetches the work into a private store, sets a depth budget for how much of it a page should carry, and writes its ideas into pages that other works feed too. Several works feed each page, so you read one author’s ideas next to what other people wrote about the same thing.
02 The graph
A notes vault keeps the links you typed. Symposium computes the rest. The links written in prose are one layer of five. The others are computed: each page to the works it came from, read from its sources:; each work to the person who wrote it, read from its author:; the reading order of a field, computed from its topic pages; and the links the prose forgot, where a page names another and never links it. The pipeline rebuilds all five from frontmatter on every change, so they stay true to the pages.
03 Provenance
Credit follows the works a page cites. Each page lists the works it was built from, and the pipeline computes credit from that list alone, page to work and work to author. If a page traces to no author, the build fails.
04 Between fields
Symposium exists for the links between fields. Each field grows as its own lobe. The good questions sit between lobes, where an idea in one field already has a name in another.
Planned: bridges, a kind of page that puts what one author says beside what an author in another field says, each claim sourced, and labels the link as one neither of them drew. If a real work already draws it, the bridge cites that work and drops the label.
05 Growth
It grows where you walk. As you read, the wiki records your trail in your browser and shows you what is one link away in the reading map. A reader’s agent reads that trail and ranks what lies just past its edge: topics named but not yet written, links that led nowhere, connections back to places you already visited. It writes those first, a little in every field and the most wherever readers keep returning.
Built now: frontier pages, unexplored places drawn dim that hold a name and the real works found for it and nothing else, and the loop that ranks an exported trail into jobs. Each job passes the same checks as any ingest, and before a person accepts a new paragraph, the tools show it beside the passage in its sources that supports it.
Planned: linking your own agent, so the loop runs on your trail instead of the maintainer’s.
06 Upkeep
Change one work and the wiki knows what it touched. Rewrite a work and the wiki flags every page built from it stale until someone rereads each against the new version. A page records what its sources said on the day someone wrote it. Each change runs the same pass: intake, then credit, then regenerating the outlines and catalogues, then two checks. Every page must trace to an author, and every link must resolve. The deploy runs both checks first and publishes nothing if either fails.
07 Architecture
Two halves are built, and a third is on the way.

The pipeline, private. Full texts, a summary of each work, and the tools that read, distil, link, credit and check. The texts belong to their authors, so this half stays private.
The wiki, public. Concept pages only. Each cites the works it rests on and links out to the originals.
Your agent, planned. Linked to your trail, it grows the map in the direction you are going, through the same checks. The model carries what the works say to you and adds no claims of its own.

Where to go

Sections: the fields, each with an outline
Authors: every writer and the pages built from them
Learn: guided paths with a finish line
The reading map: what you have read and what is next

index.title: Symposium
index.content:
Symposium

A research wiki. Each field is split into single ideas you can read in order, and every claim traces to a named author.

See the whole wiki in three dimensions

Sections

































































SectionCoversOutlinePsychologyThe science of mind and behaviourOutline · 160 pages from 150 sourcesNeuroscienceHow nervous systems compute, learn and control behaviourOutline · 63 pages from 53 sourcesMachine LearningHow machines learn from data: architectures, training, evaluation, and the systems built on themOutline · 90 pages from 44 sourcesPhilosophyKnowledge, mind, value and how to liveOutline · 37 pages from 20 sourcesBiologyHow living things are built, run and changeOutline · 22 pages from 6 sourcesEconomicsMoney, incentives, strategy and the systems they makeOutline · 13 pages from 6 sourcesSociologyHow media, institutions and groups shape what people doOutline · 11 pages from 1 sourcesMathematicsStructures, proofs and the language the other sciences are written inOutline · 8 pages from 5 sourcesInformation TheoryHow information is measured, compressed and sent through noiseOutline · 8 pages from 5 sourcesComputational FinancePricing, risk and markets, worked out numericallyOutline · 8 pages from 5 sourcesPhysicsThe laws of matter, energy, space and timeOutline · 11 pages from 5 sources
How to use it

Open a field’s outline. It lists every page in reading order, grouped by domain, with one line on what each page holds.
Read a page. The line above the title says which domain you are in and how far through it. Previous and Next at the bottom follow the outline.
Test yourself. Questions sit beside the claims they test. Once you have met one, Review brings it back at growing intervals.
Check the source. A small number in the text points to the work a claim came from. Every page ends with its works cited: the authors, and a link to each original.

Learn has shorter guided paths with a finish line. The reading map shows what you have read and what is one link away.
Page types

























TypeWhat it isconceptOne idea, technique, or phenomenonentityOne named mechanism, structure, person, or systemtopicA domain’s overview pagesynthesisA report that answers one question across a whole field
431 pages: 173 entities, 205 concepts, 49 topics and 4 synthesis reports.
More

Authors: every writer, their works, and the pages built from them
Submit a source: propose an article, paper, or file for review
Settings: account, sync, backups, and appearance

learn.title: Learn
learn.content:
Learn
A path is a fixed list of lessons through one field, with a finish line. Pick one and continue from the next unread lesson. Questions from lessons you have read come back in Review.
The paths load below. With JavaScript off, read the same pages from each field’s outline.

map.title: Reading Map
map.content:
Reading Map

This map shows the wiki’s ideas. Circles represent pages and lines represent links. The brighter route traces your last ninety days of reading, while a ring marks an unread page one link from a page you have read. Hover over or focus a circle to see its name, then open the page to continue reading.

Reading it
Choose a field above the map for a closer view. Follow a section hub’s link to open the map with that hub’s field selected.
Use the table to compare three measures for each field. explored gives more weight to the pages with the most connections, connected counts links whose two pages you have read, and pages gives the plain count.
The reading recorder marks a page seen when you arrive and read after you spend enough visible time with most of its prose.
Where this is kept
Your browser keeps those signals as the working copy for your reading map and card schedule. Sign in from Settings to add both to a recoverable cloud copy and carry them between devices. Another signed-in device can continue from the same place, with the map’s recent route intact. Review provides export and import.
You lose an unsigned local copy when you clear site data. On iPhone, install the site to keep that copy through a week away.
Without JavaScript, you can read this description. You need the browser record and JavaScript for your reader-specific view.

review.title: Review
review.content:
Review
Review cards due today. You will see cards you graded while reading and unseen cards from pages the reading recorder has marked read. You will encounter a page’s context before any of its cards appear here.
Press Space or Enter to reveal an answer. Use 1 2 3 4 to grade it Again, Hard, Good, or Easy. You can see the interval each grade will set. Choose or continue a curriculum from Learn.

How scheduling and storage work
The scheduler gives each new card one-minute and ten-minute learning steps before a five-day interval. After a lapse, it halves the earned interval and gives you a short relearning step. Set daily limits from the mortarboard in the toolbar.
Progress stays on this device unless the site has account sync and you sign in. Export and import work with or without sync. Clearing site data deletes the local copy; on iPhone, install the site to protect that copy from Safari’s short script-storage lifetime. Manage your account and cloud copy in Settings.

sections/biology/concepts/body-compositi.title: Body Composition
sections/biology/concepts/body-compositi.content:
Body Composition
Body composition is the proportion of fat mass, lean muscle mass, and bone in the human body.
flowchart TD
  B[Body composition] --> F[Fat mass]
  B --> M[Lean muscle mass]
  B --> O[Bone]
  F --> H[Metabolic and hormonal signal]
  M --> P[Physical capability signal]
  H --> A[One input to perceived attractiveness]
  P --> A

In short

Optimal ranges are 10 %–15 % body fat for men and 18 %–25 % for women, with adequate muscle.
Low body fat signals metabolic health and capability; muscle mass signals testosterone‑driven fitness.
Progressive overload resistance training and balanced nutrition reach these ranges.

In detail
These ranges mark optimal health and attractiveness:

Men: 10 %–15 % body fat with sufficient muscle mass.
Women: 18 %–25 % body fat with toned musculature.

Low body fat signals metabolic health and physical capability, and adequate muscle mass signals testosterone‑driven fitness. Progressive overload resistance training and balanced nutrition reach these ranges.


                  
                  What do the two halves of body composition each signal? 
                  
                

Low body fat reports metabolic health and physical capability; adequate muscle mass reports testosterone-driven fitness. They are separate readouts, which is why either alone is incomplete.


Connects to

health-signaling-theory: body composition is one of the four signals the theory treats as a readout of systemic health
Attraction-as-Health-Signaling: the entity page places fat distribution against the full detection system
hormone-optimization: body fat percentage governs hormone production, and hormone levels govern fat distribution
byproduct-signaling: observers can interpret the same physique differently even though appearance cannot reveal its history or motive
nutrition-and-cognition: the diet side of the same intervention, tracked for its cognitive rather than aesthetic effects
Biology: hub



Works cited

ixcarus, Why Attraction Is Health Signaling (And How to Optimize It)
ixcarus, The Complete Testosterone And Estrogen Optimization Guide
ixcarus, You Are Aging At A Speed You’re Choosing: The Neurobiology of Aging

sections/biology/concepts/chemiosmosis.title: Chemiosmosis
sections/biology/concepts/chemiosmosis.content:
Chemiosmosis
Chemiosmosis is the making of ATP by a proton gradient: energy released as electrons move down a transport chain pumps protons across a membrane, and their flow back through ATP synthase drives ATP synthesis.
In short

Most of the ATP from aerobic glucose breakdown, about 90%, comes from chemiosmosis, not from glycolysis or the citric acid cycle.
An electron transport chain of four complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane pumps protons out of the matrix.
The only way back in for those protons is through ATP synthase, which turns like a generator and joins phosphate to ADP.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and ends up as water.
The ATP yield depends on how many protons are pumped, which is why it varies.

How it works

Electrons enter. NADH hands two electrons to complex I, which pumps four protons. FADH2 hands its electrons to complex II, which skips complex I’s pump.
Electrons are carried along. Ubiquinone (Q), which dissolves in the membrane’s fatty core, takes electrons to complex III. Complex III pumps more protons and passes electrons one at a time to cytochrome c.
Oxygen is reduced. Complex IV holds an oxygen molecule between iron and copper ions until it has gained its electrons, and the oxygen then takes up protons to form water.
The gradient builds. Protons pile up in the intermembrane space. Because they are charged, this is an electrochemical gradient: a difference in concentration and in charge.
ATP is made. Protons cannot cross the membrane’s lipid core. They come back only through ATP synthase, and their flow turns parts of the enzyme, which adds phosphate to ADP.

The same mechanism powers the light reactions of photosynthesis, where it is called photophosphorylation.
Example: two poisons
The mechanism explains what two poisons do.

Dinitrophenol makes the inner membrane leaky to protons. Protons run back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, so the gradient no longer drives ATP synthesis. It was sold as a weight-loss drug until 1938.
Cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase in complex IV. Electrons back up, pumping stops, the gradient collapses and ATP synthesis stops with it.

Why the yield varies
Electrons from FADH2 skip a pump, so they make less ATP than electrons from NADH. NADH made in the cytoplasm has to be shuttled into the mitochondrion. The liver passes its electrons to NAD⁺ and the brain to FAD, so the brain gets less ATP from the same glucose. Some intermediates are also drawn off to build amino acids, nucleotides and lipids. Overall, glucose breakdown captures about 34% of the energy in glucose, and the rest is released as heat.
Related

Mitochondrion: the organelle whose cristae carry the chain
lactate-carbon-dioxide-balance: Ray Peat’s account of what switches this respiration off under stress
Cellular-Energy-and-Metabolism
Biology



Works cited

Mary Ann Clark, Matthew Douglas and Jung Choi, 7.4 Oxidative Phosphorylation - Biology 2e — OpenStax
Mary Ann Clark, Matthew Douglas and Jung Choi, 4.3 Eukaryotic Cells - Biology 2e — OpenStax

sections/biology/concepts/cold-and-heat-.title: Cold and Heat Therapy
sections/biology/concepts/cold-and-heat-.content:
Cold and Heat Therapy
Deliberate cold and heat exposure are forms of Hormesis: a bounded stress may provoke adaptation while a larger dose causes harm. That dose dependence is the central claim and the central safety limit. The mechanistic percentages and protocols below are reports from popular sources, not individualized medical advice; temperature extremes can be dangerous, especially with cardiovascular, respiratory, pregnancy, fainting, medication, or heat-illness risks.
flowchart TD
  H[Hormesis — harmful at high dose, beneficial at low] --> C[Cold exposure]
  H --> T[Heat exposure]
  C --> C1[Norepinephrine up 200 to 300 percent]
  C --> C2[Demargination — white blood cells enter circulation]
  C --> C3[Brown fat activated, dopamine elevated for hours]
  T --> T1[Heat shock proteins repair misfolded proteins]
  T --> T2[Growth hormone elevated, if you cool between rounds]
  T --> T3[Interferon production and cardiovascular conditioning]
  C --> X[Contrast — sauna, cold plunge, repeat, end cold]
  T --> X

In short

Hormesis is the central claim and the central safety limit: a bounded stress provokes adaptation while a larger dose harms.
Brief cold immersion is reported to raise norepinephrine about 200-300%, mobilise white blood cells, and activate brown fat.
Sauna is associated with heat shock proteins, growth hormone release, interferon production, and reduced cardiovascular disease risk.
The sources do not establish that contrast-therapy benefits are additive across people.
Temperature extremes carry real risk, so the protocols are source reports, not individualized medical advice.

Hormesis: The Principle
Hormesis is a biological dose response in which a substance or condition that is harmful at high doses is beneficial at low doses. The immune system’s response to pathogens, the muscle’s response to resistance training, and the bone’s response to impact loading all follow this pattern: controlled stress produces a net positive adaptation.
The same principle applies to cold and heat exposure: the body adapts to brief, controlled exposure to temperature extremes in ways that benefit multiple physiological systems.


                  
                  What is hormesis? 
                  
                

The pattern where something harmful at high dose is beneficial at low dose. The controlled stress provokes an adaptation that leaves the system better off than the exposure cost it.


Cold exposure claims and source protocols
Norepinephrine spike: Cold water immersion (14°C/57°F) for 20 seconds produces a norepinephrine increase of approximately 200-300%. Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter and hormone involved in attention, focus, mood elevation, and metabolic activation. This is the mechanism behind the immediate alertness and euphoria reported after cold exposure.
Demargination: Cold stress triggers marginated white blood cells to enter active circulation, causing a sharp increase in the bloodstream’s immune cell count for several hours after exposure. This temporary immune mobilization is part of the association between cold exposure and improved immune resilience.
Brown adipose tissue activation: Cold exposure activates brown fat (a metabolically active fat that generates heat by burning calories). Regular cold exposure increases the amount and activity of brown fat, improving insulin sensitivity and metabolic rate.
Dopamine elevation: the sources associate sustained cold exposure with a longer-lived dopamine change than a brief digital reward. They do not establish that cold “adds to baseline without debt” for every dose or make that contrast a clinical category.


                  
                  How does cold-exposure dopamine differ from a cheap dopamine spike? 
                  
                

The source contrasts a longer-lived cold-associated change with rapid repeated rewards. It does not show that every cold exposure improves mood or carries no compensatory cost.


Mental toughness training: Entering cold water activates the sympathetic nervous system and the fear response. Choosing to stay, breathe through it, and remain calm in a physiologically uncomfortable state is a deliberate exercise in nervous system regulation under stress. The essays claim that this skill transfers to all other high-stress situations.


                  
                  What transferable skill is trained by staying in the cold? 
                  
                

Staying regulated while the sympathetic system is firing. Choosing to breathe and remain calm inside genuine physiological discomfort is the same capacity every other high-stress situation calls on.


Protocols reported by the sources:

Cold shower: 30-90 seconds at the coldest available setting, minimum 3× per week
Cold immersion: 2-4 minutes in water at 10-15°C, 2-3× per week; produces stronger effects
Contrast therapy: alternating hot and cold; enhances recovery and vagal tone
Morning timing: cold exposure in the morning with natural light provides the strongest circadian entrainment and metabolic benefit

Heat exposure claims and source protocols
Heat shock proteins (HSPs): Elevated heat triggers the production of heat shock proteins, molecular chaperones that repair misfolded proteins through a mechanism implicated in aging and neurodegenerative disease prevention. Epidemiological studies associate regular sauna use with reduced Alzheimer’s risk, and the HSP mechanism is one proposed pathway.


                  
                  What do heat shock proteins do? 
                  
                

Act as molecular chaperones that repair misfolded proteins — a mechanism implicated in ageing and neurodegeneration, and one proposed pathway for sauna’s association with reduced Alzheimer’s risk.


Growth hormone release: Prolonged heat exposure (2×20-minute sauna sessions with brief cooling periods) has been shown to produce significant growth hormone elevation, reaching up to 200-300% above baseline in some studies. Growth hormone is involved in tissue repair, muscle protein synthesis, and fat metabolism.
Interferon production: Heat exposure stimulates interferon production. These antiviral cytokines form part of the innate immune response and provide one possible mechanism for the association between regular sauna use and reduced respiratory illness incidence.
Cardiovascular conditioning: The cardiovascular demands of sauna (elevated heart rate, peripheral vasodilation) produce adaptations similar to moderate aerobic exercise. Regular sauna use is independently associated with reduced cardiovascular disease risk in long-term Finnish cohort studies.
Protocols reported by the sources:

Traditional sauna: 80-100°C, 15-20 minute sessions, 3-4× per week
Lower benefit threshold: even 2-3× per week shows significant health associations
Cool down between rounds for maximum hormonal effect (cooling resets the growth hormone signal)
Minimum effective temperature: approximately 80°C; lower temperatures produce fewer effects
Hydration: significant fluid loss; replace electrolytes after sessions



                  
                  Why cool down between sauna rounds rather than staying in? 
                  
                

The cooling resets the growth hormone signal. Two twenty-minute rounds separated by a cool-down produce the large GH elevation that one continuous session does not.


Cold and Heat Together: Contrast Therapy
The essays claim that alternating cold and heat amplifies several responses relative to either alone. Their summaries do not establish that the listed benefits are additive across people or that contrast is superior for a given outcome:

The temperature differential amplifies the cardiovascular training effect
Rapid immune cell mobilization followed by systemic heat further activates innate immune functions
The vagal tone benefits of controlled cold exposure are enhanced when followed by parasympathetic recovery in heat
Hormonal responses (norepinephrine, growth hormone) are additive

The sequence they report is sauna → cold → repeat → end cold. Because rapid temperature shifts add cardiovascular stress, this is descriptive source content rather than a recommendation to perform it without appropriate screening and supervision.

sections/biology/concepts/endosymbiotic-.title: Endosymbiotic Theory
sections/biology/concepts/endosymbiotic-.content:
Endosymbiotic Theory
Endosymbiotic theory holds that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from bacteria that were swallowed by host cells and kept alive inside them instead of being digested.
In short

Endosymbiosis is a mutually beneficial relationship in which one organism lives inside another.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are about the size of bacteria and, like bacteria, have their own DNA and ribosomes.
On this account, aerobic bacteria became mitochondria and photosynthetic cyanobacteria became chloroplasts.
Ray Peat accepts the idea as possible but objects that it stops people asking how organelles form, and he prefers a self-assembly model.

The argument
Symbiosis is any close, long-term relationship between two species that depend on each other. In endosymbiosis one partner lives inside the other. The human gut is an everyday case. Its microbes make vitamin K, which we cannot make ourselves, and in return they get shelter, moisture and a steady food supply.
The theory rests on three resemblances between bacteria and the two organelles:

They are about the same size.
Both organelles carry their own DNA. The chloroplast’s genome sits on a single circular chromosome, which is the way prokaryotes keep theirs.
Both have their own ribosomes.

The proposed history is that a host cell took in aerobic bacteria and autotrophic cyanobacteria without destroying them. Over millions of years each became specialised: the aerobes into mitochondria, the cyanobacteria into chloroplasts.
Example
A plant cell holds both organelles, and both run their own genetic machinery. The chloroplast makes sugar from carbon dioxide, water and light. The mitochondrion in the same cell burns that sugar for ATP. On the endosymbiotic account these are two kinds of former bacteria, one photosynthetic and one aerobic, working inside one host. An animal cell has only the mitochondrion, which is why animals have to eat.
Where it is disputed
In Mitochondria and mortality1, Ray Peat says he has no trouble believing that organelles can pass between species, or that mitochondria could have come from bacteria. What he rejects is believing something because it could have happened. He compares it to Francis Crick’s suggestion that life arrived on space dust, which in his view explains nothing and stops people looking for an answer closer to home. His alternative, presented here as his position, extends Sidney Fox’s proteinoid microspheres. Organelles, like primitive cells, would condense out of solution as separate phases. Their growth or breakdown would depend on pH, salts and other solutes, carbon dioxide above all. He values the model because it suggests experiments. The textbook presents the bacterial origin as the account the evidence strongly supports.

sections/biology/concepts/genetic-determ.title: Genetic Determinism
sections/biology/concepts/genetic-determ.content:
Genetic Determinism
Genetic determinism is the view that an organism’s traits are the products of the specific proteins its specific genes encode. Ray Peat rejects it as ideology, and he argues that metabolism reshapes proteins and so steers development and heredity.
In short

On the standard picture, information runs one way: DNA is copied into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein.
Molecular geneticists named this one-way flow the Central Dogma. Peat argues that retroviruses, prions and directed mutation have broken it.
He argues that carbon dioxide and sugars chemically alter proteins after they are made, so a protein’s behaviour depends on the metabolic state of the cell.
He reads a tissue’s nutritional needs as developmental, set by its history, more than inborn.
These are Peat’s positions. The textbook holds that variation comes before the environment’s selection and is not produced by it.

The standard flow
DNA in the nucleus is transcribed into messenger RNA. The mRNA travels to ribosomes, which translate its base sequence into a specific order of amino acids. Enzymes, hormones, antibodies, pigments, structural parts and receptors are all made this way. In evolution, the textbook treats mutation as the ultimate source of new alleles. It holds that variation is already present before an environmental change, and that antibiotics, for example, select resistance genes without causing them.
Peat’s critique
In Genes, Carbon Dioxide and Adaptation1, Peat says the Central Dogma was framed to rule out the Lamarckian inheritance of acquired characters. He lists three counter-examples. Retroviruses use RNA as a template for DNA. The scrapie prion passes on information as protein alone. John Cairns’ directed mutations appear even in bacteria.
His mechanism is the carbamino reaction. Every protein has amine groups, which react spontaneously with carbon dioxide (and, through glycation, with sugars). That changes a protein’s electrical charge, shape and affinity for water and fat. The change is quick and reversible while carbon dioxide is present, but under metabolic stress without it the changes tend to become permanent. Peat calls this the clearest case of metabolism acting on biological structure. On this view the same gene can give a protein that behaves differently depending on the cell’s metabolic state. He links the idea to lactate-carbon-dioxide-balance.
Worked example: the riboflavin cornea
Peat cites an experiment on rats. They were made deficient in riboflavin (vitamin B2) until their corneas showed signs of it, then returned to a standard diet. The standard diet no longer met the needs of the eye tissue. For the rest of the study, only several times the normal dose kept the signs of deficiency away. On his reading, a developmental change had permanently raised the tissue’s requirement. A need that looks inborn was set by what the tissue went through, which is why he stresses prenatal nutrition and avoiding severe deficiency.
How far he takes it
Peat accepts that about 2% of human diseases involve an inherited abnormal protein. He calls it arbitrary to blame genes for cancer, diabetes or depression, and he traces determinism to the racial-hygiene writing of Konrad Lorenz. These are polemical claims. The textbook does not engage with them.

Hormone Optimization
Hormone optimization uses lifestyle and environmental changes to support natural levels of sex hormones: testosterone in men and estrogen in women. Modern environments expose people to endocrine disruptors (plastics, processed foods, chronic stress) that suppress these hormones.

  B --> O[Visible health signals]
  K --> O

In short

Endocrine disruptors such as plastics, processed foods and chronic stress suppress testosterone and estrogen.
Sleep, sunlight, stress management, resistance training and adequate protein support natural hormone levels.
Optimized hormone levels enhance secondary sexual characteristics, which improves perceived attractiveness.

In detail
Practical Recommendations

Minimize exposure to plastics and processed foods.
Prioritize sleep, sunlight, and stress management.
Use resistance training and adequate protein to boost testosterone through natural means.
For women, maintain healthy body fat percentages to support estrogen production.

Optimized hormone levels enhance secondary sexual characteristics (e.g., facial masculinity, breast development), which improves perceived attractiveness.


                  
                  Why is stress management a hormonal intervention rather than a soft one? 
                  
                

Because chronic cortisol lowers testosterone directly. Stress is not adjacent to the endocrine system here — it is one of the suppression pathways acting on it, alongside plastics and processed food.

sections/biology/concepts/lactate-carbon.title: Lactate and Carbon Dioxide Balance
sections/biology/concepts/lactate-carbon.content:
Lactate and Carbon Dioxide Balance
The lactate and carbon dioxide balance is Ray Peat’s model of cellular energy. A cell sits in one of two states, a glycolytic stress state that makes lactic acid or an efficient respiring state that makes carbon dioxide, and the ratio of the two products decides which.
This is Peat’s position, set out in Mitochondria and mortality1 and Genes, Carbon Dioxide and Adaptation2. Textbook physiology describes the same pathways but not this model.
In short

Peat holds that lactic acid and carbon dioxide have opposite effects on mitochondria: carbon dioxide stabilises and builds them, lactate degrades them.
He treats lactate as a cause of the respiratory shutdown seen in stress and disease, not only a sign of it.
Each state feeds itself, so a cell tends to slide fully into one or the other.
He reads the Crabtree and Randle effects as the machinery of the stress state, and the Pasteur effect as normal control.
He proposes that the same ratio guides development and evolution, by changing protein shape directly.

The two states
Peat starts from three named effects:

Pasteur effect: oxygen restrains glycolysis to the rate at which respiration can burn its product. He calls this a sensible control, and it fails in cancer.
Crabtree effect: excess glucose suppresses respiration. It is usually described in tumours, but Peat argues that it runs through the whole body during stress, as respiration shuts down and glycolysis takes over.
Randle effect: free fatty acids block the oxidation of glucose. High lactate means a lot of sugar is being burned, so the body releases fatty acids, which suppress glucose oxidation further. He says estrogen promotes this.

Put together, these effects push a stressed cell toward glycolysis, which yields many times less energy than oxidation. The cell makes more lactate and less carbon dioxide, and that tips it further. Peat calls shutting down the more efficient pathway during stress maladaptive. He suggests that the products of glycolysis compete physically with carbon dioxide for binding sites such as lysine, which would amount to a phase change in the mitochondrion.
The other state also reinforces itself. When resting carbon dioxide production is high, circulation and oxygen delivery stay good and glycolysis stays low. The same amount of activity then helps a person in this state and harms one in the stress state.
Example: altitude and thyroid
Thyroid hormone and adaptation to high altitude both increase the number of mitochondria, while diabetes, an energy-deficient state, does not. Peat’s explanation is that tissue carbon dioxide rises in both of the first two cases. Thyroid raises carbon dioxide production, and at altitude the Haldane effect keeps carbon dioxide from leaving through the lungs. He says that muscles adapted to low oxygen or high carbon dioxide are 50% more efficient, and adds that glucose makes more carbon dioxide per unit of oxygen than fat does.
The mechanism he proposes
In Genes, Carbon Dioxide and Adaptation2, carbon dioxide reacts on its own with the amine groups of proteins to form carbamino groups, which changes their charge, shape and affinity for water. Peat argues that this lets carbon dioxide reshape hormones, receptors and enzymes reversibly, and that losing it under stress lets those changes become permanent. See genetic-determinism.
Related

sections/biology/concepts/natural-select.title: Natural Selection
sections/biology/concepts/natural-select.content:
Natural Selection
Natural selection is the greater reproduction of individuals whose inherited traits suit their environment, which shifts the makeup of a population over generations.
In short

It follows from three facts: traits are inherited, more offspring are born than can survive, and offspring vary in heritable ways.
It is the only known mechanism of adaptive evolution.
It works only on variation with a genetic basis, and that variation is already present before the environment changes.
Populations evolve; individuals do not.
Evolution by selection has no goal. Ray Peat disputes that it is undirected.

How it works
Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace reached the mechanism independently and presented it together in 1858. Their argument has three premises:

Inheritance. Most traits pass from parent to offspring. Neither man knew how.
Overproduction. Organisms can produce more offspring than resources can support, so each generation competes. Both men took this idea from Malthus.
Heritable variation. Offspring differ, and the differences are inherited.

The conclusion follows. The variants that compete best leave more offspring, so their traits become more common. Darwin called this “descent with modification”. A trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its present environment is an adaptation, and since environments change, the direction of selection can reverse.
New variation comes from mutation, the ultimate source of new alleles, which can lower fitness, raise it or leave it unchanged. Sexual reproduction reshuffles existing alleles into new combinations. Variation without a genetic basis, such as height from better nutrition, is not passed on.
Worked example: the Grants’ finches
Peter and Rosemary Grant have measured the medium ground finch on Daphne Major every year since 1976. Bill depth varies and is inherited. A wet El Niño year left few large hard seeds and plenty of small soft ones, so small-billed birds survived and bred. In the years after, the average bill in the population was measurably smaller. When large seeds came back in 1987, the trend stopped. No individual bill changed. The population average moved because small-billed parents left more offspring.
What it is confused with
Bacteria exposed to an antibiotic do not gain resistance because of it. The resistance gene was already present at low frequency, and the antibiotic kills the cells that lack it. The textbook cites experiments showing that resistance mutations do not arise from the antibiotic itself. Selection also does not make species “better”: it tracks a changing environment.
Ray Peat’s dissent. In Genes, Carbon Dioxide and Adaptation1, Peat argues that the “directed mutations” reported by John Cairns and others show bacteria producing useful mutations in response to conditions. He also holds that metabolism, through the ratio of carbon dioxide to lactic acid, guides development and evolution, and he objects to calling evolution random. This is his position. It runs directly against the textbook account above. See genetic-determinism.

sections/biology/concepts/posture-and-mo.title: Posture and Movement
sections/biology/concepts/posture-and-mo.content:
Posture and Movement
Posture and movement quality act as both outward signals and learned internal states. Upright carriage and coordinated movement are visible proxies for physical capability1. They also run a feedback loop: the nervous system learns repeated alignment and eventually experiences that position as neutral2.
In short

Repeated head-forward hours train the brain’s body map until true neutral feels like an overcorrection.
Durable correction is retraining: strength, mobility, repeated exposure to neutral alignment, and an environment that supports it.
Posture is the cheapest, most immediate health signal to change, though making it the default takes longer.

The proprioceptive map
The brain maintains a continuously updated model of where the body is in space. Hours spent with the head forward and shoulders rounded train that map, weaken the muscles that would hold neutral alignment, and make an objectively neutral position feel like an overcorrection. A reminder to “sit straight” must compete with a motor program reinforced by thousands of repetitions.
Posture also changes breathing mechanics. Rounding the thorax limits diaphragmatic range and promotes shallow chest breathing, which is associated with sympathetic activation and reduced cognitive clarity. The link runs through these mechanics; it does not rest on the looser claim that confidence alone changes body chemistry.
Correction is retraining
Durable correction combines capacity, mobility, sensory evidence, and environment:

strengthen deep cervical flexors and the muscles that position the shoulder blades;
lengthen the chest and compressed tissues at the base of the skull;
repeatedly expose the nervous system to neutral alignment, including wall drills;
place phones and monitors at eye level and make the chair support the intended position.

Equipment placement connects posture to environmental-design. A screen that keeps pulling the head forward forces conscious reminders to compete with the room all day. Changing the room lets each repetition reinforce the intended map.
As an attractiveness signal, posture is unusually cheap and immediate to begin changing. That immediate visual adjustment is distinct from the slower retraining required to make it the body’s default.


                  
                  What makes posture the first move among the health signals? 
                  
                

Its cost. Every other signal takes money or time; posture can be corrected immediately at no expense, which puts it ahead of the interventions that need either.

Skin Health

Clear, even-toned skin signals low inflammation, balanced hormones, adequate nutrition and good sleep.

Appearance is not a diagnosis; skin conditions have many causes and may need clinical treatment.

In detail
The claim is causal: skin can be downstream of sleep, inflammation, nutrition, and endocrine state. A person’s appearance does not provide a diagnosis; skin conditions can have many causes and may require clinical treatment rather than lifestyle inference.

sections/biology/entities/biological-age.title: Biological Age
sections/biology/entities/biological-age.content:
Biological Age

Biological age measures cellular condition rather than calendar time and can change substantially. At least one 2023 study measured an average reversal of around three years in eight weeks.

flowchart TD
  A[Chronological age] --> D[Different biological clocks]
  D --> E[Epigenetic marks]
  D --> T[Telomeres]
  D --> M[Metabolic immune and organ function]
  E --> B[Composite biological age]
  T --> B
  M --> B
  L[Sleep stress movement and diet] --> D

In short

Dozens of biological clocks tick at once, and which one runs fast is not fixed.
Growth and maintenance compete: growth hormone is pro-aging, and slower development tracks with longer life.
Feeling younger than your calendar age predicts better health, slower cognitive decline, and longer life.
A 2023 epigenetic-clock study cut biological age by around three years in eight weeks.

Many Clocks, Not One
Biological age has no single value. Your passport may say 35 while the heart runs like 28, the immune system like 48, and the metabolism “like someone who hasn’t stood up in twenty years.” Dozens of clocks tick at once, each responding to different inputs.
A grandmother’s observation makes the point. Her hands were worn and veined, “this is where time lives,” while her eyes stayed exactly what they had always been. Different parts age at different speeds, and which clock runs fast is not fixed.


                  
                  Why is there no single number for "your biological age"? 
                  
                

Dozens of clocks run at once and respond to different inputs. The heart can read 28 while the immune system reads 48 on the same passport age.


Measurement
The Horvath clock reads chemical marks on DNA to estimate cellular age. Results show people ten, fifteen or twenty years younger biologically than someone of identical calendar age, “and the gap between those two numbers is almost entirely written by how you’ve been living.”


                  
                  What does the Horvath clock actually read? 
                  
                

Chemical marks on DNA. It estimates cellular age from the epigenetic layer, which is why two people of identical calendar age can differ by fifteen or twenty years on it.


Growth Versus Maintenance
One finding qualifies most optimisation advice: the periods when you feel most vital, infancy and puberty, are when you age fastest. Slower development and later puberty correlate with longer life; animals bred to grow fast and mature early die young. Growth hormone is pro-aging, and animals engineered with very little live longest by a wide margin. “The body can build or the body can maintain. It struggles to do both hard at the same time.”


                  
                  Why are the periods of greatest vitality also the periods of fastest ageing? 
                  
                

Because building and maintaining compete. Growth hormone is pro-aging, and the body struggles to do both hard at once — which is why slower development and later puberty track with longer life.


The Subjective Age Effect
People who genuinely feel younger than their calendar age show better health, slower cognitive decline and longer lives than same-age people who feel every year of it. People in their late twenties who describe their prime as behind them are pointing learned helplessness at their own body. Most who fall apart swapped training for nostalgia and called it aging.


                  
                  What does subjective age predict, independently of calendar age? 
                  
                

Health, rate of cognitive decline and lifespan. People who genuinely feel younger than their years outperform same-age people who feel every one of them.




                  
                  Why does the source call "my prime is behind me" at twenty-nine learned helplessness? 
                  
                

Because it is a belief about uncontrollability applied to the body, and it becomes self-confirming — most people who fall apart swapped training for nostalgia and named the result aging.


The mind writes the story and the body reads it back.
Reversal
A 2023 study using epigenetic clocks produced an average reduction of around three years of biological age in eight weeks through diet, sleep, movement, stress work and targeted supplementation. Larger reversals take longer, “but the direction is proven.”


                  
                  What did the 2023 epigenetic-clock study establish? 
                  
                

That the direction reverses. Around three years of biological age came off in eight weeks via diet, sleep, movement, stress work and supplementation — the size is modest, the reversibility is the finding.
