sections/machine-learning/concepts/compo.title: Component-Wise RAG Evaluation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/compo.content:
Component-Wise RAG Evaluation
Component-wise RAG evaluation measures retrieval evidence separately from generation behaviour, because an end-to-end answer score cannot locate a RAG failure. The separation in Primers • Retrieval Augmented Generation1 lets practitioners improve ingestion, candidate discovery, reranking, and synthesis independently.
flowchart LR
  I[Ingestion] --> R[Candidate retrieval]
  R --> K[Reranking]
  K --> G[Generation]
  R --> C[Measure context precision and recall]
  G --> F[Measure groundedness and answer relevance]
  C --> D[Locate missing-evidence failures]
  F --> D[Locate synthesis failures]
  D --> O[Join component results to product outcome]

In short

Context precision is the share of retrieved material that is relevant; context recall is the share of required evidence recovered.
A faithful answer can be wrong from a wrong source, and a correct answer can be ungrounded.
Component scores must join latency, cost, permissions and user outcome, and automated judges add another fallible component.



                  
                  Why can an end-to-end answer score not diagnose a RAG system? 
                  
                

It cannot tell whether evidence was missed during retrieval or mishandled during generation.




                  
                  What is the difference between context precision and context recall? 
                  
                

Precision asks how much retrieved material is relevant; recall asks how much required evidence was recovered.


Retrieval measures include context precision, the share of retrieved material that is relevant, and context recall, the share of required evidence recovered. Context relevance asks whether passages address the query. Measuring these properties requires a reference set or judge and should happen before generation can obscure what was available.
Generation measures include groundedness or faithfulness to retrieved evidence, answer relevance, semantic similarity, exact match, string presence, and entity recall. A faithful answer can be wrong because the retrieved source was wrong; a factually correct answer can be ungrounded because the model used parametric memory. Both distinctions matter.
Diagnostic matrix

low retrieval recall + poor answer: missing evidence;
high retrieval quality + poor groundedness: synthesis failure;
high groundedness + wrong answer: corpus or reference failure;
good component scores + poor product outcome: metric or task mismatch.

Practitioners should combine component metrics with latency, cost, permissions, user outcome, and adversarial slices. Automated model judges can scale evaluation but introduce another fallible component.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/conte.title: Context Engineering
sections/machine-learning/concepts/conte.content:
Context Engineering
Context engineering decides what a model sees on each call. Context determines the upper limit of agent capability1: the model cannot act on information it never receives, so context becomes the binding constraint before model quality.
flowchart TD
  X[Context — the observation space, and it holds the tool definitions] --> L[Sets the upper limit of agent capability]
  D[Dynamic prompts, agent skills, the status bar] --> X
  A[Attention made distance within the window free] --> W[The window itself is finite]
  W --> P[More relevant information exists than fits]
  P --> C1[Compression, when the trajectory outgrows the window]
  P --> C2[Retrieval from an external store]
  P --> C3[Memory hierarchies]
  K[Stable parts first, volatile parts last] --> KV[The KV cache survives across turns]
  KV --> LC[Lower latency and cost]



                  
                  Why is context the binding constraint before model quality is? 
                  
                

The model cannot act on what was never put in front of it. However capable the policy, its ceiling is set by what the context actually contains.


In short

The model cannot act on information it never receives, so context binds before model quality does.
Tool definitions live in the context, so the observation space describes the action space.
Putting stable prompt parts first and volatile parts last keeps the KV cache valid, lowering latency and cost.
Compression, retrieval and memory hierarchies all answer one problem: more relevant information exists than fits.
Attention made distance within the window free, leaving the window itself as the constraint.

Context is the observation space
In Bojie Li’s mapping onto reinforcement learning, Agent = LLM + Context + Tools corresponds to policy + observation space + action space. Context is what the agent can perceive. Tool definitions live in the context, so what the agent “sees” includes what it can do. The observation space contains a description of the action space, complicating the eyes/hands metaphor.


                  
                  Where does the eyes/hands split between context and tools break down? 
                  
                

Tool definitions live in the context. So the observation space contains a description of the action space — what the agent sees includes what it can do.


The engineering, concretely

KV-cache-friendly design. Order the prompt so the stable parts come first and the volatile parts last, allowing the cache to survive across turns. Prompt ordering alone produces this latency and cost property, showing how an implementation detail of Transformer inference dictates application architecture.



                  
                  Why does prompt ordering affect latency and cost?
                  
                

The KV cache survives only up to the first change. Putting the stable parts first and the volatile parts last keeps the cached prefix valid across turns — an inference detail that dictates application architecture.



System prompt optimisation: prompt engineering as one technique within the broader practice of context engineering.
Dynamic prompts and agent skills: assembling the context per call from the task’s needs, rather than shipping one static prompt.
The agent status bar: injecting meta-information about the trajectory so the model can reason about its place in a long task as well as what was said.



                  
                  What does an agent status bar give the model that the transcript alone does not? 
                  
                

Where it is in the task. The conversation records what was said; injected meta-information about the trajectory lets the model reason about its own progress through a long run.



Context compression: explicit strategies for trajectories that outgrow the window.

Why it exists at all
Every source in this section that covers agents encounters the same finite context window:

LLM Powered Autonomous Agents2 names finite context length as its first limitation and notes that vector stores extend reach, though their representational power is weaker than full attention.
rag-vs-long-context treats retrieval and window capacity as complementary: retrieval saves tokens and isolates evidence, while long context preserves material a retriever might omit.
Context compression, retrieval, and memory hierarchies address the same problem: more relevant information exists than fits.

Within retrieval, context quality begins before prompting. retrieval-chunking-boundary determines whether qualifications stay attached to claims, while component-wise-rag-evaluation distinguishes a context-selection failure from a generation failure.


                  
                  What single problem do compression, retrieval and memory hierarchies all answer? 
                  
                

That more relevant information exists than fits. Each is a different way of choosing what makes it into a finite window.


Context engineering brings long-term-dependency to the application layer. Attention made distance within the window free, leaving the window itself as the constraint. Context engineering governs how an application spends that finite budget.


                  
                  What did attention do to the long-dependency problem rather than solve? 
                  
                

It moved it. Distance within the window became free, and the window itself became the constraint — so the problem reappears one layer up as how to spend a finite context budget.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/convo.title: Convolutional Networks
sections/machine-learning/concepts/convo.content:
Convolutional Networks
A convolutional network is an ordinary neural network with two extra assumptions about images, and those two assumptions are the entire invention1. Everything else — learnable weights, dot products, non-linearities, a loss on class scores — carries over from the fully-connected model unchanged.
In short

Local connectivity ties each neuron to a small receptive field across the full input depth.
Parameter sharing assumes a feature useful at one position is useful everywhere, cutting a first AlexNet layer from ~105 million weights to ~35,000.
Size-preserving convolutions leave downsampling to max pooling, and stacked 3×3 filters beat one big receptive field.
Any FC layer converts to a conv, and strided convolutions are replacing pooling.

The two constraints
Local connectivity. A fully-connected neuron facing a 200×200×3 image needs 120,000 weights, and you want many such neurons — parameters explode and overfitting follows. Convolutional neurons instead connect to a small spatial region, the receptive field, but always to the full input depth: connectivity is local in width and height, complete across channels.
Parameter sharing. The heavier reduction: assume a feature useful at one position is useful everywhere. All neurons in a depth slice share one filter, so a first AlexNet layer collapses from ~105 million weights to ~35,000. With shared weights the layer’s forward pass is literally a convolution of each filter with the input — which is where the name comes from.


                  
                  When should parameter sharing be relaxed? 
                  
                

When inputs have centered structure that makes position matter — faces are the canonical case, where eye-specific features belong near the eyes and nowhere else. Dropping sharing turns the layer into a locally-connected one: still spatially local, but every location learns its own weights.


The arithmetic and the stack
Three hyperparameters control a conv layer’s output: number of filters (depth), stride, and zero-padding, with size given by (W − F + 2P)/S + 1. The house discipline: P = (F−1)/2 at stride 1 keeps convolutions spatially size-preserving, leaving downsampling entirely to max pooling (2×2, stride 2, zero parameters, discarding 75% of activations, routing gradients through the max index). Stacking small filters beats one big receptive field: three 3×3 layers see 7×7 but add two non-linearities and cost 27C² rather than 49C² parameters — hence VGG’s homogeneous design, and the canonical pattern INPUT → [[CONV → RELU]*N → POOL?]*M → [FC]*K.
Two conversions matter in practice. Any FC layer is equivalent to a conv whose filter matches its input volume, so converting lets one forward pass score every position of a larger image at once. And pooling itself is on the way out — strided convolutions replace it, and generative models train better without it.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/diffu.title: Diffusion Guidance
sections/machine-learning/concepts/diffu.content:
Diffusion Guidance
Diffusion guidance steers the reverse process toward a condition such as a class label or text representation. It takes two routes1.
flowchart TD
  G[Steer the reverse process] --> C[Classifier guidance]
  G --> F[Classifier-free guidance]
  C --> S[Separate noisy-image classifier supplies a gradient]
  F --> M[One model learns conditional and unconditional predictions]
  S --> A[Stronger condition adherence]
  M --> A
  A --> T[Higher scale trades diversity for alignment and artifacts]

In short

Classifier guidance steers the reverse score with the gradient of a separate classifier trained across noise levels.
Classifier-free guidance trains one model with and without the condition and scales the difference of its predictions.
A higher guidance scale improves alignment while reducing diversity, and guidance does nothing for sampling speed.

In detail


                  
                  How does classifier-free guidance avoid a separate classifier? 
                  
                

One model learns both conditional and unconditional predictions, whose difference steers sampling.




                  
                  What does a higher diffusion guidance scale trade away? 
                  
                

Diversity and sometimes artifact-free samples, in exchange for stronger condition adherence.


Classifier guidance uses the gradient of a separately trained noisy-image classifier to modify the unconditional reverse score. The classifier must operate across diffusion noise levels, and its gradient points sampling toward regions associated with the desired class.
Classifier-free guidance trains one model with and without the condition by sometimes dropping conditioning. At sampling time, conditional and unconditional predictions are combined; scaling their difference strengthens adherence to the condition without requiring a separate classifier.
Increasing the guidance scale incurs a tradeoff. Stronger conditioning can improve prompt or class alignment while reducing diversity and producing artifacts or oversaturated samples. Training must make both the unconditional and conditional branches accurate enough for their difference to provide a useful direction.
Separation from generation speed
Guidance determines where the reverse trajectory is steered. Fewer-step samplers, distillation, consistency models, and latent diffusion determine the cost of traversing that trajectory. A method can change one without solving the other.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/diffu.title: Diffusion Noise Prediction
sections/machine-learning/concepts/diffu.content:
Diffusion Noise Prediction
A diffusion model can train without simulating every forward step, by predicting the noise added at one sampled timestep1. The forward Gaussian process has a closed form for sampling a corrupted (x_t) directly from clean data (x_0) at a chosen timestep. Training samples (t), adds known noise (\epsilon), and asks a network to predict that noise from (x_t) and (t).
flowchart LR
  X[Clean sample] --> N[Choose a timestep and add known noise]
  N --> C[Corrupted sample]
  C --> M[Network predicts the added noise]
  M --> L[Denoising loss compares predicted and known noise]
  L --> R[Learned reverse denoising direction]

In short

A closed-form forward process lets training corrupt clean data directly at any chosen timestep.
The simplified objective is squared error between the known added noise and the network’s prediction.
The simplified epsilon loss is one of several diffusion objectives, and weighting, schedules and sampler still alter behaviour.

In detail


                  
                  Why can diffusion training corrupt a clean sample at any chosen timestep directly? 
                  
                

The forward Gaussian process has a closed form, so earlier corruption steps need not be simulated.




                  
                  What target does the standard simplified diffusion objective predict? 
                  
                

The known noise added to the clean sample.


The original variational lower bound decomposes into a terminal term without learned parameters, Gaussian KL terms for intermediate reverse transitions, and a decoder term at the final step. Under the DDPM parameterization, the relevant mean-prediction terms can be expressed as weighted denoising losses. The widely used simplified objective trains on squared error between sampled and predicted noise.
Noise prediction parameterizes the reverse process. It does not show that the model stores clean images or merely removes visible static. Across noise levels, the network estimates the direction needed to move a corrupted sample toward higher data density, linking DDPM training to noise-conditioned score estimation.
Boundary
Loss weighting, variance schedules, reverse variance, prediction target, and sampler alter behaviour. The practical and influential simplified epsilon loss remains one of several diffusion objectives; other bound terms and modelling choices still matter.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/distr.title: Distributed LLM Training
sections/machine-learning/concepts/distr.content:
Distributed LLM Training
Distributed LLM training partitions model state, activations, sequences, and examples across devices while keeping one optimization run coherent. The 405B Llama-3 run in The Llama 3 Herd of Models1 posed this systems problem on as many as 16,384 H100 GPUs.
In short

Tensor, context, pipeline, and data parallelism are ordered so the most bandwidth-hungry dimensions sit within tighter network boundaries.
FP32 gradient accumulation keeps convergence stable across layouts, and the configurations reach 38 to 43 percent model-FLOPs utilization.
Automated recovery kept effective training time above 90 percent through 466 interruptions in 54 days.
Infrastructure limits can push a team away from the fitted compute optimum.

Four dimensions of parallelism
The run combines four methods. Tensor parallelism splits weight tensors. Pipeline parallelism assigns layer stages to different ranks and moves micro-batches through them. Context parallelism divides long input sequences. Fully sharded data parallelism partitions optimizer state and gradients while workers process different examples.
The team orders the dimensions as tensor, context, pipeline, and data parallelism. The first dimensions need the most bandwidth, so ranks place them within tighter network boundaries. Data-parallel communication can tolerate more latency because workers prefetch parameter shards and reduce gradients without blocking the same parts of the computation.
Pipeline schedules need balance as well as partitioning. The team removes a Transformer layer from the first and last stages to offset embedding and loss work, interleaves stages, and lets operators tune contiguous micro-batch count. Context parallelism splits a sequence into paired chunks and gathers key and value tensors while each rank keeps its query chunk. Grouped-query attention makes those gathered tensors smaller.
Numerical and hardware constraints
A valid partition must fit parameters, optimizer state, gradients, and activations into device memory. The team builds memory and performance estimators to compare configurations before a run. It accumulates and reduces gradients in FP32 to avoid convergence changes across parallel layouts, while BF16 carries much of the model computation. The reported configurations reach 38 to 43 percent model-FLOPs utilization.
The physical cluster shapes the software choices. Each eight-GPU server uses NVLink. A three-layer Clos network connects up to 24,000 GPUs, with full bisection bandwidth inside 3,072-GPU pods and oversubscription between pods. The scheduler and parallel layout reduce cross-pod traffic. A distributed file system supplies 240 petabytes and absorbs bursty checkpoints at up to 7 terabytes per second.
Reliability becomes training efficiency
Synchronous training lets one failed component stop thousands of peers. During a 54-day period, the team records 466 interruptions, including 419 unexpected events. Hardware accounts for most diagnosed failures, with GPUs forming the largest group. Automated recovery, checkpointing, watchdogs, and communication traces keep effective training time above 90 percent; operators intervene by hand three times in that period.
Stragglers pose a separate problem because a slow device can retain correct outputs while delaying the whole job. The team ranks suspect communication groups and records collective traces to locate slow hosts. It also observes a 1 to 2 percent daily throughput swing from temperature effects on GPU clocks.
Connection to scaling
scaling-laws chooses parameter count, batch size, token count, and update count. Distributed training makes that allocation executable. A large critical batch offers data parallelism, a large model requires tensor and pipeline partitioning, and a 128K context calls for context parallelism. Infrastructure limits can push a team away from the fitted compute optimum even when the loss model supplies a clear target.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/embed.title: Embedding
sections/machine-learning/concepts/embed.content:
Embedding
An embedding is a token’s vector and the space it inhabits, where directions carry meaning. A transformer expresses each operation as an edit to positions in this space.
flowchart LR
  T[Token] --> WE[W_E lookup — one column per vocabulary item]
  WE --> V[A vector encoding that token and nothing else]
  P[Position, encoded in the same vector] --> V
  V --> A[Attention and MLP blocks edit the position]
  A --> C[A vector that has soaked up the surrounding context]
  C --> WU[W_U unembedding — one value per vocabulary token]
  WU --> L[Logits]
  L --> S[Softmax — a distribution over next tokens]
  CS[Context size — the attention pattern is its square] -->|a hard ceiling| A

Training operates on continuous values, so models must encode language as numbers. The learned encoding develops a legible geometry.
In short

W_E starts each token as a context-free lookup, and attention and MLP blocks then enrich it with context.
Directions in the space carry meaning, and the dot product measures how far a vector points along one.
Context size is a hard ceiling, because the attention pattern grows with the square of the context.
W_U turns the last vector into logits, and during training every final-layer vector predicts what follows it.

The lookup table is only the starting point
The first matrix, W_E, has one column per vocabulary item. In GPT-3, that means 50,257 columns × 12,288 dimensions = 617,558,016 weights. At that moment a vector is a lookup with no input from its surroundings: it encodes one token and nothing else.
The network then enriches that vector with context. That is the primary goal: each vector soaks up meaning richer and more specific than individual words can represent1. A vector that began as king can end up encoding a king who lived in Scotland, who took the throne by murdering his predecessor, described in Shakespearean language.
A mystery novel ending “Therefore the murderer was…” shows the requirement2. The final vector, which started life embedding was, must absorb everything in the context relevant to the answer because it is the only vector used for the prediction.


                  
                  What is a token's vector at the moment it leaves the embedding matrix? 
                  
                

A lookup with no input from its surroundings — it encodes that token and nothing else. Everything that follows exists to make that stop being true.




                  
                  Why must the last vector in a mystery novel carry the whole plot?
                  
                

Because it is the only vector used for the prediction. A vector that started life embedding “was” has to have absorbed everything in the context relevant to naming the murderer.


Directions have meaning, and the dot product tests them

Nearest neighbours of tower share a recognisable character.
woman − man ≈ king − queen. Sanderson qualifies the classic example: in the model he used, queen sits farther off than the difference predicts, “presumably because the way queen is used in training data is not merely a feminine version of a king.” Family relations demonstrate it better.
Italy − Germany + Hitler lands near Mussolini. Some directions appear to encode Italian-ness, others Axis leadership.



                  
                  Why does Sanderson qualify the king − man + woman ≈ queen example?
                  
                

In the model he used, queen sits farther off than the difference predicts — presumably because queen is not used in training data as merely a feminine king. Family relations demonstrate the property more cleanly.


The dot product turns a hunch about a direction into a measurement: positive when aligned, zero when perpendicular, negative when opposed. Take cats − cat as a candidate plurality direction and dot it against nouns. Plurals score consistently higher, and one, two, three, four give increasing values, as though the direction quantitatively measures how plural the model finds a word.


                  
                  How do you test whether a direction in embedding space means what you think? 
                  
                

Dot it against words you have opinions about. Take cats − cat as a candidate plurality direction and plurals score higher; one through four give increasing values, which is the direction measuring degree rather than just membership.


This is the machinery every later block reuses: Attention in transformers, step-by-step — Deep Learning Chapter 62 scores key–query alignment by dot product, and How might LLMs store facts — Deep Learning Chapter 73 reads MLP rows as directions whose dot product with a vector asks a question about it.
Position is in there too
Embeddings also encode where a token sits through positional-encoding, so a single vector’s entries tell you both what the word is and where it is in the context.
Context size is a hard ceiling
GPT-3’s context was 2048 tokens, so the data flowing through is a 2048-column array of ~12k-dimensional vectors. Sanderson attributes early ChatGPT’s tendency to lose the thread in long conversations to that limit. Enlarging it is nontrivial because the attention pattern is the square of the context size.


                  
                  Why is enlarging the context window not simply a matter of allocating more memory? 
                  
                

The attention pattern is the square of the context size. Doubling the window quadruples that cost, which is why the limit that made early ChatGPT lose the thread was hard to lift.


Unembedding, and how many predictions get made
W_U maps the last vector to ~50,000 values, one per token. It has the same shape as W_E with rows and columns swapped, adding another ~617M parameters. Those raw unnormalised values are the logits; softmax turns them into a distribution.
Using only the final vector looks wasteful given thousands of context-rich vectors sitting in that layer. During training, every vector in the final layer simultaneously predicts what follows it, so one passage acts as many training examples. Masking is required, because later tokens must not leak backwards into earlier predictions2.


                  
                  What are logits, and what turns them into a prediction? 
                  
                

The raw unnormalised values the unembedding matrix produces, one per vocabulary token. Softmax converts them into a probability distribution.




                  
                  Every final-layer vector predicts what follows it. What does that buy, and what does it require? 
                  
                

It buys training efficiency — one passage becomes many training examples. It requires masking, because a prediction made at an early position must not see the later tokens that would give away its answer.


How many meanings can a space hold?
A space can hold more meanings than its dimension count; superposition explains how.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/estim.title: Estimation and Uncertainty
sections/machine-learning/concepts/estim.content:
Estimation and Uncertainty
A sample statistic estimates an unknown population quantity: the sample mean targets expectation, and sample variance targets dispersion. Super VIP Cheatsheet: Machine Learning1 places parameter estimation between probability definitions and machine-learning algorithms.
flowchart LR
  P[Unknown population quantity] --> S[Sample statistic]
  S --> B[Sampling bias]
  S --> V[Sampling variance]
  S --> D[Approximate sampling distribution]
  D --> E[Standard error model]
  E --> C[Confidence interval]
  C --> M[Match precision claims to data generation]

In short

Estimator bias and sampling variance are properties of a sampling procedure, and they underlie the bias-variance tradeoff.
A confidence interval expresses repeated-sampling coverage, not the probability that a fixed parameter lies in one realized interval.
Dependence, heavy tails, selection, small samples and misspecification can invalidate routine approximations.

In detail


                  
                  How do estimator bias and sampling variance differ? 
                  
                

Bias is the expected offset from the target; variance is how estimates change across possible datasets.




                  
                  What does a frequentist confidence interval describe? 
                  
                

Repeated-sampling coverage, not the probability that a fixed parameter lies in one realized interval.


Estimator bias is the difference between an estimator’s expected value and the parameter it targets. Sampling variance describes how much the estimate changes across possible datasets. Both are properties of a sampling procedure rather than one observed number, and they underlie the bias-variance-tradeoff in predictive modelling.
The central limit theorem motivates an approximately normal sampling distribution for suitably normalized sums or means under its conditions. Confidence intervals combine an estimate with a standard-error model to express repeated-sampling coverage. Under a frequentist interpretation, this coverage does not assign a probability that a fixed parameter lies in one realized interval.
The cheatsheet is a compact formula reference and does not enumerate all regularity assumptions. Dependence, heavy tails, selection, small samples, and model misspecification can invalidate routine approximations. The data-generating process should therefore determine reported precision.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/evalu.title: Evaluation Metrics
sections/machine-learning/concepts/evalu.content:
Evaluation Metrics
An evaluation metric encodes a decision about which errors matter, so choosing one is part of modelling and is no reporting formality. Every claim about a machine learning system rests on a metric.
flowchart TD
  Q[What decision must the metric support] --> C[Classification errors]
  Q --> R[Regression fit]
  Q --> G[Generated text quality]
  Q --> K[Ranking quality]
  Q --> P[Component behaviour]
  P --> E[End-to-end outcome]



                  
                  Why is choosing a metric a modelling decision rather than a reporting one? 
                  
                

Each metric encodes a judgement about which errors matter. Picking one has already decided what the system is allowed to get wrong.


In short

Classification metrics all derive from the four confusion-matrix cells and differ only in their denominators.
Clustering metrics without ground truth describe the partition, not its correctness.
Perplexity measures predictive fit, and burstiness catches the endless repetition perplexity misses.
A RAG system needs retrieval and generation scored separately, because an aggregate cannot tell which failed.
A reward model is a learned metric, capped near 73% labeler agreement and valid only where it has data.

The classical core
The 2018 CS229 foundation comes from VIP Cheatsheet: Machine Learning Tips and Tricks1. False negatives are Type II errors and false positives are Type I. Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F₁ each have an interpretation, and the ROC equivalences are explicit: TPR = recall = sensitivity, FPR = 1 − specificity. F₁ is a hybrid metric useful for unbalanced classes, which says when to use it as well as what it is.
Regression model selection uses criteria that penalise parameter count: Mallow’s Cₚ, AIC, BIC, and adjusted R². Fit alone is not evidence.
Without ground truth, assessment becomes difficult. The substitutes in VIP Cheatsheet: Unsupervised Learning2, the silhouette coefficient and the Calinski-Harabaz index, measure whether clusters are dense and well separated. They describe the partition rather than its correctness, answering a question adjacent to the intended one. Reward-Model has the same gap.


                  
                  What do clustering metrics like the silhouette coefficient actually measure? 
                  
                

Whether the clusters are dense and well separated — a property of the partition, not of its correctness. With no ground truth available, the metric answers a question adjacent to the one being asked.


Classification: the confusion matrix and its readings
Accuracy, precision, recall, F₁, sensitivity, specificity, negative predictive value, ROC, AUROC, equal error rate, and DET curves all derive from the same four cells. They differ in their denominators.
Precision/recall and sensitivity/specificity are two communities’ readings of the same matrix with different denominators, which causes many metric errors3.


                  
                  Why is precision/recall confused with sensitivity/specificity so often? 
                  
                

They are the same confusion matrix read by two communities using different denominators. The cells are identical; only what each figure is divided by differs.


F₁ becomes misleading under negative-class imbalance, where a healthy-looking score measures the wrong thing. A medical-diagnosis example makes the problem concrete: a false negative and a false positive are not comparable events, and a single number cannot make them comparable.


                  
                  What does the medical-diagnosis example establish about single-number scores? 
                  
                

That a false negative and a false positive are not comparable events. A missed diagnosis and a false alarm cost different things, and any single number has already assumed they cost the same.


Generative text: two instruments, two questions

Perplexity — how well the model predicts held-out data.
Burstiness — the diversity and variability of its output.

The two measures answer different questions. A model can score well on perplexity while repeating itself endlessly; burstiness catches that failure.


                  
                  What failure does perplexity miss that burstiness catches? 
                  
                

Endless repetition. A model can predict held-out data well while producing no variety at all, so a good perplexity score says nothing about the diversity of what it generates.



BLEU — precision-oriented n-gram overlap, built for translation.
ROUGE / ROUGE-L — recall-oriented, built for summarisation. More reference sentences always improve the estimate.
BERTScore — embedding similarity instead of n-gram overlap, so paraphrase stops being penalised as error.



                  
                  Why is BLEU precision-oriented and ROUGE recall-oriented? 
                  
                

Because of the tasks they were built for. Translation asks whether what was produced is correct — precision. Summarisation asks whether what mattered was kept — recall.




                  
                  What error does BERTScore stop punishing? 
                  
                

Paraphrase. Scoring by embedding similarity rather than n-gram overlap means a correct answer in different words is no longer counted as wrong.


Each domain has its own family: regression, object detection, generative images, GANs, speech, clustering, code generation, compression, and recommender systems. No single number covers that range.
The major metric families have focused graph pages:

classification-error-tradeoffs — denominators, thresholds, and asymmetric errors
regression-loss-geometry — absolute, squared, relative, and variance-based summaries
reference-based-text-evaluation — lexical overlap versus semantic similarity
rank-aware-evaluation — relevance, position, normalisation, and beyond-accuracy goals

Measure the components, not just the system
Retrieval and generation are evaluated separately in Primers • Retrieval Augmented Generation4. A RAG system that answers badly may have retrieved perfectly but generated poorly, or retrieved garbage and generated from it faithfully. An aggregate score cannot distinguish these failures, which call for opposite fixes.
When the metric is itself a model
RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback5 carries this idea to a learned metric. The Reward-Model fits comparisons rather than following a formula, so it inherits the properties of a metric along with new ones:

Its ceiling is the agreement of the people who produced its data: roughly 73% inter-labeler agreement.
It is only valid where it has seen data, and the policy being trained actively searches for the regions where it is wrong. Hence the KL penalty pinning the policy near its starting point.
Human preference is not a single function. Huyen prefers the losing response in a published example and says so; the metric averages a disagreement rather than approximating a fact.



                  
                  What does a learned metric inherit that a formula-defined one does not? 
                  
                

A training distribution. It is only valid where it has seen data — and unlike a formula, an optimiser can be pointed at the regions where it is wrong.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/explo.title: Exploration vs. Exploitation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/explo.content:
Exploration vs. Exploitation
An agent must balance finding better actions against using what it has found: pure exploitation blocks the first, and pure exploration blocks the second. The balance is one of the most fundamental challenges in reinforcement learning, and its optimum remains an open problem1.
flowchart LR
  U[Under-exploration — a sub-optimal policy locked in] --- K[One knob — epsilon, UCB, Thompson sampling, temperature]
  K --- O[Over-exploration — effort spent on actions that yield nothing]
  K --> C[Exploration costs samples, often millions of interactions]
  C --> D[Disqualifying where each interaction costs money, time or hardware]
  R[RLHF inverts it — the policy explores too eagerly] --> P[A KL penalty against the SFT policy constrains exploration]

In short

Over-exploration wastes effort; under-exploration locks in a sub-optimal policy, and ε-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling are only heuristics.
Exploration costs samples, often millions of interactions, which can disqualify a method where each one costs money, time or hardware.
The Q-learning max is pure exploitation; nothing in the update says how to find actions worth maximising over.
Sampling temperature is the same knob in language models: near zero loops, higher values add novelty and errors.
RLHF inverts the trade-off, using a KL penalty to stop the policy exploring into the reward model’s mistakes.

The two failure directions

Over-exploration — effort spent on actions that yield nothing.
Under-exploration — a sub-optimal policy locked in because a better one was never tried.

The standard attacks are ε-greedy (act randomly with probability ε), upper-confidence-bound algorithms (prefer actions whose value is uncertain), and Thompson sampling (sample from a posterior over action values). All are heuristics for a problem with no general solution.


                  
                  What does an upper-confidence-bound method prefer, and why is that exploration? 
                  
                

Actions whose value is uncertain, not merely high. Uncertainty is where new information lives, so favouring it buys knowledge rather than immediate return.


Why it is expensive rather than merely hard
Exploration costs samples, and sample inefficiency is the practical blocker on real deployment1: state-of-the-art methods can require millions of environment interactions. In robotics, healthcare, and autonomous driving, each interaction costs money, time, or hardware. That cost can disqualify a method from deployment. Experience replay helps without solving the problem.


                  
                  Why does sample inefficiency disqualify RL in robotics or healthcare rather than merely slow it? 
                  
                

Because each interaction has a real cost in money, time or hardware. Methods needing millions of environment interactions are unaffordable in those settings, not just protracted.


Sparse and delayed rewards make it worse. When success arrives only after a long sequence of actions, the agent may need very many trials just to stumble onto the sequence once, and then still has to work out which action mattered.


                  
                  What two separate difficulties does a sparse, delayed reward create? 
                  
                

Finding the rewarded sequence at all, which may take very many trials, and then working out which of its actions earned the reward. Discovery and credit assignment are distinct problems.


The formal setting, compressed
VIP Cheatsheet: Deep Learning2 gives the machinery in half a page: a Markov-Decision-Process as (S, A, {P_sa}, γ, R), the value function, the optimal Bellman equation, value iteration, and Q-learning as the model-free update

Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[R(s,a,s′) + γ·max_a′ Q(s′,a′) − Q(s,a)]

The max in that update expresses exploitation in one symbol. The formula contains no account of how the agent finds actions worth maximising over. ε-greedy, UCB, and Thompson sampling supply that missing exploration step.
The data consequences depend on on-vs-off-policy-learning. On-policy methods must explore with the policy being improved and rapidly age out old experience; off-policy methods can reuse trajectories from another behaviour policy, but inherit distribution-mismatch and stability problems.


                  
                  Where is exploration in the Q-learning update? 
                  
                

Nowhere. The max is exploitation stated in one symbol; nothing in the equation says how the agent finds actions worth maximising over. ε-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling are all bolted on to supply exactly that gap.


The same knob, elsewhere in the field
Sampling temperature. The trade-off appears outside RL in The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks3. Lowering the softmax temperature makes a language model more confident and conservative; raising it yields more diversity at the cost of more errors. Karpathy shows both extremes: near-zero temperature collapses into a literal infinite loop about startups, while higher temperatures produce novelty and misspellings. One scalar controls the balance between exploration and exploitation.


                  
                  What happens to generated text at near-zero sampling temperature, and why? 
                  
                

It collapses into a literal infinite loop. Always taking the most confident token is pure exploitation, so the model re-enters the same state and repeats — Karpathy’s example loops endlessly about startups.


Agent trial-and-error. LLM Powered Autonomous Agents4 describes Reflexion resetting the environment when a heuristic judges the trajectory inefficient. The reset stops exploitation of a bad path and opens another for exploration. Weng also notes that LLMs struggle to revise a plan after an unexpected error, failing to explore when the error requires it.
RLHF’s KL penalty. RLHF reverses the trade-off5. An over-eager policy will find regions where the Reward-Model is mistakenly generous. The KL term against the SFT policy constrains exploration, keeping the model inside the space where its reward signal can be trusted. Unconstrained exploration creates the failure here.


                  
                  Where does the exploration/exploitation trade-off invert, and why? 
                  
                

In RLHF. Because the reward signal is only trustworthy near the training distribution, unconstrained exploration finds the reward model’s mistakes — so the KL penalty deliberately limits exploring rather than encouraging it.


Sample efficiency as a research frontier. AI Agents in Depth: Design Principles and Engineering Practice6 devotes a section of its post-training chapter to improving sample efficiency. Li gives data and environment priority over algorithms because the setting in which exploration occurs determines the return from costly samples.


                  
                  If exploration is expensive, what is the lever Li says matters most? 
                  
                

The environment and data, over the algorithm. Since every sample costs, the thing you explore in determines the return on exploring more than the rule choosing what to try.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/gener.title: Generative Learning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/gener.content:
Generative Learning
Generative learning algorithms model what the data itself looks like — p(x|y), the features of each class — and classify by turning that around with Bayes rule. Discriminative algorithms (logistic regression, and most of deep learning) skip the detour and learn p(y|x) directly. Comparing the two directions is a first lesson in what modelling assumptions buy and cost1.
In short

GDA’s shared covariance makes the decision boundary straight and p(y=1|x) necessarily logistic, but the converse fails.
GDA’s stronger assumptions need less data when they hold, while logistic regression’s weaker ones usually win at scale.
Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given y, cutting 2⁵⁰⁰⁰⁰ − 1 parameters to 2 × 50,000.
Laplace smoothing keeps a never-seen word from zeroing the whole product.

Gaussian discriminant analysis
GDA assumes the continuous features of each class are multivariate normal: y ∼ Bernoulli(φ), x|y=0 ∼ N(μ₀, Σ), x|y=1 ∼ N(μ₁, Σ). Both classes share one covariance matrix Σ — only the means differ — which is why the fitted Gaussian contours have identical shape and orientation, and why the decision boundary p(y=1|x) = 0.5 comes out exactly straight. The four parameters (φ, μ₀, μ₁, Σ) have closed-form maximum-likelihood estimates: class frequency, class means, and a pooled covariance.
The punchline is the relationship to logistic regression: under these assumptions, p(y=1|x) is necessarily a logistic function of x. The converse fails — many non-Gaussian data-generating processes (Poisson, for one) also produce logistic p(y|x).


                  
                  When does GDA beat logistic regression, and when does logistic regression win? 
                  
                

GDA makes stronger assumptions, so when they hold it is asymptotically efficient — no algorithm beats it in the large-data limit — and it needs less data to do well. Logistic regression makes weaker assumptions, so on non-Gaussian data it almost always wins at scale. In practice that robustness is why logistic regression is used more.


Naive Bayes
For discrete features, modelling p(x|y) naively explodes: a 50,000-word vocabulary means 2⁵⁰⁰⁰⁰ − 1 parameters for a joint multinomial. Naive Bayes cuts through this with one strong assumption — features are conditionally independent given y — collapsing the joint into ∏ⱼ p(xⱼ|y): 2 × 50,000 parameters, each interpretable as “the fraction of spam emails containing word j.”
Two refinements matter:

Laplace smoothing — maximum likelihood assigns probability zero to any word never seen, and one zero factor annihilates the whole product (the 0/0 spam filter). Adding 1 to each numerator and k to each denominator keeps the estimates a valid distribution and never zero.
Event models for text — the Bernoulli event model asks which words appear; the multinomial event model models the email as a word sequence, ignoring position but counting multiplicity, and usually does better for text.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/gradi.title: Gradient Descent
sections/machine-learning/concepts/gradi.content:
Gradient Descent
Gradient descent moves the parameters against the gradient of the cost at a pace set by the learning rate α. The same update rule applies to nearly everything in this section:

θ ← θ − α∇J(θ)

VIP Cheatsheet: Supervised Learning1 introduces the rule once, then reuses it for linear regression, logistic regression, and neural networks. Those models differ in their loss and hypothesis class while sharing the optimiser.
flowchart TD
  B[Take a batch] --> F[Forward propagate to obtain the loss]
  F --> G[Backpropagate — the chain rule, for the gradients]
  G --> U[Update — the parameters move against the gradient at rate alpha]
  U --> B
  S[Batch size — a full batch, or one example per update in SGD] --> B
  A[Alpha schedule — fixed, or adaptive per parameter as in Adam] --> U
  N[Newton's method — second order, far fewer steps] -->|the Hessian is unaffordable at scale| U
  U --> R[A point where the gradient vanishes in its basin — nothing global]



                  
                  What distinguishes one model from another, if they all share the same optimiser? 
                  
                

The loss and the hypothesis class. Linear regression, logistic regression and a neural network differ in what they are fitting and what they are penalised for — the update rule is the same for all three.


In short

Linear regression, logistic regression and neural networks share one optimiser and differ in their loss and hypothesis class.
Batch size, momentum, adaptive rescaling such as Adam, and schedules on α are the axes of variation.
Newton’s method can take fewer iterations, but the Hessian is unaffordable at modern parameter counts.
Gradient descent finds a point where the gradient vanishes in its starting basin, with no guarantee of global optimality.

Batch size changes the gradient estimate

Batch gradient descent — update on a batch of examples.
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) — update per training example.

Batch size provides one axis of variation. Momentum changes the update state, adaptive optimisers such as RMSProp and Adam rescale coordinates using gradient history, and schedules change α over time. VIP Cheatsheet: Deep Learning2 names Adam as the then-current standard, while The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks3 reports RMSProp or Adam specifically “to stabilize the updates.”


                  
                  What is Adam or RMSProp chosen for in practice? 
                  
                

Stability, not speed. Per-parameter adaptive rates keep updates from blowing up, which is the reason Karpathy gives for using them.


Backpropagation is not a different algorithm
It is the chain rule, applied to get the gradients a layered model needs:

∂L(z,y)/∂w = (∂L/∂a)(∂a/∂z)(∂z/∂w)

and then the same update, w ← w − η·∂L/∂w. VIP Cheatsheet: Deep Learning2 gives the loop in four steps: take a batch, forward propagate to obtain the loss, backpropagate to get the gradients, use the gradients to update the weights.
The second-order alternative
Newton’s method finds θ with ℓ′(θ) = 0 via θ ← θ − ℓ′(θ)/ℓ″(θ), generalising to Newton-Raphson with the Hessian: θ ← θ − (∇²ℓ)⁻¹∇ℓ. It can converge in fewer local iterations, but forming and inverting a Hessian at modern parameter counts is unaffordable in most cases. Large-scale deep-learning optimisers therefore use predominantly first-order methods, though Newton updates do not always converge faster and some optimisers approximate second-order information.


                  
                  Newton's method converges in far fewer steps. Why is deep learning first-order anyway? 
                  
                

The Hessian. Forming and inverting a second-derivative matrix over a modern network’s parameter count is unaffordable, and that single cost is why the whole field stays first-order.


Where the identities come from
matrix-calculus-for-learning collects the gradient, Hessian, trace, and matrix-derivative identities that the compiled sheet supplies for the normal equations θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, Newton-Raphson, and backpropagation. The sheet is a compact identity reference rather than a derivation of every validity condition.
What it does not guarantee
Gradient descent does not guarantee global optimality. It finds a point where the gradient vanishes in the basin where it started. Its success on non-convex objectives remains an empirical fact that the field relies on without a full explanation. It also provides the mechanism for scaling-beats-knowledge-engineering, since gradient descent over more data and parameters is the “learning” half of Sutton’s two scalable methods.


                  
                  What does gradient descent actually guarantee about the point it reaches? 
                  
                

Only that the gradient vanishes there, within whatever basin it started in. Nothing about global optimality — that it works on non-convex objectives is an empirical fact the field relies on without fully explaining.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/harne.title: Harness Engineering
sections/machine-learning/concepts/harne.content:
Harness Engineering
The harness is everything built around the model, and it separates an agent demo from an agent product. AI Agents in Depth: Design Principles and Engineering Practice1 calls the LLM the Model and the rest the Harness:
flowchart TD
  A[Agent system] --> M[Model]
  A --> H[Harness]
  H --> C[Context]
  H --> T[Tools]
  H --> N[Constrain]
  H --> V[Verify]
  H --> R[Correct]


Agent = LLM + [Context + Tools + Constrain + Verify + Correct] = Model + Harness

The first two bracketed terms are the original formula Agent = LLM + Context + Tools. The three added are safeguards: Constrain (what the agent may and may not do), Verify (whether it did the thing correctly), Correct (how to recover when it did not).


                  
                  What three terms does the harness add to Agent = LLM + Context + Tools?
                  
                

Constrain, Verify and Correct — what the agent may do, whether it did it correctly, and how to recover when it did not. The first two terms describe capability; these three describe reliability.


In short

The harness adds Constrain, Verify and Correct to Agent = LLM + Context + Tools.
It absorbs the bare ReAct loop’s failures: hallucinated tools, wrong tool choice, no recovery from error.
Once competitors have comparable models, their harnesses distinguish them.
MAST found 14 multi-agent failure modes; simple fixes improved ChatDev by only 15.6%.
Without a Verify layer, prompt tuning cannot stop an agent reporting “completed” on unchecked work.

What it is a response to
Bojie Li bases his framing on observed failures rather than an architectural preference. The basic ReAct loop works but remains fragile in three specific ways: the model hallucinates tools or parameters that do not exist, picks the wrong tool, or cannot recover from an error. The harness exists to absorb those failures.


                  
                  Which three failures of the bare ReAct loop does a harness exist to absorb? 
                  
                

Hallucinating tools or parameters that do not exist, picking the wrong tool, and being unable to recover from an error.


Once competing systems have access to comparable models, their harnesses distinguish them. Li uses “Model” rather than “LLM” because the principles apply to anything that can reason and call tools.


                  
                  Once competitors have comparable models, where does the difference between their agents live? 
                  
                

In the harness. The model becomes a commodity component; what is built around it — constraints, verification, recovery — is what still differs.


The same observation, three times
Three sources make the same observation:

LLM Powered Autonomous Agents2 — model output is unreliable, since LLMs may make formatting errors and occasionally exhibit rebellious behavior, so much agent demo code focuses on parsing model output. Weng identifies the symptom in 2023 without naming the discipline.
Primers • Agents3 — the workflow/agent distinction is a harness decision: how much of the control flow is code a human wrote versus decisions the model makes at run time.
AI Agents in Depth: Design Principles and Engineering Practice1 — names it, gives it an equation, and devotes the book to it.

The deepened primer turns those safeguards into three design surfaces. agent-control-boundary decides which transitions remain deterministic; tool-interface-design makes actions legible, bounded, validated, and recoverable; reflection-evaluator-loop adds critique and external checks instead of trusting a single pass. Together, they specify concrete harness choices beyond the model’s capabilities.
Evidence that it cannot be patched in later
In the 2025 MAST study, researchers annotated ~150 execution traces across MetaGPT, ChatDev, AG2, and Magentic-One (inter-annotator κ = 0.88). They found 14 failure modes in three groups: system design flaws, inter-agent alignment failures, and missing task verification. Simple fixes improved ChatDev by only 15.6%. The authors concluded that these fundamental design flaws require a system redesign rather than patches to one component.
The third group marks an absent Verify layer. If an agent can report “completed” without any mechanism to confirm that the result meets requirements, prompt tuning cannot close the gap.


                  
                  What does MAST's "missing task verification" group correspond to in harness terms? 
                  
                

The Verify layer, absent. An agent that can report “completed” with nothing checking the result against requirements has a hole prompt tuning cannot close.


Li adds two failure modes from engineering practice beyond MAST’s dialogue-based taxonomy: concurrency conflicts when multiple agents share a file system, and cascading amplification of errors across agents.
single-vs-multi-agent-economics traces these costs to each new agent boundary, which serializes context and creates another coordination and verification surface. Multi-agent architecture earns that burden only when decomposition or independent checking produces measured gains.


                  
                  Which two multi-agent failures does MAST's dialogue-focused taxonomy miss? 
                  
                

Concurrency conflicts when several agents share a file system, and cascading amplification of an error across agents. Both come from engineering practice rather than from conversation traces.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/hybri.title: Hybrid Retrieval
sections/machine-learning/concepts/hybri.content:
Hybrid Retrieval
Hybrid retrieval combines signals with different failure modes: lexical methods such as TF-IDF or BM25, dense embedding similarity, graph relationships, structured SQL, and metadata filtering1.
flowchart LR
  L[Sparse lexical channel] --> P[Pooled candidates]
  D[Dense semantic channel] --> P
  G[Graph or relational channel] --> P
  M[Metadata and permission filters] --> P
  P --> F[Normalize scores or fuse ranks]
  F --> R[Rerank with richer matching]
  R --> E[Evidence set for generation]

In short

Sparse retrieval keeps exact terms; dense retrieval catches paraphrases.
Candidates from several channels are pooled, fused, then reranked.
The union helps only when one channel recovers what another misses.

In detail


                  
                  Why combine sparse and dense retrieval? 
                  
                

They fail differently: sparse retrieval preserves exact terms, while dense retrieval catches paraphrases.




                  
                  What happens after hybrid retrieval pools candidates from several channels? 
                  
                

Scores are normalized or rank-fused before the candidates are reranked.


Sparse lexical retrieval preserves exact names, rare terms, and identifiers but misses paraphrases. Dense retrieval finds semantic neighbours but can return plausible yet irrelevant passages. Graph or relational paths exploit explicit entities and constraints but depend on extracted structure and query formulation. Metadata filters enforce tenant, date, document type, or access boundaries before or after scoring.
A hybrid system retrieves from several channels, normalizes or rank-fuses their scores, and passes a pooled candidate set to reranking. The union can improve recall only if one channel recovers what another misses; naive concatenation can instead multiply duplicates and noise.
Boundary
The primer’s early suggestion that graph retrieval requires exact matching is an oversimplification; vector-plus-graph systems exist within the broader period covered by the evolving primer. Complementary evidence signals provide the durable concept, independent of a fixed database taxonomy.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/instr.title: Instruction Tuning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/instr.content:
Instruction Tuning
Instruction tuning uses supervised examples from many tasks to update a pretrained language model, with each input phrased as a natural-language request. Wei and colleagues designed FLAN to transfer the pattern of responding to instructions to task types absent from its tuning mixture.
In short

Natural instructions lifted held-out FLAN results to 55.2, against 37.3 for bare inputs and outputs.
Instruction tuning helped the 68B and 137B models but hurt models from 422 million through 8 billion parameters.
It helps tasks users would state as requests and adds little where the format already matches next-token prediction.

The FLAN procedure
Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners1 starts with the 137-billion-parameter LaMDA-PT model. Researchers converted 62 datasets into instructional form, grouped them into twelve task clusters, and wrote ten templates per dataset. To test one cluster, they tuned a checkpoint on the other clusters. This split excludes related datasets as well as the named evaluation set, giving zero-shot a stricter meaning than dataset-level holdout.
Natural wording mattered. A model tuned on bare inputs and outputs averaged 37.3 across four held-out clusters. Dataset-name prefixes raised the result to 46.6 or 47.0, while natural instructions reached 55.2. Adding datasets within the training clusters also helped more than adding template paraphrases once the mixture had enough datasets.
Scale and task format set the boundary
Instruction tuning helped the 68-billion and 137-billion parameter models on held-out tasks, but it hurt models from 422 million through 8 billion parameters in the paper’s scale ablation. The authors suggest that smaller models may use their capacity to fit the tuning mixture without retaining enough capacity for transfer.
The method worked best when users would state the task as a request, including translation, question answering, and natural-language inference. It offered little benefit on several sentence-completion tasks whose format already matched next-token-prediction. FLAN also failed some simple instructions, retained a 1,024-token context, and carried the biases of its labeled tuning datasets.
Distinct from RLHF
FLAN uses supervised task targets and ordinary gradient-based finetuning. It does not train a reward model or optimize against human preference rankings, which belong to RLHF. Few-shot prompting and prompt tuning remained compatible with the resulting checkpoint.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/knowl.title: Knowledge Distillation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/knowl.content:
Knowledge Distillation
Knowledge distillation trains a deployable student model to reproduce the output distribution of a cumbersome teacher, which may be an ensemble or a large regularised network. Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean’s formulation treats the teacher’s input-output mapping as the transferable knowledge, so the student can use a smaller or different architecture.
In short

A teacher’s probabilities over wrong classes encode how it generalises, and the student learns that class structure from every case.
Dividing logits by a temperature T exposes small probabilities; the soft-target gradient is multiplied by T² to compensate.
A distilled speech model reached 60.8% frame accuracy against the ten-model ensemble’s 61.1%.
A small student may not match every low-probability relation, and intermediate temperatures worked best for a 30-unit student.

Soft targets teach relationships between classes
A hard label identifies one correct class. The teacher also assigns probabilities to the alternatives, and their relative sizes are evidence about the teacher’s generalisation. An image labelled BMW may receive more probability for another vehicle than for a carrot. The student learns that class structure from every training case.
High-entropy targets provide more information per case and reduce variance in the gradients between cases. The student can train from the original labelled data or from a separate transfer set, including unlabelled examples, because the teacher supplies a target distribution.
Temperature reveals the teacher’s small probabilities
The method divides teacher and student logits by a temperature T before softmax. Raising T spreads probability mass across classes that would sit near zero at the ordinary temperature of 1. The student matches this softened distribution during training and uses temperature 1 at inference.
When labels are available, the method combines two losses: cross-entropy against the teacher at high temperature and cross-entropy against the correct labels at temperature 1. It gives the hard-label objective a smaller weight and multiply the soft-target gradient contribution by T², compensating for the way its magnitude shrinks as temperature rises. The derivation also makes squared-error logit matching a high-temperature special case after zero-centring the logits.
Reported transfers
On MNIST, the paper’s smaller network reduced its test errors from 146 to 74 after learning from a larger model’s soft targets; the teacher made 67 errors. In the speech experiment, a ten-model ensemble improved frame accuracy from 58.9% to 61.1%, and one distilled model reached 60.8%. It also retained the ensemble’s reduction in word error rate.
Soft targets act as a regulariser as well as a compression signal. With 3% of their speech data, hard targets produced 44.5% test frame accuracy while soft targets from a full-data model produced 57.0%, close to the 58.9% full-data baseline. These results support the claim that teacher outputs carry regularities absent from one-hot labels.
Boundaries
Distillation targets the teacher’s output behaviour, and a student with limited capacity may fail to match every low-probability relation. Intermediate temperatures worked best for a student with only 30 hidden units per layer. The paper’s specialist-model experiment also stopped before compressing the complete specialist ensemble, leaving that deployment step open.
Related Entities & Topics

sections/machine-learning/concepts/layer.title: Layer-Wise Representations
sections/machine-learning/concepts/layer.content:
Layer-Wise Representations
A layer-wise representation is the vector at one sequence position after a particular block has modified it. Repeated Transformer blocks produce a series of representations from the initial embedding to the final vector used for prediction. Each vector records computational state at a different depth.
In short

Each block alternates attention, which moves information between positions, and an MLP, whose edit the residual connection adds.
Depth composes local changes, so stacked blocks can respond to position relationships no single layer distinguishes.
The evidence supports an operation-level account only, with no fixed sequence of syntax, fact, or reasoning layers.

Alternating operations change the vectors
Each block performs two operations1. self-attention lets positions exchange information, so a token vector can incorporate features from surrounding tokens. The multilayer perceptron then processes each position independently: an up-projection, nonlinearity, and down-projection produce an edit that the residual connection adds to the incoming vector.
The same pattern repeats with different learned parameters. Sanderson’s worked example supposes that an earlier attention block has already moved first-name information into the vector for a surname. An MLP can then test directions in that combined vector and add another direction. He presents this as a simplified structural reading and warns that superposition makes one-feature-per-neuron accounts rare in real models.
Depth composes local changes
Position gives an example2. One T5 attention layer groups every relative offset beyond 128 tokens into the same bucket, so that layer cannot distinguish those distances. Later blocks can combine information gathered through shorter offsets and respond to longer-range relationships. The network gains that sensitivity by composing repeated vector updates.
The two sources support an operation-level account of depth. Attention moves information between positions; MLPs edit each position; residual connections preserve and add to the prior vector. Neither work presents probing evidence for a fixed sequence of syntax, fact, or reasoning layers.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/learn.title: Learning Theory
sections/machine-learning/concepts/learn.content:
Learning Theory
Learning theory turns the practice of fitting training data into guarantees about unseen data. It builds from two elementary probability lemmas to the result many call the most important theorem in the field1. On the way it answers three questions: why low training error says anything about test error, how much data suffices, and what the right measure of a hypothesis class’s complexity is.
In short

Hoeffding’s inequality plus the union bound make training error close to generalization error for every hypothesis in a finite class at once.
Enlarging the class lowers bias but grows the variance term, and sample complexity is logarithmic in |H|.
VC dimension measures complexity without parameter counting, making sample complexity linear in VC(H).
Past the interpolation point test error descends again, so the classical U-curve is not the whole curve.

Uniform convergence for finite classes
The training error ε̂(h) of a fixed h is the sample mean of a Bernoulli — so Hoeffding’s inequality bounds its distance from the true generalization error ε(h). But ERM does not evaluate one h; it picks the best of k. The union bound upgrades the guarantee to hold simultaneously for every h ∈ H:
P(|ε(h) − ε̂(h)| ≤ γ for all h ∈ H) ≥ 1 − 2k·exp(−2γ²n)
Under this uniform convergence, ERM’s choice ε(ĥ) lands within 2γ of the best possible error in the class. The bound’s shape is the bias/variance tradeoff made formal: enlarging the class H can only lower min_h ε(h) (bias), but grows the √(log k / n) term (variance). Sample complexity comes out logarithmic in |H| and quadratic in 1/γ.
VC dimension: complexity without parameter counting
Real classes are infinite, and parameter counting is unreliable — the same class of linear classifiers can be written with d or with 2d+2 parameters. The fix is the Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension: the size of the largest set a hypothesis class can shatter (realize every labelling of). Linear classifiers in 2-D have VC dimension 3 — they shatter some triple, but no set of four.


                  
                  Why must VC(H) = 3 for 2-D linear classifiers even though some triples cannot be shattered? 
                  
                

The definition needs only one set of size D that the class shatters, not all sets. Three points in general position can be labelled all eight ways by some line; certain degenerate arrangements (collinear points) cannot — but existence, not universality, sets the dimension.


Vapnik’s theorem replaces |H| with VC(H) in the uniform convergence bound, making sample complexity linear in the VC dimension — which for most classes is roughly linear in parameters anyway, but now with a definition that never depended on parameterization.
Where the classical picture bends
The exact decomposition behind bias-variance-tradeoff is test error = irreducible noise + bias² + variance, and it has its own limit: in the overparameterized regime, past the point where the model can interpolate the data, test error descends again (double descent). The notes attribute this to implicit regularization by optimizers such as gradient descent selecting minimum-norm solutions among the many that fit. The classical U-curve remains the first resort; it is just not the whole curve.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/long-.title: Long-Term Dependency
sections/machine-learning/concepts/long-.content:
Long-Term Dependency
A long-term dependency occurs when a prediction needs information from far back in a sequence. This problem has organised sequence modelling and driven much of its architectural history.
flowchart LR
  D[Distant information must affect a later prediction] --> R[Plain recurrent path carries many steps]
  R --> L[LSTM gates preserve selected state]
  L --> A[Attention creates direct access across positions]
  A --> C[Distance cost becomes total context cost]
  D --> P[Delayed reward creates the same credit-assignment shape]

In short

Vanilla RNNs can represent long dependencies but fail to learn them by training as the gap grows.
LSTM gating makes persistence the default, and attention gives every position one-hop access to every other.
Attention turns distance into total-length cost, so the finite context window becomes the binding constraint, with retrieval reaching beyond it.
RL credit assignment under delayed rewards has the same structure, and none of its partial bridges solves it generally.

The two sentences
A minimal pair states it1:

“The clouds are in the ___” — the answer is sky, and everything needed is right there.
“I grew up in France… I speak fluent ___” — recent words say the answer is a language. A word that may be arbitrarily far back determines which language.

As that gap grows, vanilla recurrent networks lose the ability to bridge it in practice. RNNs can represent such dependencies, and a human can hand-pick parameters that solve toy versions. Training fails to learn them for reasons established by Hochreiter (1991) and Bengio et al. (1994).


                  
                  Why is the RNN long-dependency failure practical rather than theoretical? 
                  
                

RNNs can represent such dependencies — a human can hand-pick parameters that solve toy versions. What fails is learning them by gradient descent, not representing them.


Three answers, in order
Gating. The LSTM adds a cell state that information traverses unchanged unless a gate alters it, inverting the default from decay to persistence. Gating supported roughly a decade of progress.
Attention. self-attention gives every position one-hop access to every other position, removing the recurrent path. Distance stops mattering entirely, but total sequence length carries a quadratic cost. The Transformer thus converts long-range dependency from a depth problem into a width problem, making the finite context window the binding constraint.


                  
                  In what sense does attention convert the long-dependency problem rather than solve it?
                  
                

It turns a depth problem into a width problem. Distance becomes free, and total sequence length becomes the cost — which is why the finite context window is now the binding constraint.


Retrieval. Dependencies that exceed any feasible context window can sit outside the model in Retrieval-Augmented-Generation or in the external vector store that agent literature calls long-term memory. Weng notes the trade-off: a vector store extends reach, but its representational power is weaker than full attention.
The same problem in reinforcement learning
Credit assignment under sparse and delayed rewards is hard2: when success arrives only after many steps, identifying which early action earned it becomes difficult. This has the structure of a long-term dependency with a reward signal instead of a token. temporal-difference-bootstrap shortens the feedback path by updating from an observed reward plus a successor estimate, while reward shaping and eligibility traces supply other partial bridges. None provides a general solution.


                  
                  How is RL credit assignment the same problem as long-term dependency? 
                  
                

Both ask which distant thing accounts for something here — an early action for a late reward, an early word for a late prediction. Same structure, and the mitigations rhyme: reward shaping and eligibility traces where sequence models use gating.


Evidence that models do learn it
LSTM cells track state across long spans3: one that switches on inside a URL and off outside, one giving a position-in-scope coordinate across a [[ ]] environment, and one counting through “www”. Karpathy’s samples also show the failure: generated C code has correct local syntax, yet its functions return values despite a void signature. The mismatch is a long-range interaction failure in text that remains locally fluent.


                  
                  What does a void function that returns a value diagnose in generated code?
                  
                

A long-range interaction failure. The local syntax is correct because it depends on nearby tokens; the signature is far enough back that the model no longer holds it. Fluent in form, wrong across distance.
