sections/machine-learning/concepts/matri.title: Matrix Calculus for Learning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/matri.content:
Matrix Calculus for Learning
Matrix calculus expresses how scalar objectives change with vector or matrix parameters. The gradient, Hessian, trace, determinant, transpose, and inverse identities recur across linear models, PCA, Newton-style optimization, and neural-network backpropagation1.
flowchart TD
  O[Scalar objective] --> G[Gradient — first-order sensitivity]
  O --> H[Hessian — local curvature]
  G --> D[Choose a descent direction]
  H --> S[Rescale a step by curvature]
  T[Trace and matrix identities] --> C[Compact differentiable forms]
  C --> G

In short

The gradient records first-order sensitivity and selects a local descent direction.
The Hessian describes local curvature and can rescale a step accordingly.
Identities cannot replace shape checks or regularity conditions, and layout conventions can transpose results.

In detail


                  
                  How do a gradient and a Hessian differ? 
                  
                

The gradient gives first-order sensitivity; the Hessian describes local curvature through second derivatives.




                  
                  Why can a matrix-calculus identity sheet not prove an optimizer is well behaved? 
                  
                

Shape, invertibility and regularity conditions still have to hold.


For a scalar-valued function, the gradient has the shape of the parameter and records first-order sensitivity. The Hessian collects second derivatives and describes local curvature; positive semidefiniteness links curvature to convexity under appropriate conditions. Trace identities often turn sums and quadratic forms into expressions that differentiate compactly.
These operations connect to gradient-descent: the gradient selects a local descent direction, while Hessian information can rescale a step according to curvature. Eigendecomposition and singular-value decomposition connect linear algebra to principal components, rank, and stable factorization.
Boundary
A sheet of identities cannot replace shape checks or regularity conditions. Gradients require a scalar output in the convention used by the source; inverses require nonsingularity; Hessian-based conclusions are local; and equivalent-looking numerator- versus denominator-layout conventions can transpose results. The refresher helps readers navigate derivations, while a proof must establish that an optimization problem is well behaved.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/multi.title: Multi-Hop Retrieval Planning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/multi.content:
Multi-Hop Retrieval Planning
A multi-hop question contains evidence dependencies: the first result identifies an entity, relation, or constraint needed to formulate the next query. One-shot RAG fails here because the original query may not resemble every supporting passage1.
flowchart LR
  Q[Original multi-hop question] --> D[Decompose the first information need]
  D --> R[Retrieve evidence]
  R --> U[Update entities relations and unresolved variables]
  U --> N[Construct the next query]
  N --> R
  U --> S[Synthesize only when the evidence chain closes]

In short

Each hop’s result supplies the entity or constraint needed for the next query.
A wrong entity early redirects every later search while the final answer stays fluent.
Stop on evidence support, with per-hop provenance, never after a fixed number of searches.

In detail


                  
                  Why can one-shot retrieval fail on a multi-hop question? 
                  
                

The original query may not resemble passages whose identity is only revealed by an earlier result.




                  
                  Why must a multi-hop system retain provenance at every hop? 
                  
                

An early wrong entity can redirect every later search while leaving a fluent final answer.


The system decomposes the question into intermediate information needs, retrieves for the first need, updates state with the evidence, and constructs the next query. A final answer is synthesized only after the chain connects the original question to supporting passages. Hierarchical retrieval is a constrained form in which hops move from document to section to chunk.
Each hop introduces branching and error propagation. A wrong entity in step one can redirect all later retrieval; a fluent final answer may hide a broken chain. Systems need per-hop provenance, explicit unresolved variables, evidence deduplication, and a stopping condition based on support rather than a fixed number of searches.
agentic-retrieval-routing can choose sources and hops dynamically, while a deterministic planner can encode known dependency patterns. Both approaches require evaluation of intermediate retrieval.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/next-.title: Next-Token Prediction
sections/machine-learning/concepts/next-.content:
Next-Token Prediction
Next-token prediction trains a model to assign a probability to each token given the tokens before it. A sequence probability is the product of these conditional probabilities1, so generation and likelihood evaluation are two uses of the same model.
In short

A causal mask lets every position predict its successor in parallel during training without answers leaking backward.
Web text contains task demonstrations, so reducing next-token loss can produce zero-shot behavior, unevenly across tasks.
In T5’s controlled comparison, denoising transferred better downstream, while causal prediction stayed the direct fit for decoder-only generation.

Causal computation
A decoder-only Transformer uses a causal attention mask so position i cannot read positions after i. During training, every position can predict its own successor in parallel while the mask prevents answers from leaking backward. During generation, the model samples or selects one token, appends it to the context, and repeats.
On the representation side2, a token begins as an embedding, then repeated attention and MLP blocks alter its vector with contextual and parameterized information. The final representation supplies the next-token distribution after unembedding.
An objective that contains task demonstrations
Radford and colleagues argue that web documents contain sequences that look like task input followed by task output. Translation pairs, question-answer exchanges, and article summaries all contribute ordinary next-token loss. A model can reduce that loss by inferring which task the surrounding text demonstrates. Their GPT-2 experiments found zero-shot behavior without task-specific parameter updates, though results ranged from competitive reading comprehension to weak summarization and question answering.
One pretraining objective among several
Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer3 compares causal language modeling with denoising in a controlled text-to-text setup. Denoising produced better downstream transfer across the authors’ main benchmarks, while causal prediction remained the direct fit for decoder-only generation. pretraining-objectives separates this choice from architecture: researchers can train an encoder-decoder model with a prefix language-model objective or adapt denoising targets to a decoder-only model.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/offli.title: Offline Policy Evaluation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/offli.content:
Offline Policy Evaluation
Offline policy evaluation (OPE) estimates how a target policy would perform without deploying it. It works from logs generated by a behaviour policy1, and the desired policy may choose actions the dataset rarely or never contains, so its outcomes are counterfactual.
flowchart TD
  L[Logged behaviour-policy data] --> O[Estimate target-policy value]
  O --> D[Direct outcome model]
  O --> I[Importance reweighting]
  O --> R[Doubly robust combination]
  O --> Q[Fitted action-value evaluation]
  O --> M[Learned transition and reward model]
  O --> C[Check coverage bias variance and horizon error]

In short

The target policy may pick actions the log rarely or never contains, so its outcomes are counterfactual.
Direct models risk bias, importance weights risk high variance, and doubly robust methods keep both failure surfaces.
No estimator creates support where none exists, so results need coverage slices, uncertainty and safe online checks.

In detail


                  
                  What makes offline policy evaluation fundamentally counterfactual? 
                  
                

The target policy may choose actions that the behaviour-policy log rarely or never contains.




                  
                  What tradeoff separates direct methods from importance sampling in OPE? 
                  
                

Direct models introduce model bias; importance weights can introduce very high variance.


The estimators group by what they trust:

Direct methods fit rewards or outcomes and simulate the target policy; model error creates bias.
Importance sampling reweights logged outcomes by target-to-behaviour action probabilities; large ratios create high variance.
Doubly robust methods join a direct model with importance correction, reducing dependence on either one while retaining both failure surfaces.
Fitted Q evaluation learns the target policy’s action values through Bellman updates on the log.
Model-based evaluation learns transitions and rewards, then simulates; compounded model error can dominate long horizons.

No estimator creates support where none exists. If the target policy systematically selects unseen actions, neither weighting nor a learned model can provide strong evidence without assumptions. Results should therefore be sliced by coverage, accompanied by uncertainty, and checked against limited online tests where safe.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/on-vs.title: On- vs Off-Policy Learning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/on-vs.content:
On- vs Off-Policy Learning
On- and off-policy learning differ in whether experience comes from the policy being learned about. The data-generating policy is the behaviour policy, and the policy being evaluated or improved is the target policy1.
flowchart TD
  P[Policy being learned about] --> O[On-policy]
  P --> F[Off-policy]
  O --> S[Current target policy generates data]
  S --> C[Matched distribution but continual collection]
  F --> D[Another policy or replay log generates data]
  D --> R[Reuse data with coverage and correction risk]

In short

On-policy data match the current action distribution, but every update makes old experience stale.
Off-policy learning reuses data from other policies for sample efficiency, yet target actions may be poorly represented in the log.
Importance sampling corrects some mismatch, at the cost of high variance over long trajectories.

In detail


                  
                  What determines whether learning is on-policy or off-policy? 
                  
                

Whether the data-generating behaviour policy is the same policy being learned about.




                  
                  What does off-policy learning gain and risk? 
                  
                

It gains data reuse and sample efficiency but risks distribution mismatch and unstable correction.


On-policy methods collect trajectories from the current target policy. Their data match the current action distribution, which simplifies estimation, but policy updates make old experience stale and require continual interaction. SARSA and common policy-gradient loops are examples.
Off-policy methods learn a target policy from experience produced by another policy: an exploratory behaviour policy, an older checkpoint, human demonstrations, or a replay buffer. Q-learning is the standard tabular example. Data reuse can improve sample efficiency and supports offline learning, but target actions may be poorly represented in the log.
Importance sampling corrects some mismatch by weighting actions according to target-to-behaviour probability ratios. Large ratios create high variance, especially over long trajectories. Value-function approximation and bootstrapping can add instability when coverage is weak.
Operational consequence
Freshness, replay, clipping, and drift monitoring control the distance between behaviour and target distributions. This same mismatch makes offline-policy-evaluation difficult because it asks what a different policy would have done using only actions another policy selected.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/optim.title: Optimizers
sections/machine-learning/concepts/optim.content:
Optimizers
An optimizer is the update rule that turns gradients into parameter steps. The lineage runs from vanilla SGD to Adam, every variant reads as a particle rolling down the loss landscape, and the verdict is to use SGD+Nesterov Momentum or Adam1.
In short

Momentum lets the gradient control a velocity, so consistent directions accelerate and oscillating ones cancel.
Nesterov momentum evaluates the gradient at the look-ahead position x + μv.
Adagrad’s cache only grows and stops training early; RMSprop makes it a leaky moving average, and Adam adds momentum.
Second-order methods are hopeless at scale, so first-order methods own large-scale deep learning.
Step decay, gradient checks, log-scale random hyperparameter search and ensembles make up the rest of the craft.

Momentum changes what the gradient integrates
Vanilla SGD steps directly against the gradient. Momentum instead gives the gradient control of a velocity: v = μv − α·dx; x += v. The physical reading is exact — loss is hill height, negative gradient is force, so gradient is acceleration rather than displacement. The consequence is directional: velocity accumulates in any direction with consistent gradient while oscillating directions cancel. The hyperparameter μ (typically 0.9) is misnamed momentum — physically it is friction, damping the system so it can stop at the bottom.


                  
                  Why does momentum help on ravines but hurt nowhere? 
                  
                

On consistently-graded directions it adds the steps up, accelerating progress; across steep oscillating directions the alternating signs cancel in the velocity average, dampening the zig-zag vanilla SGD suffers. The cost is overshoot past a minimum, which friction bleeds off.


Nesterov momentum sharpens this with a look-ahead: since momentum alone is about to move x by μv, evaluate the gradient there (x + μv) rather than at the stale current position — stronger convergence guarantees for convex functions, slightly better practice everywhere.
Adaptive per-parameter learning rates
A second family abandons one global learning rate. Adagrad divides each parameter’s step by √(accumulated squared gradients): frequently-updated parameters slow down, rarely-updated ones speed up. Its flaw is monotonicity — the accumulated cache only grows, so the effective rate collapses and training stops early. RMSprop fixes exactly that by making the cache a leaky moving average (cache = decay·cache + (1−decay)·dx²), keeping equalization without decay. Famously, its publication is slide 29 of Hinton’s Coursera course.


                  
                  What makes Adam "RMSProp with momentum," and what is bias correction for? 
                  
                

Adam keeps RMSProp’s adaptive denominator v but replaces the raw gradient in the numerator with a smoothed moving average m. Both m and v start at zero, so early estimates are biased toward nothing; dividing each by (1 − βᵗ) at step t corrects the warm-up, which otherwise makes the first steps tiny.


The practical payoff shows at saddle points: vanilla SGD stalls where curvature cancels, while adaptive methods see near-zero gradient along the flat direction, inflate that direction’s effective rate, and escape.
The rest of the craft

Learning-rate annealing — high rates carry too much kinetic energy to settle into narrow minima. Step decay (halve every k epochs, or when validation error plateaus) beats exponential/1-t schedules on interpretability.
Second-order methods — Newton’s method uses curvature via the inverse Hessian but is hopeless at scale (a million parameters → ~3.7 TB of Hessian); L-BFGS approximates it yet resists mini-batching, so first-order methods own large-scale deep learning.
Verification before trust — centered-difference gradient checks judged on relative error; overfitting 20 examples to zero loss before any full run.
Hyperparameters — search log-scale (effects are multiplicative), random rather than grid, coarse-to-fine.
Ensembles — averaging independent models, checkpoints, or a running weight average buys reliable final percent; knowledge-distillation compresses them back.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/polic.title: Policy Gradients
sections/machine-learning/concepts/polic.content:
Policy Gradients
Policy-gradient methods learn a randomized policy π_θ(a|s) directly by gradient ascent on expected total payoff — no model of transitions or rewards required, only the ability to sample trajectories and observe payoffs. The family runs from REINFORCE through PPO1.
In short

The log-derivative trick turns the gradient of expected payoff into an expectation estimable from sampled trajectories.
Transition-dynamics terms have zero gradient and vanish, so no model of the environment is needed.
Subtracting a state-dependent baseline, ideally the value function, leaves the gradient unbiased and cuts variance.
PPO reuses one batch for several updates through importance ratios, and clipping stops overshoot from stale data.

REINFORCE: the log-derivative trick
The obstacle is that η(θ) = E_τ∼P_θ[f(τ)] averages over a distribution that depends on θ — you cannot differentiate under an expectation whose sampling process moves. (This is the same problem VAEs solve with reparameterization; unavailable here because f — the payoff — cannot be differentiated at all.) The rescue is algebraic:
∇_θ E[f(τ)] = E[(∇_θ log P_θ(τ)) · f(τ)]
The transition-dynamics terms inside log P_θ(τ) have zero gradient and vanish — precisely the terms we couldn’t evaluate anyway. What remains is estimable from sampled trajectories:
∇_θη(θ) ≈ (1/n) Σᵢ (∇_θ Σₜ log π_θ(aₜ⁽ⁱ⁾|sₜ⁽ⁱ⁾)) · f(τ⁽ⁱ⁾)
The reading gives the algorithm its character: ∇log π is the direction that makes a sampled trajectory more likely; multiplying by its payoff f(τ) reinforces good trajectories strongly and bad ones weakly.


                  
                  Why can any state-dependent function B(sₜ) be subtracted from the payoff without biasing the gradient? 
                  
                

Because E[∇_θ log π_θ(aₜ|sₜ)] = 0 for any fixed state — the score of a distribution has zero mean. So the added term E[∇log π · B(sₜ)] vanishes exactly, while subtracting a well-chosen B (approximately the value function) cancels the bulk of the payoff’s random variation, cutting estimator variance dramatically.


Baselines and PPO
That zero-mean fact yields the baseline: subtracting B(sₜ) leaves the expected gradient unchanged but reduces variance, with the value function V(sₜ) as the near-optimal choice — estimated crudely, since errors affect only variance, never the mean. This value-function baseline is what makes the method effectively actor-critic: the policy (actor) ascends the advantage R≥t − V_old(sₜ) computed by the learned critic.
PPO addresses the data inefficiency of on-policy methods — vanilla REINFORCE allows one gradient update per batch of sampled trajectories. Importance-sampling likelihood ratios rₜ(θ) = π_θ(aₜ|sₜ)/π_{θ_old}(aₜ|sₜ) convert old-policy samples into local surrogate objectives, letting several updates reuse one batch. The famous clipping caps each per-timestep contribution: once an action’s probability has moved beyond [1−ε, 1+ε] relative to the old policy, the objective stops rewarding further movement in that direction — preventing overshoot from stale data. Advantages replace raw reward-to-go inside the clipped term, and generalized advantage estimation refines them further.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/posit.title: Positional Encoding
sections/machine-learning/concepts/posit.content:
Positional Encoding
Positional encoding gives a Transformer the sequence order it would otherwise lack, because self-attention treats its inputs as a set. Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer1 uses relative position biases instead of adding a fixed vector for each absolute position.
In short

T5 adds a learned scalar per query-key offset to the attention logit, per head, shared across layers.
Offsets fall into 32 buckets, so one layer cannot tell apart two distances beyond 128 tokens.
Stacked layers compose shorter offsets, letting the whole network respond to relationships beyond one layer’s range.

T5’s relative position scheme
For each query-key pair, T5 finds the offset between their sequence positions and adds a learned scalar to the attention logit before the model computes attention weights. Each attention head has its own learned biases. The model shares those position parameters across layers.
T5 groups offsets into 32 buckets. Bucket widths grow logarithmically through a distance of 128 tokens, and every larger offset maps to the same far-distance bucket. One attention layer therefore cannot distinguish two relative distances once both exceed 128.
Repeated blocks change that boundary. A later layer can combine information that prior layers gathered across shorter offsets, so the complete network can respond to relationships beyond one layer’s direct range. This effect comes from composition across layer-wise-representations, not from a hidden absolute position index.
Other schemes in the comparison
T5’s design contrasts with the sinusoidal signals in the original Transformer and learned absolute position embeddings. All three restore order information, but relative biases attach the signal to the distance between a query and key inside attention.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/post-.title: Post-Training
sections/machine-learning/concepts/post-.content:
Post-Training
Post-training changes a pretrained language model’s behavior or skills with smaller, targeted datasets and objectives. In Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training1 it is a staged engineering process: choose capabilities, curate and decontaminate data, optimize the model, then test both target gains and regressions.
In short

Supervised fine-tuning uses demonstrations, preference optimization uses comparisons, and a verifiable-reward stage handles program-checkable answers.
Each stage starts from the previous checkpoint and can trade one skill for another, as Tulu 3’s safety decline shows.
Data design, such as unique prompts and on-policy responses, often controls the result more than the algorithm name.

Stages serve different data shapes
supervised-fine-tuning trains on prompt-response demonstrations. preference-optimization trains on comparisons between responses; Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model2 derives a loss that performs this stage without a separate reward model or an online RL loop. Tulu 3 adds a later reinforcement-learning stage for tasks whose answers or format constraints a program can verify.
Post-training can also install a narrow interface skill. Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools3 fine-tunes ordinary next-token prediction data augmented with API calls that help predict later text. The model retains its language-modeling objective while learning when to request a calculator, search system, translator, calendar, or question-answering model.
A pipeline creates regression surfaces
Each stage starts from the previous checkpoint and can trade one skill for another. Tulu 3’s safety score peaked after SFT, then declined after preference tuning and verifiable-reward training. Its held-out tests also showed that gains on one instruction-following benchmark transferred poorly to new constraint types. Tulu 3’s stage-by-stage suite measures intended capabilities beyond the objective used in each run.
Data design often controls the result more than the algorithm name. Tulu 3 found benefits from unique prompts, on-policy responses, skill-specific mixtures, license tracking, and evaluation decontamination. Duplicating prompts with new response pairs offered little gain. Toolformer found that useful API calls could be rare enough to require tool-specific corpus filters.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/prefe.title: Preference Optimization
sections/machine-learning/concepts/prefe.content:
Preference Optimization
Preference optimization trains a language model from comparisons between responses to the same prompt. Each example marks one response as preferred and another as rejected, supplying information that a set of demonstrations cannot express.
In short

RLHF fits a reward model and optimizes against it, while DPO turns the same comparisons into one offline classification loss.
The DPO loss weights pairs by how badly the implicit reward orders them, and a naive unweighted objective could produce degenerate text.
Tulu 3 chose length-normalized DPO, which beat the base checkpoint where standard DPO, SimPO, and the tested PPO runs did not.
Preference optimization inherits its labels’ limits, including judge biases and offline data that cannot respond to later generations.

Explicit and implicit reward routes
The conventional RLHF route fits a Reward-Model to the comparisons, then uses reinforcement learning to raise its scores while a KL penalty keeps the policy near a reference model. Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model1 derives Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which expresses the latent reward as a log-probability ratio between the policy and its reference. Substituting that expression into a pairwise preference model yields a binary classification loss over preferred and rejected completions. DPO trains the policy and an implicit reward representation in one offline step.
The DPO loss does more than raise one response’s probability and lower the other’s. It compares both changes with the reference model and weights pairs according to how badly the implicit reward orders them. The authors found that a naive unweighted preferred-versus-rejected objective could produce degenerate text. Its β coefficient regulates departure from the reference.
Data construction controls what the preference means
Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training2 built synthetic preferences by sampling four responses from a pool of models and scoring helpfulness, instruction following, honesty, and truthfulness. It included responses from the SFT checkpoint to provide on-policy coverage. Ablations favored more unique prompts and a mixture of used and unused SFT prompts; repeating prompts with different response pairs produced little aggregate gain.
Tulu 3 used length-normalized DPO to reduce preference judges’ tendency to favor longer responses. In its tested algorithm sweep, that variant beat the base checkpoint while standard DPO, SimPO, and the tested PPO runs did not. The team chose it for cheaper iteration, then cached reference log-probabilities and separated chosen and rejected forward passes to fit larger models.
Preference optimization still inherits its labels’ limits. A model judge can encode length, style, or factuality errors, and offline data cannot respond to generations produced later in training. Tulu 3 found little benefit from its tested online DPO setup, so the report records that path as an unresolved engineering choice rather than a general failure of online methods.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/pretr.title: Pre-training Evaluation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/pretr.content:
Pre-training Evaluation
Pre-training evaluation measures the base checkpoint before instruction-tuning changes its behavior. For Llama-3 in The Llama 3 Herd of Models1 it combines likelihood, task scores, robustness checks, adversarial sets, long-context probes, and contamination analysis.
In short

Downstream accuracy is forecast in two fits, task likelihood against FLOPs and then a sigmoid from likelihood to accuracy.
Larger base checkpoints vary less across multiple-choice formats, but adversarial math and question answering still cost substantial ground.
N-gram contamination checks can miss transformed copies or flag common language, leaving some sets’ cleanliness unresolved.
Scores from the instruction-tuned model cannot establish what pre-training learned, so the two stages are reported separately.

Forecast before the run
Ordinary scaling-laws predict next-token loss, while a flagship decision needs estimates for downstream tasks. The team uses two links. First, it relates the negative log-likelihood of the correct task answer to pre-training FLOPs for compute-optimal small models. Second, it relates that likelihood to task accuracy with the small scaling models and older Llama 2 checkpoints.
On ARC Challenge, this method extrapolates across four orders of magnitude in compute and gives a close forecast for the 405B checkpoint. The method does not assume that a smooth loss change maps to a smooth accuracy change; the second fit uses a sigmoid to capture the task’s response curve.
Evaluation suite
The standard base-model suite covers reading comprehension, code, commonsense, mathematics, long context, and aggregate knowledge tests. The team recomputes competitor results where model access permits and uses published scores when access prevents a fresh run. For finite benchmark samples, it reports 95 percent confidence intervals under a Gaussian approximation and warns that these intervals omit other sources of variation.
Long-context evaluation combines task datasets with targeted retrieval probes. The models recover needles placed across contexts up to 128K tokens, then face multi-needle and long-document question sets that demand more than retrieval of one string. During context extension, the training team also requires short-context scores to recover after each length increase.
Robustness and adversarial checks
Multiple-choice scores can depend on labels, answer order, examples, and prompt wording. The team changes each factor on MMLU. Its larger base checkpoints show less variation across these formats, though the paper treats that result as a measured property of this family rather than a general benchmark guarantee.
Adversarial evaluations pair altered question-answering, mathematics, and paraphrase sets with their standard counterparts. Llama 3 retains paraphrase performance but loses substantial ground on adversarial math and question answering. A high average benchmark score can therefore hide a specific sensitivity.
Contamination analysis
The team marks an evaluation example as contaminated when enough of its tokens belong to matching 8-grams in the pre-training corpus. It selects a threshold per dataset based on the largest measured clean-versus-full score difference. Some datasets show both high overlap and a large estimated performance gain; others show overlap with little gain.
The paper lists two limits. An n-gram method can miss transformed copies or flag common language, and some benchmarks have too few clean examples after filtering to estimate a difference. The team withholds a contamination result in those cases and leaves the set’s cleanliness unresolved. training-data-engineering covers the organizational and corpus controls used before this audit.
Keep base and chat claims separate
Post-training adds instruction following, preference alignment, tool use, and safety behavior. Scores from the instruction-tuned model cannot establish what pre-training learned. The paper reports the two stages in separate sections and changes evaluation protocols to match their roles. That separation also helps diagnose whether a regression comes from corpus and scale choices or from later alignment data.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/pretr.title: Pretraining Objectives
sections/machine-learning/concepts/pretr.content:
Pretraining Objectives
A pretraining objective determines which prediction error supplies the updates during pretraining. Two main families compete: predicting each next token from its left context and reconstructing text that a corruption process has damaged.
In short

Causal language modeling can include many latent tasks, because ordinary documents contain questions with answers and articles with summaries.
Denoising beat causal language modeling and deshuffling on the main T5 transfer benchmarks, while denoising variants differed little.
T5 corrupts 15% of tokens in spans averaging three tokens, and a 50% rate hurt GLUE and SQuAD.
Objective and architecture are separate choices, so an objective should not stand in for an architecture name.

Causal language modeling
Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners1 factorizes a sequence probability into one conditional probability per token. GPT-2 minimizes error on next-token-prediction over WebText. The authors argue that this single objective can include many latent tasks because ordinary documents contain questions followed by answers, source sentences followed by translations, and articles followed by summaries.
Causal masking prevents a position from seeing future tokens. A decoder-only model can then use the same operation during training and generation, though it processes an input prefix from left to right rather than forming bidirectional representations of that prefix.
Denoising and span corruption
Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer2 compares causal language modeling, token deshuffling, BERT-style masking, and several denoising variants under one text-to-text framework. Denoising beat causal language modeling and deshuffling on the main downstream transfer benchmarks.
Small changes among denoising variants mattered less. Reconstructing the whole original sequence, predicting only removed tokens, replacing spans with sentinels, and dropping corrupted tokens produced similar aggregate performance. Sequence length and training cost therefore guided the final choice.
T5 corrupts 15% of tokens in contiguous spans averaging three tokens. It replaces each span in the input with a unique sentinel and asks the decoder to emit only the missing spans, separated by corresponding sentinels. This target remains shorter than the original sequence. A 50% corruption rate hurt GLUE and SQuAD, while rates of 10%, 15%, and 25% stayed closer.
Objective and architecture are separate choices
Raffel and colleagues apply language-model and denoising objectives to encoder-decoder, decoder-only, and prefix-language-model structures. Their encoder-decoder denoising combination performed best, but the experiment shows why an objective should not stand in for an architecture name. GPT-2 identifies both: a decoder-only Transformer trained causally.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/pretr.title: Pretraining
sections/machine-learning/concepts/pretr.content:
Pretraining
Pretraining updates a model on a large, data-rich objective before anyone adapts it to a narrower task. The corpus, objective, architecture, and compute budget all affect what transfers.
In short

Pretraining improved every T5 baseline task except high-resource English-to-French translation, where task data already sufficed.
Unsupervised pretraining followed by task-specific finetuning beat mixing supervised and unsupervised tasks in one run.
Heuristic cleaning beat unfiltered C4 on every reported task, and repeating a small corpus many times degraded transfer.
Lower pretraining loss does not establish factual reliability or task completion, so each paper evaluates transfer directly.

The transfer pipeline
Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer1 treats pretraining as the first phase of a controlled pipeline. Its T5 experiments train a Transformer on unlabeled text, then use labeled task data to finetune the same parameters. Pretraining improved every baseline task except high-resource English-to-French translation, where the task dataset already supplied enough examples to make the gain small.
The paper also compares joint multitask training with staged transfer. Mixing supervised and unsupervised tasks in one run required careful sampling rates and underperformed unsupervised pretraining followed by task-specific finetuning. Multitask pretraining followed by a separate finetuning phase recovered performance close to the staged baseline.
Corpus quality and coverage
Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners2 uses WebText, a 40 GB collection of more than eight million web documents selected through Reddit links. The authors sought broad domains and naturally occurring task demonstrations, then found that larger GPT-2 variants transferred better while every model still underfit the corpus.
T5 uses the much larger C4 corpus. Heuristic cleaning beat unfiltered C4 on every reported task. Narrow in-domain corpora could help a matching downstream benchmark, but repeating a small corpus hundreds or thousands of times degraded transfer. Their final models trained on about one trillion tokens without exhausting C4.
Adaptation after pretraining
Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners3 starts FLAN from LaMDA-PT, a 137-billion-parameter model pretrained on 2.49 trillion BPE tokens. instruction-tuning then updates that base model on many labeled tasks phrased as requests. Its zero-shot gains show that later supervision can change how a pretrained model uses text interactions without replacing the base architecture.
Pretraining does not establish factual reliability or task completion by itself. GPT-2 produced factual errors and weak results on several tasks, T5’s English-only corpus limited translation, and FLAN still failed simple instructions. Each paper evaluates transfer rather than treating lower pretraining loss as sufficient evidence of useful behavior.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/rag-v.title: RAG vs Long Context
sections/machine-learning/concepts/rag-v.content:
RAG vs Long Context
Long context and retrieval allocate evidence differently: long context sends more of the corpus into the model, while RAG searches first and sends a selected subset1.
flowchart TD
  E[Evidence allocation choice] --> L[Long context sends more of the corpus]
  E --> R[RAG searches then selects a subset]
  L --> C[More cross-document context with higher cost and attention competition]
  R --> S[Lower input cost with retrieval-coverage risk]
  L --> H[Hybrid retrieval plus a moderately long context]
  R --> H
  H --> V[Validate quality recall latency cost and failure severity]

In short

Long context keeps cross-document detail but its cost and attention competition grow with input length.
RAG cuts input cost, but retrieval coverage bounds the answer.
Decide on validation data; a larger window does not make retrieval obsolete by itself.

In detail


                  
                  How do long context and RAG allocate evidence differently? 
                  
                

Long context sends more of the corpus; RAG searches first and sends a selected subset.




                  
                  What is the characteristic evidence failure of each approach? 
                  
                

Long context may ignore available evidence; RAG may exclude the needed evidence before generation.


Long context preserves cross-document details a retriever might omit and simplifies pipelines for bounded corpora. Its memory use, latency, throughput costs, and attention competition grow with input length. Capacity cannot guarantee utilization; under position sensitivity the model uses evidence in the middle of a long prompt less reliably.
RAG reduces input cost and allows independent evidence updates and permissions, but ingestion, query, chunking, or ranking errors can exclude the needed passage. Retrieval coverage bounds the answer. A hybrid can retrieve documents or sections, then use a relatively long context within the selected scope.
Decision rule
Use validation data rather than context-window size alone. Measure answer quality, evidence recall, latency, cost, and failure severity across corpus sizes and query types. A larger window changes the useful retrieval granularity but does not make retrieval obsolete by itself.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/rank-.title: Rank-Aware Evaluation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/rank-.content:
Rank-Aware Evaluation
Rank-aware evaluation treats relevance and position as separate inputs. Returning the right items is insufficient if the most useful ones appear after the user has stopped looking.
flowchart LR
  R[Relevance labels] --> C[Cumulative gain]
  P[Rank position] --> D[Position discount]
  C --> G[Discounted cumulative gain]
  D --> G
  I[Ideal ordering] --> N[NDCG = DCG / ideal DCG]
  G --> N

In short

DCG discounts relevance gains at later ranks, so order matters where cumulative gain alone would tie.
NDCG divides by the ideal ordering’s gain, giving a comparable 0–1 score across lists.
NDCG can let irrelevant results escape penalty, and ranking accuracy misses novelty, diversity and satisfaction.

Cumulative gain sums relevance without order, so two permutations can tie. DCG discounts gains at later ranks. NDCG divides by the gain of the ideal ordering, placing the result on a comparable 0–1 scale across recommendation lists.


                  
                  What does normalisation add after DCG has already included rank position? 
                  
                

It compares the observed ordering with the best ordering available for that list, allowing scores from lists with different attainable gains to be averaged.


NDCG carries a caveat: irrelevant results may escape penalty depending on the relevance scheme and list length. Objectives beyond ranking accuracy therefore matter: novelty, diversity, personalisation, satisfaction, hit rate, and future impact. A recommender can rank known relevance well while remaining repetitive or unsatisfying.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/refer.title: Reference-Based Text Evaluation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/refer.content:
Reference-Based Text Evaluation
Reference-based text evaluation compares generated text with one or more accepted answers. Each metric uses one of three definitions of a match: exact surface units, contextual token similarity, or distance between embedded distributions.
flowchart LR
  C[Candidate text] --> L[Lexical overlap]
  R[Reference set] --> L
  C --> E[Embedding similarity]
  R --> E
  L --> B[BLEU: precision-oriented n-grams]
  L --> G[ROUGE: recall-oriented overlap]
  E --> S[BERTScore: contextual token matches]
  E --> M[MoverScore: transport distance]

In short

BLEU asks how much produced n-gram content the references support; ROUGE asks how much reference content the candidate recovered.
BERTScore and MoverScore match on embeddings, so paraphrases can count without shared surface n-grams.
Reference quality remains the ceiling, and no score alone establishes factuality, usefulness, style, or safety.

Developed for translation, BLEU asks how much produced n-gram content the references support. ROUGE was developed for summarisation and asks how much reference content the candidate recovered; ROUGE-L uses longest common subsequences. BERTScore replaces exact tokens with contextual embedding matches and reports precision, recall, and F₁. MoverScore measures the work required to move embedded content between candidate and reference.


                  
                  What limitation do BERTScore and MoverScore address that BLEU and ROUGE retain? 
                  
                

They allow semantically similar paraphrases to match even when surface n-grams differ. They change the definition of similarity rather than eliminating dependence on a reference.


More varied references can represent more valid phrasings, but reference quality remains the ceiling. None of these scores alone establishes factuality, usefulness, style, or safety. Perplexity measures predictive fit, and burstiness measures output variation. Neither substitutes for reference agreement.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/refle.title: Reflection-Evaluator Loop
sections/machine-learning/concepts/refle.content:
Reflection-Evaluator Loop
A reflection-evaluator loop replaces one-pass generation with four stages: produce a draft, evaluate it against a goal, convert the evaluation into actionable feedback, and revise. Reflection is a simple agentic pattern; evaluator-optimizer is a workflow in which generation and judgment have distinct roles1.
flowchart LR
  D[Produce a draft] --> E[Evaluate against explicit criteria]
  E --> F[Convert findings into actionable feedback]
  F --> R[Revise]
  R --> E
  E --> P[Stop when a candidate passes or attempts are exhausted]

In short

Self-critique can repeat the draft’s blind spots, so external checks such as unit tests matter.
The loop improves only when evaluation yields useful findings and revision addresses them.
Reliable loops need explicit criteria, bounded attempts and an escalation rule when no candidate passes.

In detail


                  
                  What are the four stages of a reflection-evaluator loop? 
                  
                

Draft, evaluate, turn findings into feedback, then revise.




                  
                  Why are external checks valuable in a reflection loop? 
                  
                

A model critiquing itself can repeat the same blind spots as its draft.


The evaluator may be the same model under a critique prompt, a separate critic agent, or an external tool. Unit tests can check generated code; search or a database can challenge factual claims. Fluent self-critique can repeat the same blind spots as the draft, so external signals matter. The loop improves only when evaluation yields useful findings and revision addresses them.
Code can fix the order and stopping rule while models supply the draft and critique, placing this pattern on the workflow side of the agent-control-boundary without requiring full autonomy. A multi-agent implementation separates generator and critic but adds communication and cost.
Failure modes
An evaluator can reward style over correctness, invent defects, or accept correlated errors. Unlimited iteration can oscillate or spend tokens without measurable gain. Reliable loops need explicit criteria, external validation where possible, bounded attempts, and a rule for escalation when no candidate passes.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/regre.title: Regression Loss Geometry
sections/machine-learning/concepts/regre.content:
Regression Loss Geometry
Regression loss geometry describes how a metric transforms residuals before aggregation. That transformation determines whether one large miss should dominate, whether the score remains in the target unit, and whether absolute or relative error matters.








































MetricTransformationWhat the summary emphasisesMAEabsolute residuallinear cost; target unitsMSEsquared residualdisproportionately large missesRMSEsquare root of MSElarge-miss emphasis in target unitsRMSLEsquared log-space residualrelative rather than absolute scaleR²explained variationfit relative to a baselineadjusted R²R² adjusted for predictorsdiscourages gratuitous parameters


                  
                  Why can MAE and RMSE rank the same models differently? 
                  
                

MAE weights residual magnitude linearly, while RMSE inherits squared-error emphasis on large misses. The disagreement reports a choice about whether tail errors should dominate.


Choose the metric to match the consequence surface. If a ten-unit miss costs exactly twice a five-unit miss, absolute error reflects that premise. If large misses cause disproportionate harm, squared error reflects a different premise. A unitless fit statistic such as R² answers neither cost question by itself.
In short

MAE weights residuals linearly in target units, while MSE and RMSE let large misses dominate.
MAE and RMSE can rank the same models differently, reporting a choice about tail errors.
The metric should match the consequence surface, and R² answers neither cost question by itself.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/regul.title: Regularization
sections/machine-learning/concepts/regul.content:
Regularization
Regularization is any device that controls a network’s capacity to prevent it from fitting noise. bias-variance-tradeoff supplies the diagnosis — training error far below test error is overfitting, and regularisation is the remedy. Neural networks use its mechanisms in four families1. What is actually done in practice is one global L2 strength set by cross-validation, plus dropout at p = 0.5 after every layer.
In short

L2 penalises peaky weight vectors and acts on the update as weight decay toward zero.
L1 drives weights to essentially exactly zero, but unless feature selection is the goal, L2 performs better.
Max-norm constraints bound each neuron’s weights, so the network cannot explode under too high a learning rate.
Dropout samples a sub-network each step, and inverted dropout scales during training so the test-time pass needs no changes.
Dropout, DropConnect, stochastic pooling and data augmentation share one idea: noise injected into the forward pass, then marginalised away.

The four mechanisms
L2 regularization adds ½λw² to the objective for every weight, with λ the regularization strength. The factor of ½ exists only so the gradient comes out as λw instead of 2λw. Its character is to penalise peaky weight vectors and prefer diffuse ones: because weights interact multiplicatively with inputs, spreading weight across all inputs a little beats concentrating it on a few inputs a lot. On the update step it has an exact reading — every weight decays linearly toward zero, W += -lambda * W, which is why the machine-learning name for the same term is weight decay.
L1 regularization adds λ|w| per weight and produces sparsity — weights driven not just small but to essentially exactly zero. A neuron under L1 ends up using only its most important inputs and becomes nearly invariant to noisy ones; L2’s final vectors are diffuse small numbers instead. They combine as elastic net (λ₁|w| + λ₂w²). The practical verdict: unless explicit feature selection is the goal, L2 performs better.


                  
                  Why does the L1 penalty zero weights out while L2 only shrinks them? 
                  
                

The L1 gradient is constant in magnitude (±λ) no matter how small w gets, so pressure toward zero never relaxes; the L2 gradient λw shrinks in proportion to w, so the pressure fades as the weight gets small and it never arrives.


Max-norm constraints impose an absolute bound ‖w‖₂ < c on every neuron’s weight vector, enforced by clamping after each ordinary update (projected gradient descent). Typical c is 3–4. The appeal is failure containment rather than generalisation polish: the network cannot explode even when the learning rate is set too high, because updates are bounded.
Dropout (Srivastava et al.) keeps each neuron active with probability p during training and zeroes it otherwise, drawing a fresh mask every forward pass. Read structurally, each training step samples one sub-network from an exponential family and updates only its parameters (which all sub-networks share); at test time, using every neuron approximates averaging predictions across that whole ensemble. The scaling bookkeeping matters: since a neuron’s expected training output is px + (1−p)·0, test-time activations must match that expectation. Inverted dropout — the recommended form — divides kept activations by p during training so the test-time forward pass needs no changes at all when dropout is moved or removed.


                  
                  What problem does inverted dropout solve relative to vanilla dropout? 
                  
                

Vanilla dropout scales activations by p at test time, coupling prediction code to a training-time hyperparameter. Inverted dropout does the scaling during training, leaving the test-time pass untouched — so changing where dropout applies cannot silently break inference.


One theme underneath
Dropout belongs to a family defined by noise injected into the forward pass, then marginalised away — analytically at test time (scaling by p) or numerically (averaging several sampled passes). DropConnect zeroes random weights instead of neurons; stochastic pooling and data augmentation are convolutional-network members of the same family. What looks like four unrelated tricks is one idea applied at different points in the network.
Practice notes from the source

Biases are normally not regularized: they lack the multiplicative interaction with inputs that gives weight penalties their meaning, and there are few enough of them that the classifier can afford to use them.
Per-layer regularization strengths are rarely used; a single global L2 strength, cross-validated, is the norm.
Dropout placement interacts with the loss: applying it in the layer directly before an L2 regression loss is specifically warned against — the loss demands exact outputs, and dropout noise makes that fragile.
Batch normalization, though motivated by initialisation rather than capacity, is part of the same setup checklist; networks using it are markedly more robust to bad initialisation.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/retri.title: Retrieval Chunking Boundary
sections/machine-learning/concepts/retri.content:
Retrieval Chunking Boundary
The chunking boundary determines what unit a retriever can return. The core tradeoff1: smaller chunks match narrow queries precisely but can detach a statement from its definition or qualification; larger chunks preserve surrounding context but introduce unrelated material and spend more of the generation budget.
flowchart TD
  B[Choose a chunk boundary] --> S[Smaller chunks]
  B --> L[Larger chunks]
  S --> P[Precise narrow matching]
  S --> C[Context can be detached]
  L --> K[More surrounding context]
  L --> N[More noise and budget use]
  B --> T[Test against corpus and query granularity]

In short

Small chunks match precisely but can detach a statement from its qualification.
Large chunks keep context but add noise and spend generation budget.
No corpus-independent optimal size exists; test candidate sizes on the corpus.

In detail


                  
                  What is the central chunk-size tradeoff in retrieval? 
                  
                

Small chunks match precisely but lose context; large chunks preserve context but add noise and cost.




                  
                  Why is there no corpus-independent optimal chunk size? 
                  
                

Document structure, query granularity, task, model limits and synthesis budget all change the useful boundary.


Fixed-size chunking is cheap and predictable, with overlap reducing boundary loss at the cost of duplicate evidence. Sentence, paragraph, recursive, and format-aware methods follow visible structure. Semantic chunking groups neighbouring units until similarity changes. Late chunking or late interaction tries to preserve broader context during representation while retaining fine-grained retrieval.
There is no corpus-independent optimal size. Document structure, embedding input limits, query granularity, retrieval metric, synthesis budget, and task type all change the boundary. Check whether a chunk makes sense without hidden surrounding text, then evaluate candidate sizes on the corpus.
Failure signature
Fragmented retrieval returns an answer-bearing phrase without its scope; oversized retrieval returns the right phrase buried in noise. Overlap can make several near-duplicates look like independent support. Evaluate chunking together with reranking and context recall and precision.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/retri.title: Retrieval-Reranking Funnel
sections/machine-learning/concepts/retri.content:
Retrieval-Reranking Funnel
A retrieval-reranking funnel separates broad candidate discovery from precise evidence selection. First-stage retrieval is a high-recall operation1: sparse, dense, or hybrid indexes cheaply return more candidates than the generator can consume.
flowchart LR
  C[Large corpus] --> R[High-recall first-stage retrieval]
  R --> P[Pooled candidate set]
  P --> K[Costlier reranking]
  K --> E[Small evidence set]
  E --> G[Generator context]
  M[Metadata permissions and budget rules] --> K

In short

A cheap first stage maximizes recall; a costlier reranker picks the evidence that earns prompt space.
One score rarely serves both scale and precision.
Reranking cannot recover a relevant item missing from the candidate pool.

In detail


                  
                  Why does a retrieval-reranking funnel use a broad first stage? 
                  
                

The first stage cheaply maximizes recall over a large corpus.




                  
                  What is the reranker buying with its extra computation? 
                  
                

More precise selection of the small evidence set that deserves prompt space.


The second stage spends more computation per candidate. Cross-encoders can jointly read query and passage; late-interaction models retain token-level matching; instruction-following rerankers apply task criteria; metadata and business rules remove ineligible results. Personalization and context-budget constraints may alter the final order even when semantic relevance is unchanged.
One score rarely serves both scale and precision. Approximate nearest-neighbour search makes a large corpus searchable; reranking decides which small set deserves scarce prompt space. Multiple retrievers require score calibration or rank fusion before comparison.
Evaluation boundary
Reranking cannot recover a relevant item absent from the candidate pool. Measure candidate recall and post-rerank precision separately through component-wise-rag-evaluation. Filtering can also encode policy or personalization errors that look like retrieval failure unless stages are logged.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/rewar.title: Reward Proxy Failure
sections/machine-learning/concepts/rewar.content:
Reward Proxy Failure
A reinforcement-learning agent optimizes the reward it receives, not the intention the designer had. Reward hacking is exploiting a proxy or loophole to raise measured reward without completing the intended task1.
flowchart LR
  I[Intended objective] --> P[Measurable reward proxy]
  P --> O[Agent optimizes the measured signal]
  O --> L[Find loophole or omitted dimension]
  L --> H[Reward rises while intended task fails]
  H --> M[Monitoring and adversarial evaluation]
  M --> R[Redesign reward constraints or oversight]

In short

Delayed or hard-to-observe objectives force proxies, and each proxy is useful but incomplete.
Reward shaping speeds credit assignment but adds targets the agent can optimize independently of the real objective.
Hacking is high reward that violates intent, and a learned reward model is still a proxy that can be exploited or drift.

In detail


                  
                  Why can a reinforcement-learning agent satisfy its reward while failing the task? 
                  
                

It optimizes the measurable proxy it receives, not the designer’s unobserved intention.




                  
                  Why can reward shaping create new failure modes? 
                  
                

Every added intermediate signal becomes another target the agent can optimize independently of the real objective.


Production systems often need proxies because the final objective is delayed or hard to observe. A coding assistant might be rewarded for suggestion acceptance, test passage, or task completion signals. Each signal is useful but incomplete: acceptance can favour superficial convenience, a narrow test can be gamed, and a completion report can be false. Combining them may still fail to recover the latent objective.
Reward shaping adds intermediate feedback to sparse tasks, accelerating credit assignment while also adding targets that can be optimized independently. Guardrails, regression tests, quality metrics, failure slices, human review, and online monitoring therefore belong in reward design. They test whether reward improvement transfers to the actual outcome.
Boundary
Poor performance and reward hacking are different. Hacking means the policy found a high-reward behaviour that violates intent; in ordinary learning failure, the policy may receive low reward. A Reward-Model can make the proxy adaptive, but its learned preferences remain a proxy and can be exploited or drift.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/safet.title: Safety Tuning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/safet.content:
Safety Tuning
Safety tuning uses targeted post-training data to teach a model when to refuse, when to comply, and how to handle requests that lack enough information or fall outside supported tasks. Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training1 treats this behavior as a distinct skill with its own data and regression suite.
In short

Safety data pairs harmful and adversarial requests with benign look-alikes, so the model learns both refusal and compliance.
Removing the safety datasets dropped Tulu 3’s 8B safety average from 93.1 to 74.7; later DPO and RL eroded part of the gain.
The scores depend on classifiers, prompts and six datasets, and do not establish deployment safety.

Refusal accuracy has two directions
Tulu 3 combines harmful and adversarial requests with benign prompts that resemble unsafe ones. Its safety data covers direct harmful requests, jailbreaks, in-the-wild interactions, and contextual noncompliance cases such as incomplete or indeterminate requests. Contrastive examples from CoCoNot help prevent broad refusal rules from blocking safe questions.
The evaluation suite measures harmful refusal and benign compliance. HarmBench, Do-Anything-Now, and jailbreak sets test whether the model rejects harmful requests. XSTest and parts of WildJailbreak also test whether superficial safety cues cause refusal of harmless requests. A useful aggregate must penalize both unsafe compliance and exaggerated refusal.
Dedicated data moved the measured skill
In Tulu 3’s SFT ablation, removing safety-specific datasets changed the 8B safety average from 93.1 to 74.7 while most other benchmark scores stayed close. The safety data is orthogonal to the rest of the SFT mix. General instruction and reasoning examples did not recover the same refusal and compliance behavior.
Later optimization can erase part of that gain. For the 8B model, the six-task safety average fell from 93.1 after SFT to 87.2 after DPO and 85.5 after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. The 70B sequence fell from 94.4 to 89.0 to 88.3. Neither later stage targeted safety, so its objectives shifted behavior learned earlier. Tulu 3’s stage-by-stage tests detect that regression after each post-training objective.
These scores remain tied to classifiers, prompts, and the six selected datasets. Tulu 3 uses WildGuard to classify refusal or compliance for several benchmarks, so classifier error enters the reported result. The suite measures response behavior under its tested attacks; it does not establish safety for deployment contexts, tool permissions, or new attack families.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/scali.title: Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering
sections/machine-learning/concepts/scali.content:
Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering
General methods that convert computation into performance eventually beat methods that encode human understanding of a domain. Sutton names and argues this claim in The Bitter Lesson1, though researchers had observed the empirical pattern before he named it.
flowchart TD
  A[Assume available compute is fixed] --> K[Encode domain knowledge]
  K --> S1[Short-term gain, and it is personally satisfying]
  S1 --> P[Plateau]
  P --> O[Then it obstructs later use of general computation]
  C[Compute arrives regardless] --> G[General methods — search and learning]
  G --> W[Keeps improving with no human in the loop]
  W --> B[The breakthrough arrives by the rejected route — hence bitter]
  T[An architecture encoding how to spend compute] --> G
  D[An architecture encoding what is true about the domain] --> K

In short

Knowledge engineering looks right only under the false assumption that available compute is fixed.
Built-in knowledge helps briefly, then plateaus and obstructs later use of general computation.
Sutton holds that only search and learning scale arbitrarily, as chess, Go, speech and vision repeated.
The Transformer complicates the claim, but it encodes how to spend compute, not what is true about the domain.

The argument
Researchers optimise as though available compute were fixed. Under that assumption, encoding domain knowledge is the only available lever. Over a horizon longer than a single research project, far more compute arrives regardless, and only methods that can absorb it keep improving.


                  
                  What false assumption makes knowledge engineering look like the right move? 
                  
                

That available compute is fixed. Under that assumption domain knowledge is the only lever; over a horizon longer than one research project, far more compute arrives anyway, and only methods that can absorb it keep improving.


The two need not conflict, but in practice they do: time spent on one is time not spent on the other, people become psychologically committed to their approach, and knowledge-based methods tend to complicate the system in ways that make it worse at exploiting general computation later.


                  
                  Beyond opportunity cost, how does built-in knowledge actively harm later progress? 
                  
                

It complicates the system in ways that make it worse at exploiting general computation. The structure added to help does not merely stop paying — it obstructs the method that would have scaled.


Sutton argues that only two things scale arbitrarily: search and learning. Both turn compute into performance without a human in the loop.


                  
                  Which two methods does Sutton say scale arbitrarily, and what do they share? 
                  
                

Search and learning. Both convert compute into performance with no human in the loop, which is why more hardware improves them without more research.


Four repeats






























DomainThe knowledge approachWhat wonChessHuman understanding of chess structureMassive deep search, Kasparov, 1997GoEncoding human knowledge to avoid searchSearch plus self-play learning, 20 years laterSpeechPhonemes, vocal tract models, word knowledgeStatistical HMMs, then deep learningVisionEdges, generalised cylinders, SIFT featuresConvolution and invariance, everything else discarded
Why it is “bitter”
In Sutton’s account, building in human knowledge helps in the short term and feels personally satisfying. It then plateaus and actively inhibits progress. The eventual breakthrough arrives by the opposing route, making the success a defeat for a favoured, human-centric approach. Sutton says researchers therefore resent the lesson and digest it incompletely instead of learning it once and remembering it.


                  
                  Why is the lesson "bitter" rather than merely surprising? 
                  
                

Because the breakthrough arrives by the route the researchers rejected. Every win for scale is a defeat for a favoured human-centric approach, so it is resented and incompletely digested instead of learned once.


The second, less-quoted half
Sutton also specifies what designers should leave out. The contents of minds are “tremendously, irredeemably complex.” Space, objects, multiple agents, and symmetries belong to the arbitrary outside world, whose complexity is endless. Build the meta-methods that find complexity, not the complexity itself. The aim is agents that can discover as people do, not agents that contain what people have discovered.


                  
                  What should be built in, if not knowledge about the domain? 
                  
                

The meta-methods that find complexity. The contents of minds are irredeemably complex and the world they describe is endless, so the buildable thing is the capacity to discover, not the discoveries.


An instance four years early
A character-level model given raw text demonstrates the same claim2. It learns spelling, syntax, quote matching, brace nesting, and markdown structure, and the researchers specified none of those features. Karpathy’s interpretability finding is the argument in miniature: nobody hardcoded that tracking whether the model is inside or outside a quote helps predict the next character.
The case that complicates it
Architecture is human design, and the unmistakably designed Transformer complicates Sutton’s argument: built-in structure may plateau, yet the biggest recent gain came from an architectural change.
The distinction lies in what the architecture encodes. The Transformer contains almost no knowledge about language: no phonemes, grammar, or parse structure. It supplies a way to spend more compute usefully through parallelism across positions and a mechanism indifferent to modality. As a general method that scales, it belongs to the category Sutton says survives. Little changes between text and vision3. The Vision Transformer’s architecture is nearly identical to the 2017 original, with images cut into patches that play the role of tokens.
Architecture still matters. Architectures that last encode how to use compute rather than what is true about the domain.


                  
                  What distinguishes an architecture that lasts from one that plateaus? 
                  
                

What it encodes. A lasting architecture encodes how to spend compute — parallelism, modality-indifference. A plateauing one encodes what is true about the domain, like phonemes or parse structure.


Related Entities & Topics

sections/machine-learning/concepts/scali.title: Scaling Laws
sections/machine-learning/concepts/scali.content:
Scaling Laws
Scaling laws estimate how model loss changes as researchers add parameters, training data, or compute. Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models1 fits power laws across each resource and then joins them into allocation rules. The Llama 3 Herd of Models2 shows a later model team using the same method to choose a frontier-scale run.
In short

Loss follows a power law in parameters, data, and compute while the other two stay large enough to avoid a bottleneck.
The 2020 Kaplan fit sends most new compute into parameters and favors stopping large models early.
The Llama team fits optimal tokens as C^0.53 and trains its 8B and 70B models past compute-optimal for inference.
The exponents come from one dataset, tokenizer, and model family, and loss forecasts do not prove downstream gains.

The three-way constraint
Kaplan and colleagues measure cross-entropy loss against non-embedding parameter count N, dataset tokens D, and training compute C. Loss follows a power law in each variable while the other two remain large enough to avoid a bottleneck. Their experiments cover six orders of magnitude in model size and more than eight in adjusted compute, yet architecture shape has a small effect across the tested Transformer configurations.
A budget cannot fund any one axis in isolation. More parameters yield diminishing returns once data limits the run. More tokens yield diminishing returns once model capacity limits it. More compute helps only when researchers assign it to a model and training schedule that can use it.
Allocation on the Kaplan frontier
The 2020 fit sends most new compute into parameters. Its compute-efficient prescription scales model size as C^0.73, critical batch size as C^0.24, and serial update steps as C^0.03. A one-epoch dataset grows as C^0.27. Under this fit, the team gains throughput from larger batches and capacity from larger models while adding little serial training depth.
This allocation connects scaling to gradient-descent. Batch size controls the noise and parallelism of each gradient estimate; update count controls the serial path; parameter count sets the work per token. Kaplan and colleagues use the gradient noise scale to estimate a critical batch size. Above that point, larger batches buy fewer steps at a rising compute cost.
The same fit favors early stopping. A large model reaches a target loss with fewer tokens and updates than a small model. The authors estimate that a compute-efficient run should stop about 10 percent above that model’s converged loss instead of training a smaller model to convergence.
A later allocation
The Meta Llama Team builds IsoFLOPs curves from models between 40 million and 16 billion parameters. It fits optimal training tokens as C^0.53 and projects a 402-billion-parameter model trained on 16.55 trillion tokens at 3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs. The team selects 405 billion parameters because its fitted loss curve has a broad minimum near that point.
The team makes a different choice for the 8B and 70B Llama-3 models. It trains them past their compute-optimal allocation to improve quality at a fixed inference budget. Compute-optimal training answers one operating question: how to minimize training loss for a training budget. Deployment cost can justify another point on the curve.
Limits
Kaplan and colleagues give their exponents as measurements from WebText2, one tokenizer, and one model family. They report weak fits in the smallest-data regime and no theory that derives the laws. Their compute estimate also omits context-dependent terms that matter for long sequences. The Llama team refits the relation on its own data.
Power-law loss forecasts do not prove gains on downstream tasks. The Llama team addresses that gap by linking task negative log-likelihood to training FLOPs, then linking likelihood to accuracy with scaling runs and older models. pretraining-evaluation covers that forecast and the benchmark checks around it.
