sections/machine-learning/concepts/self-.title: Self-Attention
sections/machine-learning/concepts/self-.content:
Self-Attention
Self-attention lets every position in a sequence look at every other position and use learned similarity to decide how much of each to absorb. It is the only operation in a Transformer that connects positions to one another.
flowchart LR
  E[Input embedding] --> P[Project to a query, a key and a value]
  P --> S[Score — this query against every key]
  S --> D[Divide by the square root of d_k, for gradient stability]
  D --> M[Softmax — positive weights summing to 1]
  M --> V[Multiply each value by its weight]
  V --> O[Sum — the output for this position]
  P --> H[Eight heads, eight representation subspaces]
  H --> C[Concatenate and project through W_O]
  O --> C

In short

Each position scores its query against every key, scales by √dk, softmaxes, and sums the weighted values.
Connecting every word to every other lets the model resolve pronouns that local attention cannot.
Multiple heads give separate representation subspaces, so one position can absorb several kinds of context at once.
Attention makes distance free and total length expensive: O(n²) in sequence length, with order restored by positional encoding.
Cross-attention takes queries from one source and keys and values from another, fusing different kinds of data.

The computation, in six steps
From The Illustrated Transformer1:

Project each input embedding into a query, a key, and a value (dimension 64 against an embedding dimension of 512, an architecture choice that keeps multi-head computation roughly constant).
Score each position against every position: dot product of this query with that key.
Divide by 8 (√dk) for gradient stability.
Softmax, so the scores are positive and sum to 1.
Multiply each value vector by its score, scaling down the irrelevant ones.
Sum the weighted value vectors to produce the output for this position.

In practice, one matrix expression performs all six steps and allows parallel computation.


                  
                  What are the three roles a query, a key and a value play? 
                  
                

The query is what this position is looking for, the key is what a position offers for matching, and the value is what actually gets carried across once the match is scored. Query·key decides how much of the value to absorb.




                  
                  Why divide the attention scores by √d k before the softmax?
                  
                

For gradient stability. Dot products grow with dimension, and large scores push the softmax into its flat region where gradients vanish.




                  
                  What does the softmax step do to the attention scores? 
                  
                

Makes them positive and sum to 1, so they act as weights over the value vectors — the irrelevant positions are scaled toward zero and drowned out of the sum.


What it is for
The canonical example is “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.” A reader resolves “it” at once, but an algorithm must bind “it” to “animal”. Self-attention performs that binding, which appears in a visualisation of the top encoder.
A harder variant comes from Primers • Transformers2: “The owl spied a squirrel. It tried to grab it with its talons but only got the end of its tail”. It makes the same point: a model attending only to nearby words cannot resolve which “it” is which, while a model connecting every word to every other can work out that the owl grabbed and the squirrel lost part of its tail.


                  
                  Why does pronoun resolution defeat a model that only attends locally? 
                  
                

The antecedent can be arbitrarily far away, and several candidates may sit nearby. Resolving which “it” is which requires connecting every word to every other, not just to its neighbours.


Multi-head: several opinions at once
Eight independently initialised sets of Q/K/V matrices produce eight outputs, concatenated and projected by a further matrix WO. The gain is representation subspaces: in the same example, one head attends to “the animal” while another attends to “tired,” so the encoding of “it” absorbs both. With a single head, the position’s own value tends to dominate.


                  
                  What failure mode does a single attention head have? 
                  
                

Its own position’s value tends to dominate the weighted sum, so little context actually gets absorbed. Several heads give several subspaces, letting one bind “it” to “the animal” while another binds it to “tired.”


What it costs
Attention compares every pair of positions, so it is O(n²) in sequence length where recurrence is O(n). Distance within the sequence becomes free because position 1 and position 500 are one hop apart, but total length becomes expensive. Long-context techniques try to reduce that n² cost.


                  
                  What does attention make free, and what does it make expensive? 
                  
                

Distance becomes free — position 1 and position 500 are one hop apart. Total length becomes expensive, because every pair of positions is compared: O(n²) where recurrence was O(n).


Removing recurrence also removes all notion of order, which is why positional-encoding has to be added back explicitly.
Cross-attention: the same idea across modalities
Cross-attention takes queries from one source and keys and values from another, fusing two different kinds of data. Its deeper significance lies in its indifference to what the sequence contains, more than in any language-specific ability, and that indifference allowed one architecture to serve text, images and audio2.


                  
                  What single change turns self-attention into cross-attention? 
                  
                

Taking the queries from one source and the keys and values from another. That one substitution lets the mechanism fuse two different kinds of data, which is what made one architecture serve text, images and audio.


Predicted before it arrived
The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks3 (May 2015) calls attention “the most interesting recent architectural innovation in neural networks,” discussing soft attention from Neural Turing Machines and the efficiency cost that motivates hard attention. Understanding LSTM Networks4 (August 2015) closes by naming attention as the next step after LSTMs. Both precede Attention is All You Need by two years.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/singl.title: Single- vs Multi-Agent Economics
sections/machine-learning/concepts/singl.content:
Single- vs Multi-Agent Economics
Architecture choice trades unified reasoning against structured coordination. Start from a single-agent baseline1: one trajectory retains the full context and token budget, avoids handoffs, and preserves global state. This suits sequential, tightly coupled work where omissions at a boundary can cascade.
flowchart TD
  T[Architecture choice] --> S[Start with one agent]
  S --> C[Preserve context coherence and token depth]
  T --> D[Task has intrinsic decomposition or independent checking]
  D --> M[Add specialist or verifier roles]
  M --> L[Pay communication and coordination costs]
  L --> E[Keep multi-agent only if measured gains exceed costs]

In short

One agent keeps full context, token budget and global state, and avoids handoffs.
Multiple agents earn their cost only through intrinsic decomposition, parallel work or independent verification.
Each added agent costs tokens, serialized information, conflicts, propagated errors and governance complexity.
Strengthen one agent first, then measure whether added roles improve the target task.

In detail


                  
                  Why is one agent the recommended baseline? 
                  
                

It preserves global context, avoids handoffs and keeps the token budget in one reasoning trajectory.




                  
                  When does a multi-agent design earn its coordination cost? 
                  
                

When intrinsic decomposition, parallel work or an independent verifier produces measured gains.


Multi-agent systems earn their cost when the task already contains semi-independent parts: parallel search, specialist roles, diverse hypotheses, or an explicit reviewer. They can also partition a long or noisy context into smaller views. Agent count adds value only when it supports task-aligned decomposition or verification.
Each additional agent adds these costs:

tokens and latency for duplicate context and communication;
information lost when state is serialized or summarized;
conflicts between concurrent actions;
error propagation through trusted handoffs;
orchestration, permission, and governance complexity.

Under a fixed compute budget, distributing tokens can leave each agent with less reasoning depth. Stronger base models can also absorb workflows that once required explicit teams. Multi-agent coordination is a deliberate escalation: strengthen planning, routing, tools, and reflection within one agent first, then measure whether added roles improve the target task.
Decision rule
Prefer one agent when coherence dominates. Escalate when decomposition is intrinsic, independent work can run in parallel, or a distinct verifier produces measurable reliability gains. Central coordination can reduce error amplification, but it becomes a bottleneck that teams must also evaluate.
Related

Works cited

sections/machine-learning/concepts/super.title: Superposition
sections/machine-learning/concepts/super.content:
Superposition
Superposition is a layer carrying far more features than it has neurons, each feature a specific combination of neurons along nearly perpendicular directions. It explains why a neuron almost never means one thing and may explain why scaling works as well as it does.
flowchart LR
  N[n dimensions hold exactly n perpendicular directions] --> R[Relax to nearly perpendicular, tolerating a little interference]
  R --> J[Johnson-Lindenstrauss — capacity grows exponentially with dimension]
  J --> T[The angular tolerance dominates the number]
  J --> M[A layer probes far more features than it has neurons]
  M --> S[A feature is a combination of neurons, not one neuron]
  S --> U[Weights look uninterpretable by property, not by accident]
  U --> SA[Sparse autoencoders as the tool for recovering features anyway]
  J --> SC[A candidate mechanism for scaling — offered as a might]

In short

Relaxing perpendicular to nearly perpendicular makes capacity grow exponentially with dimension, by a consequence of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma.
The angular tolerance dominates the count: at 85°, GPT-3’s 12,288 dimensions hold well over 40 billion directions.
A layer exploiting this probes more features than it has neurons, so a feature cannot be one neuron.
Exponential capacity may explain why scaling works so well, offered only as a candidate mechanism.

The counting argument
In n dimensions you can fit exactly n mutually perpendicular directions. That is the definition of dimension, and it looks like a hard ceiling on how many independent features a space can hold.
If you relax “perpendicular” to “nearly perpendicular,” say 85° to 95° with a little interference, the ceiling moves. A consequence of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma is that the number of nearly-perpendicular vectors you can cram in grows exponentially with dimension. In low dimensions this buys almost nothing, which is what makes the high-dimensional behaviour counterintuitive.
A space with ten times the dimensions can store far more than ten times the independent ideas.


                  
                  What does relaxing "perpendicular" to "nearly perpendicular" buy? 
                  
                

The capacity stops being n and starts growing exponentially with dimension. Tolerating a little interference between features is what lifts the hard ceiling the definition of dimension seemed to impose.




                  
                  Why is superposition counterintuitive to reason about? 
                  
                

Because in low dimensions the near-perpendicular relaxation buys almost nothing. The exponential behaviour only shows up at high dimension, so small-space intuition points the wrong way.


The numbers, after the correction
Sanderson strengthens the evidence in How might LLMs store facts — Deep Learning Chapter 71 by publishing his own error. The video’s demo pushed 10,000 vectors in 100 dimensions to pairwise angles of 89°–91°, but a bad cost function let a few pairs escape to dot products near ±1. A space of 100 dimensions is not enough for a range that tight. Corrected figures, credited to viewer Nick Yoder:






























ToleranceDimensionsCapacity89°–91°—uninteresting below ~250,000 dimensions85° (dot product 0.087)—scales very quickly85°12,288 (GPT-3 embedding)well over 40 billion, likely > 10¹⁷85°116,000 (plausible for later models)over a googol, likely > 10¹⁶⁰
The tolerance you accept dominates the answer. That is the substantive content of the correction, and it is why the original demo’s tightness mattered.


                  
                  Which parameter dominates how many features a space can hold? 
                  
                

The angular tolerance. At 89°–91° the capacity is uninteresting below ~250,000 dimensions; at 85° the same 12,288-dimensional space holds well over 40 billion directions.


What follows for interpretability
If a layer exploits this capacity, it probes far more features than it has neurons; GPT-3’s ~50,000-neuron MLP layer could be asking orders of magnitude more questions. But then a feature cannot appear as one neuron lighting up. It has to appear as a specific combination of neurons: a superposition.


                  
                  Why can't a feature be one neuron, if a layer exploits superposition? 
                  
                

There are more features than neurons. Once a layer probes orders of magnitude more directions than it has units, each feature must be carried by a specific combination of them.


Sanderson retracts his own worked example in How might LLMs store facts — Deep Learning Chapter 71. “Michael Jordan → basketball” as one neuron implementing an AND gate is a clean, correct account of the mechanics, and almost certainly not what any real neuron does. The structural account survives: rows of the up-projection are directions and columns of the down-projection are edits. The assumption that either corresponds to a single human-legible concept does not.


                  
                  Which part of the "one neuron stores one fact" account survives superposition, and which does not? 
                  
                

The mechanics survive — rows are directions that ask, columns are edits that answer. What does not survive is the assumption that either corresponds to a single human-legible concept.


Researchers can recover features with a sparse autoencoder, as in Anthropic’s Toy Models of Superposition and Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning.
The older version of the same disappointment
Seven years earlier, Analyzing our neural network2 reported the same problem at a scale of 13,002 parameters: the digit classifier’s first-layer weights, visualised, look almost random rather than like the edge detectors that motivated the architecture. The 2017 explanation was a happy local minimum; the 2024 explanation is that clean single-feature neurons may not be what a well-trained network wants in the first place.


                  
                  How did the explanation for uninterpretable weights change between 2017 and 2024? 
                  
                

From “the network settled into a happy local minimum” to “clean single-feature neurons may not be what a well-trained network wants at all.” The observation is the same; the second reading makes it a property rather than an accident.


And why it may explain scaling
Because capacity in nearly-perpendicular directions grows exponentially rather than linearly with dimension, a bigger model gets disproportionately more room for ideas. Sanderson offers this as a possible reason “why model performance seems to scale so well with size,” a mechanism-level candidate for the pattern scaling-beats-knowledge-engineering asserts empirically. He presents it only as a might.


                  
                  How would superposition explain why scaling works so well? 
                  
                

Because capacity grows exponentially with dimension rather than linearly, a bigger model gets disproportionately more room for ideas — not merely proportionally more. Sanderson offers this as a candidate mechanism, not a result.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/super.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/super.content:
Supervised Fine-Tuning
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) updates a pretrained model on prompt-response demonstrations. It teaches a base language model to answer instructions in a chosen format and supplies the checkpoint from which later preference-optimization often begins.
In short

The SFT policy generates candidates for preference labeling, initializes the trainable policy, and serves as the reference constraining preference updates.
SFT quality depends on the data mixture, and removing math or safety data cut those scores sharply in Tulu 3.
Later preference stages can revise SFT behavior, improving chat while reducing some safety and coding results.

In detail
Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model1 places SFT first in the standard RLHF pipeline. The SFT policy generates candidate responses for preference labeling, initializes the trainable policy, and serves as the reference that constrains preference updates. When researchers reuse preference data without its original SFT checkpoint, distribution shift between the data and reference model becomes a training concern.
Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training2 shows that SFT quality depends on the data mixture, not just the loss. The team built skill-specific mixtures for math, code, precise instruction following, chat, and safety, then combined and ablated them. Removing math data cut the 8B model’s MATH score from 31.5 to 23.5 and GSM8K from 76.2 to 64.1. Removing persona data hurt the skills those synthetic examples targeted. Removing safety examples left most capability scores close but cut the safety average from 93.1 to 74.7.
The Tulu 3 experiments also exposed implementation choices that change the effective training objective. Averaging per-example losses under gradient accumulation weighted batches differently according to sequence length. The team used a summed token loss to keep token weighting consistent across distributed and accumulated batches, then tuned the learning rate for that choice.
SFT sets a broad behavioral base, but later stages can revise it. Tulu 3’s preference stage improved its aggregate score and chat measures while reducing some SFT safety and coding results. The release preserves intermediate checkpoints and reports stage-by-stage deltas, which expose later optimization as a possible regression source.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/suppo.title: Support Vector Machines
sections/machine-learning/concepts/suppo.content:
Support Vector Machines
The support vector machine chooses the decision boundary that separates classes with the largest possible gap, and ranks among the best off-the-shelf supervised classifiers1. Its derivation is a chain of reformulations — margins → convex QP → Lagrange duality → kernels — each of which became a standard tool in its own right.
In short

The geometric margin is invariant to rescaling (w, b), so a scaling constraint turns margin maximization into a convex quadratic program.
The dual touches the data only through inner products, and only the support vectors carry nonzero αᵢ.
Soft margins let examples fall short of margin 1 at cost Cξᵢ, which changes the dual only to the box constraint 0 ≤ αᵢ ≤ C.
SMO solves the dual by updating pairs of αᵢ, because the equality constraint pins any single one to the rest.
Kernels replace the inner product with K(x, z), and Mercer’s theorem makes any positive semi-definite K valid.

Margins
The functional margin of an example, γ̂⁽ⁱ⁾ = y⁽ⁱ⁾(wᵀx⁽ⁱ⁾ + b), is large exactly when the classifier is confident and correct — but it scales trivially with (w, b), so on its own it measures nothing. The geometric margin divides by ‖w‖ to get actual Euclidean distance from the boundary, and is invariant to rescaling. That invariance is the hinge of the whole derivation: a scaling constraint can be imposed for free.
From optimization problem to dual
Maximizing the geometric margin becomes min ½‖w‖² subject to every example having functional margin ≥ 1 — a convex quadratic program. Introducing Lagrange multipliers αᵢ and switching to the dual (valid here because the problem is convex with strictly feasible constraints) yields:
max_α Σαᵢ − ½ ΣΣ y⁽ⁱ⁾y⁽ʲ⁾αᵢαⱼ⟨x⁽ⁱ⁾, x⁽ʲ⁾⟩ — a maximization whose objective and whose prediction rule (wᵀx + b = Σᵢ αᵢy⁽ⁱ⁾⟨x⁽ⁱ⁾, x⟩ + b) touch the data only through inner products.


                  
                  Why do most training examples end up irrelevant to the fitted SVM? 
                  
                

The KKT dual-complementarity condition forces αᵢ > 0 only where the margin constraint holds with equality — the points closest to the boundary. Those few are the support vectors; every other training point could be deleted without moving the classifier.


Soft margins and SMO
Real data is not separable, and forcing separability lets one outlier swing the boundary dramatically. ℓ₁ regularization relaxes it: examples may fall short of margin 1 by paying Cξᵢ. Strikingly, the only change to the dual is that the constraint becomes 0 ≤ αᵢ ≤ C — the box constraint. Solving the dual by naive coordinate ascent fails because the equality constraint pins any one αᵢ to the others; SMO updates pairs instead, where each pairwise step reduces to maximizing a quadratic in one variable clipped to a line-segment interval, with KKT violation as the convergence test.
Kernels complete the story
Because both objective and predictor are inner products, replacing ⟨x, z⟩ with K(x, z) runs the same algorithm implicitly in the feature space of φ — polynomial or Gaussian (infinite-dimensional). Mercer’s theorem says a function K is a valid kernel if and only if every kernel matrix it induces is symmetric positive semi-definite, which turns feature engineering into kernel selection.


                  
                  What interface change does Mercer's theorem enable? 
                  
                

You no longer need to write down (or even know) the feature map φ. Pick any similarity function K you like, verify positive semi-definiteness on finite sets, and the kernel trick guarantees some feature space exists where K is an inner product.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/tempo.title: Temporal-Difference Bootstrapping
sections/machine-learning/concepts/tempo.content:
Temporal-Difference Bootstrapping
Temporal-difference (TD) learning updates a value estimate before a trajectory ends. The one-step error is (\delta_t=r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)): observed reward plus the current successor estimate, minus the current-state estimate1.
flowchart LR
  S[Current state estimate] --> T[Add observed reward and discounted successor estimate]
  T --> E[Temporal-difference target]
  E --> D[Compute prediction error]
  D --> U[Update current value estimate]
  U --> S
  B[Bootstrapping learns before the trajectory ends] --> T

In short

TD trains the current value estimate on a learned successor estimate, which makes it bootstrapping.
It updates earlier and with lower variance than Monte Carlo, but inherits bias from an inaccurate successor estimate.
With function approximation and off-policy data that bias can destabilize learning, and sparse delayed rewards still propagate slowly.

In detail


                  
                  Why is temporal-difference learning called bootstrapping? 
                  
                

One learned successor-value estimate is used to train the current value estimate.




                  
                  What does TD gain and risk by updating before a trajectory ends? 
                  
                

It gains earlier, lower-variance updates but inherits bias from an inaccurate successor estimate.


One learned estimate trains another, which makes the update a form of bootstrapping. Dynamic programming also bootstraps but assumes known transition dynamics and takes expectations over successors. Monte Carlo methods avoid bootstrapping by waiting for a complete sampled return. TD occupies the middle: it learns from experience online while using its present model of the future.
The benefit is earlier, lower-variance updating and no requirement to wait for episode termination. The cost is bias from an inaccurate successor estimate; coupled with function approximation and off-policy data, that bias can destabilize learning. Multi-step methods and eligibility traces trade between short bootstrap targets and longer sampled returns.
TD also shows the problem of temporal credit assignment. A delayed outcome must influence earlier states through successive updates, which can be slow when rewards are sparse or horizons are long. Bootstrapping helps propagate information but does not solve the general problem.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/token.title: Tokenization
sections/machine-learning/concepts/token.content:
Tokenization
Tokenization converts text into vocabulary IDs before a model maps those IDs to an embedding. The choice fixes which strings share units, how many positions a passage consumes, and which languages the model can encode efficiently.
In short

GPT-2’s byte-level BPE starts from 256 byte symbols, so it covers every string without a 130,000-symbol Unicode base.
Merges across character categories were mostly blocked, so punctuation variants would not consume separate vocabulary slots.
T5’s fixed vocabulary mixture limits it to those languages, and FLAN’s English-oriented tokenizer partly explains why it translates into English better.

Byte-level BPE in GPT-2
Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners1 rejects both ends of a practical tradeoff. Word vocabularies need unknown-token handling and cannot assign a probability to every string. Raw bytes cover every UTF-8 string with 256 base symbols, but the authors found byte-level language models less competitive than word-level models at their scale.
Their byte-level byte-pair encoding starts with those 256 symbols and merges frequent sequences into subword tokens. A code-point implementation would need more than 130,000 Unicode symbols before adding any merged units; the byte base avoids that cost. The team also blocked most merges across character categories because a frequency-only process spent separate slots on punctuation variants such as a word followed by a period, question mark, or exclamation mark. GPT-2 used 50,257 tokens.
SentencePiece in T5 and FLAN
Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer2 uses SentencePiece with 32,000 wordpieces shared by encoder input and decoder output. The authors trained the vocabulary on ten parts English C4 to one part each German, French, and Romanian because downstream translation required all four languages. They note that this fixed mixture limits the model to languages its vocabulary can process.
Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners3 reports a 32,000-token SentencePiece BPE vocabulary for LaMDA-PT and FLAN. About 90% of its pretraining data was English, and FLAN translated into English better than out of it. The authors connect this asymmetry in part to the English-oriented tokenizer and corpus.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/tool-.title: Tool Interface Design
sections/machine-learning/concepts/tool-.content:
Tool Interface Design
A tool’s interface is part of the agent system: names and descriptions guide tool selection, schemas constrain arguments, middleware formats results, and validation and error handling determine whether a failed call can be repaired. An LLM-Agent needs more than an implemented function to use it well1.
flowchart TD
  T[Usable tool contract] --> S[Selection]
  T --> I[Invocation]
  T --> O[Outcome]
  T --> F[Recoverable failure]
  T --> B[Security boundary]

In short

A usable contract makes selection, invocation, outcome and recoverable failure legible.
Permissions, sandboxing and confirmation bound what a correct-looking call may do.
Schemas constrain syntax, not intent, and more tools can reduce reliability.

In detail


                  
                  What four things must a usable tool contract make legible? 
                  
                

Selection, invocation, outcome and recoverable failure.




                  
                  Why is a schema insufficient to make a tool call correct? 
                  
                

It constrains argument syntax, not whether the action is intended, authorized or appropriate.


A useful contract makes four things legible:

Selection: what the tool does, when it applies, and how it differs from neighbouring tools.
Invocation: required arguments, allowed values, types, and examples.
Outcome: structured results that preserve the information needed for the next decision.
Failure: specific, recoverable errors rather than an opaque exception or misleading success.

Security belongs to the same contract. Authentication, least-privilege permissions, sandboxing, confirmation for consequential actions, and limits on returned data bound what a correct-looking call may do. These controls make tool design part of harness-engineering rather than ordinary API plumbing outside the model.
Boundary
More tools can reduce reliability by making selection harder and expanding the action surface. Schemas constrain syntax, not intent; a valid call can still be the wrong action. Evaluate tool selection, argument construction, authorization, execution, result interpretation, and recovery separately.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/tool-.title: Tool-Use Tuning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/tool-.content:
Tool-Use Tuning
Tool-use tuning trains a language model to emit calls to external systems at useful points in its generation. The learned behavior covers tool selection, call timing, argument construction, and use of the returned text. A runtime outside the model still executes the call.
In short

Toolformer keeps a candidate API call only when its result lowers loss on the text that follows.
The first version allows one call per input and cannot chain tools, refine a failed search, or weigh API cost.
General instruction, preference and safety tuning do not supply tool competence without tool-specific data and evaluations.

Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools1 supplies a self-supervised recipe. Researchers show the model a few calls for each API, ask it to insert candidate calls into a language-modeling corpus, execute those calls, and retain a candidate only when its returned result lowers loss on the text that follows. Fine-tuning on the augmented corpus teaches the model from examples selected by its own prediction error.
This filter turns next-token loss into a usefulness test. A calculator call earns a place when the result helps predict a later number; a search call survives when retrieved text helps complete a factual statement. Tool-specific heuristics and thresholds remain necessary because useful examples can be rare. The Toolformer pipeline processed more than a million documents to obtain only a few thousand retained calculator calls.
At inference, Toolformer pauses generation when the model requests an API result, runs the API, inserts its response, and resumes decoding. The surrounding LLM-Agent or harness executes the call; the trained model produces its textual form.
The method’s first version allows one call per input and generates each tool’s training calls in isolation. It cannot chain tools, refine a failed search, browse several results, or include API cost in the decision. It also becomes less selective when decoding settings force more calls. These limits distinguish tool-use tuning from planning and error recovery.
Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training2 identifies tool use and agent integration as future work after building an extensive general post-training recipe. That omission marks a practical boundary: broad instruction, preference, and safety-tuning do not supply tool competence without data and evaluations designed for tool interactions.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/train.title: Training Data Engineering
sections/machine-learning/concepts/train.content:
Training Data Engineering
Training data engineering turns raw corpora into the token mixtures used for pre-training and post-training. Alongside scale, it is a main source of model quality in The Llama 3 Herd of Models1, whose Transformer architecture stays close to Llama 2.
In short

Deduplication runs at URL, document, and line level, and line filtering removes some good text in a trade evaluations favor.
Small-model scaling experiments choose a mix of about 50 percent general knowledge, 25 percent math and reasoning, 17 percent code, and 8 percent multilingual.
Generated code and math receive external checks such as unit tests, because prose-quality scores cannot establish correctness.
Contamination detection has false positives and negatives, so it cannot certify a clean measurement.

Web data pipeline
The team starts with web and non-web sources containing material through the end of 2023. It removes domains associated with high volumes of personal information, adult material, or unsafe content. A custom parser extracts text from HTML, preserves mathematical and code structure, and removes Markdown markers after experiments found them harmful for a model trained on web text.
Deduplication works at three levels. URL matching keeps the newest page version, global MinHash removes near-duplicate documents, and line-level matching removes lines that recur more than six times within a 30-million-document bucket. The team notes that line filtering also removes some good text, but its evaluations favor the trade.
Heuristics catch repeated n-grams, outlier token distributions, and other patterns missed by deduplication. Model-based classifiers rank document quality. Separate pipelines extract code and mathematical reasoning material because those domains have token distributions and document structures that differ from prose. A language identifier and language-specific filters process 176 languages before the team ranks multilingual documents.
Choosing the mix
A knowledge classifier groups web documents so the team can reduce overrepresented categories. Small-model scaling-laws experiments compare candidate mixtures before the team spends a flagship budget. The resulting pre-training mix contains about 50 percent general-knowledge tokens, 25 percent mathematics and reasoning, 17 percent code, and 8 percent multilingual data.
The team changes the mix during training by adding recent web data, increasing non-English and mathematical material, and reducing sources that later quality checks flag. During the final annealing stage, it raises the share of selected code and math data while lowering the learning rate. Forty-billion-token tests on an 8B checkpoint provide a cheaper screen for small candidate datasets than a fresh scaling study.
Post-training data needs different controls
Human preferences, rejection-sampled responses, and synthetic examples feed supervised fine-tuning and preference optimisation. The team scores topic, quality, and difficulty, then removes semantic duplicates within clusters. Reward-model scores and Llama-based judges disagree often enough that the team keeps examples accepted by either signal.
Generated code receives stronger checks. Parsers, linters, compilation, and unit tests supply execution feedback; the model revises failed attempts, and the pipeline retains dialogs that pass. Mathematical traces receive answer checks, model verification, or reward-model filtering. These controls use an external result where prose-quality scores cannot establish correctness.
Evaluation boundaries
The team excludes common benchmark training sets from annealing and assigns a separate organization to procure pre-training data so model developers cannot tune against the evaluation set. Its contamination study still finds high overlap estimates on some benchmarks. pretraining-evaluation treats contamination detection as evidence with false positives and negatives; it cannot certify a clean measurement.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/trans.title: Transfer Learning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/trans.content:
Transfer Learning
Transfer learning reuses a network trained on one task as the starting point for another. Almost nobody trains a convolutional network from scratch, because datasets of sufficient size are rare. A model pretrained on something large (ImageNet: 1.2M images) is used instead, as an initialisation or a fixed feature extractor1.
In short

Fixed feature extraction freezes the pretrained network and trains only a linear classifier on its CNN codes.
Fine-tuning works because early layers hold generic features while later layers grow specific to the original classes.
New-dataset size and similarity to the pretraining distribution select among four strategies.
Even with a large, very different dataset, initialising from pretrained weights still beats random initialisation.

The three strategies
Fixed feature extraction. Remove the pretrained classifier head and run the rest of the network frozen: every image becomes an activation vector (“CNN codes”), and only a linear classifier trains on top. Cheap and effective when data is scarce.
Fine-tuning. Continue backpropagation into some or all of the pretrained layers. The justification is representational: early layers hold generic features (edge detectors, colour blobs), while later layers grow specific to the original classes — a significant share of an ImageNet network’s capacity may exist to distinguish dog breeds. Fine-tune what you keep; freeze what would overfit.
Pretrained models as infrastructure. Since training takes weeks on multi-GPU clusters, released checkpoints (model zoos) are the normal starting point — transfer learning as default practice rather than technique.


                  
                  Why does fine-tuning usually use two different learning rates? 
                  
                

The pretrained weights are already good and should move slowly; the freshly initialised classifier head must train fast just to catch up. One rate for both either distorts the representation early or starves the new head.


The decision procedure
Two axes — new-dataset size and similarity to the pretraining distribution — select among four cases:




















Similar to originalVery differentSmall datasetLinear classifier on CNN codesLinear classifier on earlier-layer activationsLarge datasetFine-tune through the full networkFine-tune throughout — even here, pretrained beats random
The lower-right cell is the interesting one: with enough data you could start from scratch, but in practice initialising from pretrained weights still wins.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/unsup.title: Unsupervised Learning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/unsup.content:
Unsupervised Learning
Unsupervised learning finds structure in data with no labels at all. Its three classical instruments in CS229 Lecture Notes1, clustering, latent-variable density estimation, and projection, are one subject: each is an optimization algorithm in disguise, and the same failure (local optima) and remedy (restarts) recur across all three.
In short

k-means is coordinate descent on a non-convex distortion, so it decreases monotonically but can stall in local optima.
EM handles a latent component choice by alternating soft posterior guesses with weighted maximum likelihood.
EM’s likelihood never decreases because each iteration is coordinate ascent on the ELBO, a bound that generalizes to any latent-variable model.
PCA’s optimal k-dimensional subspace is the top k eigenvectors of the empirical covariance matrix.

Clustering: k-means
Given points and a chosen k, k-means alternates two steps until convergence: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its assigned points. The assignment step is exactly coordinate descent on the distortion function J(c, μ) = Σᵢ‖x⁽ⁱ⁾ − μ_{c⁽ⁱ⁾}‖² — first minimizing over cluster assignments c with centroids fixed, then over centroids μ with assignments fixed. That reading explains both its guarantee (J decreases monotonically) and its weakness: J is non-convex, so k-means can stall in local optima. The standard mitigation is multiple random restarts, keeping the run with lowest distortion.
Density estimation: EM
The mixture of Gaussians model posits a hidden choice z of component, then x drawn from that component’s Gaussian. If z were observed, maximum likelihood would be trivially GDA-like; the entire difficulty is that z is latent. The EM algorithm iterates:

E-step — compute wⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾ = p(z⁽ⁱ⁾ = j | x⁽ⁱ⁾), the posterior “soft” guess of each point’s component;
M-step — re-fit φ, μ, Σ by weighted maximum likelihood, the weights being those soft guesses.



                  
                  Why does EM's likelihood never decrease between iterations? 
                  
                

The E-step chooses Q(z) = p(z|x; θ) so the evidence lower bound touches log p(x; θ) exactly at the current θ; the M-step then raises the bound, carrying the true likelihood up with it. Each iteration is coordinate ascent on the ELBO, alternating maximization over Q and over θ.


That argument generalizes far beyond Gaussians: for any latent-variable model, Jensen’s inequality supplies the ELBO lower bound, the posterior makes it tight, and maximizing it in θ gives monotone improvement — the same bound that later reappears throughout variational inference.
Projection: PCA
Principal components analysis asks for the k-dimensional subspace retaining the most variance. Maximizing the projected variance (1/n)Σ(xᵀu)² over unit u reduces to finding the top eigenvector of the empirical covariance matrix Σ; the top k eigenvectors give the optimal basis, where “optimal” holds under both readings — maximum retained variability among orthonormal bases, and minimum reconstruction error. Applications listed run from compression and visualization to preprocessing for supervised learning (fewer dimensions means smaller hypothesis classes) and noise reduction — the eigenfaces method being the classic example.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/value.title: Value, Return, and Advantage
sections/machine-learning/concepts/value.content:
Value, Return, and Advantage
Return is an observed outcome, while value and advantage are expectations built around it1.
flowchart TD
  T[One sampled trajectory] --> G[Realized discounted return]
  G --> V[State value averages return from a state]
  G --> Q[Action value averages return after an action]
  Q --> A[Advantage compares action value with state value]
  V --> A
  V --> B[Bellman relation links present and successor value]

In short

Return is realized on one trajectory; value is the expected return under a particular policy.
Advantage subtracts the state value as a baseline, which can reduce policy-gradient variance.
These are definitions that algorithms only estimate, and an accurate value can still be misaligned with the intended task.

In detail


                  
                  How does return differ from value in reinforcement learning?
                  
                

Return is realized on one trajectory; value is an expectation over possible returns under a policy.




                  
                  What does advantage measure? 
                  
                

How much better or worse an action is than the policy’s average action in that state.



Return (G_t) is the discounted reward realized from time (t) onward along one sampled trajectory.
State value (V^\pi(s)) is the expected return from state (s) when policy (\pi) is followed.
Action value (Q^\pi(s,a)) is the expected return after taking action (a) in (s), then following (\pi).
Advantage (A^\pi(s,a)=Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s)) measures how much better or worse that action is than the policy’s average action in the state.

Return varies between trajectories even from the same state. Value averages over that stochasticity and is tied to a particular policy. Advantage subtracts a baseline, letting policy-gradient updates emphasize relative performance rather than the absolute scale of outcomes; this can reduce gradient variance.
The Bellman relation makes value recursive: present value equals expected immediate reward plus discounted successor value. temporal-difference-bootstrap turns that relation into an incremental learning target.
Boundary
These quantities are definitions; practical algorithms estimate them. Function approximation, limited coverage, changing policies, and long horizons introduce error. An accurate value for the specified reward can also be misaligned with the intended task when reward-proxy-failure is present.
Related

sections/machine-learning/concepts/varia.title: Variational Autoencoders
sections/machine-learning/concepts/varia.content:
Variational Autoencoders
A variational auto-encoder is what EM becomes when the latent-variable model is parameterized by neural networks. It carries the evidence lower bound from mixture models into deep learning1.
In short

The VAE posterior is intractable, so the ELBO, valid for any Q, is optimized over a Gaussian family set by encoder networks.
The approximation can sit far from the true posterior, but some approximation is necessary for feasibility.
The reparameterization trick moves sampling into parameter-free noise ξ, so gradients for the encoder pass through cleanly.
Few high-dimensional distributions allow analytic densities and reparameterization at once, with Gaussians the canonical exception.

From EM’s problem to VAE’s structure
The model: a standard-normal latent z ∈ Rᵏ, decoded by a network g(z; θ) into the mean of x|z ∼ N(g(z; θ), σ²I). For Gaussian mixtures, the E-step posterior p(z|x; θ) was analytically computable; here it is intractable. The ELBO remains a valid lower bound for any choice of Q, so instead of computing the exact posterior we optimize it over a chosen family:
max over Q ∈ 𝒬, θ of ELBO(Q, θ)
The family choice defines the architecture. Each Qᵢ is Gaussian whose mean and variance are functions of the data — Qᵢ = N(q(x⁽ⁱ⁾; φ), diag(v(x⁽ⁱ⁾; ψ))²) with q and v neural networks called the encoder, and g(z; θ) the decoder. This has a cost: such Qᵢ can be far from the true posterior, but some approximation is necessary for feasibility.


                  
                  How does VAE training differ from EM's alternating maximization? 
                  
                

EM alternates an exact E-step (posterior maximization of Q) with an M-step. Here nothing has a closed form, so plain gradient ascent updates φ, ψ and θ simultaneously on the ELBO. The M-step’s inner maximization is traded for one more set of gradients.


The reparameterization trick
One gradient is easy: ∇θ moves inside the expectation because p(x,z; θ) depends on θ but the sampling distribution doesn’t. The gradients for φ and ψ are hard for the mirror-image reason — the sampling distribution depends on those parameters, and ∇E{z∼Q_φ}[f(φ)] ≠ E[∇f] when z’s distribution shifts.
The trick rewrites sampling as a deterministic transform of parameter-free noise:
z = q(x; φ) + v(x; ψ) ⊙ ξ,  ξ ∼ N(0, I)
The randomness now enters through ξ, which carries no parameters, so the gradient passes cleanly through q and v and is estimated by sampling ξ. The method has a boundary: few high-dimensional distributions admit analytic densities and reparameterization at once — Gaussians being the canonical exception Kingma & Welling catalogue alternatives for.

sections/machine-learning/entities/diffu.title: Diffusion Models
sections/machine-learning/entities/diffu.content:
Diffusion Models
Diffusion models form a family of generative models that destroys data with noise in a fixed forward process and learns only the reverse. Researchers drew inspiration from non-equilibrium thermodynamics and formalised the approach across Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015), noise-conditioned score networks (Song & Ermon, 2019), and DDPM (Ho et al., 2020).
flowchart LR
  X[Data] --> F[Forward — small Gaussian noise over T steps, on a fixed schedule]
  F --> G[Isotropic Gaussian noise]
  X -->|closed form, straight to any timestep| J[Jump to a random step and denoise there]
  J --> R[Reverse — the only learned part, predicting the noise]
  R --> S[Sampling, over many reverse steps]
  S --> C[The price paid — slow sampling]
  C --> A[Fewer steps, distillation, consistency models, latent diffusion]
  CF[Classifier-free guidance — interpolate conditional and unconditional] --> R

In short

Diffusion pays for tractability in slow sampling, a price that distillation and latent spaces can attack.
A closed-form jump to any timestep lets training denoise there without simulating the chain.
Conditioning on x0 makes the reverse posterior Gaussian, so the variational bound becomes computable.
Classifier-free guidance steers sampling without a separate classifier, trading prompt adherence against diversity.

The bargain each generative family strikes
Each generative family pays a different price for tractability1:

























FamilyPrice of tractabilityGANUnstable adversarial training, reduced sample diversityVAEOptimises a surrogate loss rather than the desired objectiveFlowArchitecture constrained to be invertibleDiffusionSlow sampling: many reverse steps per sample
Diffusion pays in inference time rather than in training stability or architectural freedom. That turned out to be the affordable price, since inference cost can be attacked by distillation and by moving to a latent space, while adversarial instability cannot be engineered away as cleanly.


                  
                  What price does diffusion pay for tractability, and why was it the affordable one? 
                  
                

Slow sampling — many reverse steps per sample. It was affordable because inference cost yields to distillation and latent-space training, whereas a GAN’s adversarial instability cannot be engineered away as cleanly.


Forward: fixed and closed-form
A Markov chain adds small Gaussian noise over T steps under a variance schedule βt. As T → ∞ the result is isotropic Gaussian noise.
The reparameterisation trick makes training feasible by sampling xt directly from x0 in closed form. Training jumps to a random timestep and learns to denoise there instead of simulating the chain step by step.


                  
                  What makes diffusion training feasible despite the chain having many steps? 
                  
                

xt can be sampled directly from x0 in closed form. Training jumps to a random timestep and denoises there, so it never has to simulate the chain step by step.


Reverse: the only learned part
The true reverse conditional needs the whole dataset and is intractable. Additional conditioning on x0 makes the reverse posterior Gaussian and tractable, which makes the objective computable.


                  
                  The true reverse conditional is intractable. What makes the training objective computable anyway? 
                  
                

Conditioning additionally on x0. The reverse posterior is then Gaussian, so the variational bound reduces to KL divergences between Gaussians, which have closed forms.


The variational lower bound then decomposes into a constant term (no learnable parameters, ignorable), a sum of KL divergences between Gaussians (closed form), and a final discrete decoder term. diffusion-noise-prediction carries the practical DDPM simplification: sample one timestep and predict its added noise ε rather than parameterising the reverse mean directly.
Unlike a VAE, the latent has the same dimensionality as the data and the inference procedure is fixed rather than learned. The model’s entire job is denoising.


                  
                  How does a diffusion latent differ from a VAE latent? 
                  
                

It has the same dimensionality as the data, and the procedure that produces it is fixed rather than learned. Nothing about the encoder is trained — the model’s entire job is denoising.


Conditioning is what made it useful

Classifier guidance: steer the reverse process with the gradient of a separately trained classifier.
Classifier-free guidance: train conditional and unconditional predictions jointly and combine them at sampling time. diffusion-guidance makes the resulting trade explicit: stronger conditioning can improve prompt adherence while reducing diversity or introducing artifacts.



                  
                  What does classifier-free guidance remove from the classifier-guidance recipe? 
                  
                

The separately trained classifier. Conditional and unconditional models are trained jointly and interpolated at sampling time, so steering needs no second network — which is what text-to-image systems actually run on.


Speed, attacked four ways
Four approaches reduce sampling cost: fewer sampling steps, progressive distillation, consistency models, and latent diffusion, which runs the whole process in a compressed latent space instead of pixel space.
A note on the date
Lilian Weng published the page in July 2021 and revised it repeatedly: classifier-free guidance, GLIDE, unCLIP and Imagen in 2022; latent diffusion in 2022; and distillation, consistency models and a model-architecture section in 2024. The publication date understates what the page now contains.

sections/machine-learning/entities/gpt-2.title: GPT-2
sections/machine-learning/entities/gpt-2.content:
GPT-2
GPT-2 is a 1.542-billion-parameter, decoder-only Transformer trained for next-token-prediction rather than for any one downstream benchmark. It is the largest model in the four-model WebText family evaluated by Radford and colleagues.
In short

Without finetuning it set new results on seven of eight language-modeling datasets and reached 55 F1 on CoQA.
Task performance varied sharply, from near-baseline summaries to 4.1% exact answers on Natural Questions.
It shows capacity and diverse causal pretraining producing emerging task behavior, without being a reliable general-purpose system.

Architecture and input
The family scales from 117 million parameters and 12 layers through 345 million and 24 layers, 762 million and 36 layers, to GPT-2 at 48 layers1. GPT-2 has a 1,600-dimensional model state and a 1,024-token context window.
The architecture follows the original GPT with several changes. GPT-2 moves layer normalization to the input of each residual sub-block, adds a final normalization after the last self-attention block, and scales residual-layer initialization by the inverse square root of the number of residual layers. It uses a batch size of 512 and a 50,257-entry byte-level BPE vocabulary.
Training corpus
GPT-2 trained on WebText, a 40 GB corpus containing more than eight million documents. Its pages came from Reddit outbound links that had at least three karma, using reader votes as a quality heuristic, and the collection was then deduplicated and cleaned. Wikipedia was excluded because many evaluation datasets draw from it. All four models still underfit WebText at the end of training.
Zero-shot evaluation
GPT-2 received no finetuning for the paper’s reported zero-shot tasks. It set new results on seven of eight language-modeling datasets and reached 55 F1 on CoQA without the benchmark’s 127,000-plus training examples. It also reached 70.70% accuracy on the Winograd Schema Challenge.
Task performance varied sharply. A TL;DR: cue induced summaries, but their aggregate ROUGE score only slightly exceeded three random article sentences. French-to-English translation reached 11.5 BLEU while English-to-French reached 5 BLEU. On Natural Questions, GPT-2 answered 4.1% exactly, although accuracy reached 63.1% for the 1% of questions to which it assigned the highest confidence.
Limits
The paper documents factual errors, retrieval-like shortcuts, and memorization of frequently repeated passages. Train-test overlap supplied a small, consistent boost but did not explain most reported gains. The authors present GPT-2 as evidence that capacity and diverse causal pretraining can produce emerging task behavior, not as a reliable general-purpose system.

sections/machine-learning/entities/llm-a.title: LLM Agent
sections/machine-learning/entities/llm-a.content:
LLM Agent
A system in which a language model controls the process: it decides what to do next, calls tools, and carries state across steps.
flowchart TD
  S[Agentic system] --> W[Workflow — a human wrote the code paths]
  S --> A[Agent — the model directs its own process]
  A --> P[LLM as policy]
  A --> C[Context as observation space]
  A --> T[Tools as action space]
  P --> PL[Planning — decomposition, reflection, refinement]
  C --> M1[Short-term — in-context, bounded by the window]
  C --> M2[Long-term — an external vector store, retrieval renamed]
  T --> TU[Tool use — the hard part is knowing when and how]
  PL --> R[ReAct — thought, action, observation interleaved]
  R --> RF[Reflexion — detect an inefficient trajectory and reset]

In short

A workflow follows code paths a human wrote; an agent directs its own process, and the two fail differently.
Agent = LLM + Context + Tools maps onto policy, observation space and action space.
Weng’s components are planning, memory and tool use; knowing when and how to call a tool is the hard part.
Reflection-style loops make trial and error possible, while long-horizon planning stays brittle.
Multi-agent failures are design flaws: simple fixes gained ChatDev only 15.6%.

Two definitions, and the argument between them
Following Anthropic’s framing, there are two kinds of agentic system1:

Workflow — LLMs and tools orchestrated through code paths a human wrote.
Agent — the LLM directs its own process, deciding how to use tools and sequence work.

They fail in different ways and require different evaluations. Much disagreement about “agent reliability” comes from people describing different architectures.
agent-control-boundary makes this a continuum rather than a label: a system can leave retrieval or tool choice to the model while keeping permissions, termination, and other transitions deterministic.


                  
                  What separates a workflow from an agent? 
                  
                

Who chose the control flow. In a workflow a human wrote the code paths the model and tools move through; in an agent the model directs its own process and sequences the work.


One formula, two decompositions
AI Agents in Depth: Design Principles and Engineering Practice2 compresses the whole object to Agent = LLM + Context + Tools and maps its parts as LLM ↔ policy, Context ↔ observation space, Tools ↔ action space. In this formulation, an agent is a reinforcement learning agent whose policy happens to be a language model.


                  
                  What is the reinforcement-learning reading of Agent = LLM + Context + Tools?
                  
                

LLM ↔ policy, Context ↔ observation space, Tools ↔ action space. It makes an LLM agent an RL agent whose policy happens to be a language model, rather than a slogan.


That formula and Weng’s three components below describe the same decomposition at different levels. Li’s Context absorbs Weng’s memory, while planning becomes part of the policy rather than a separate component. The production form adds three safeguards: Agent = Model + Harness, covered under harness-engineering.
Three components
LLM Powered Autonomous Agents3 supplies the decomposition the field settled on:
Planning covers subgoal decomposition, reflection, and refinement. Chain of Thought spends test-time compute breaking a task into steps. Tree of Thoughts generates several thoughts per step and searches the resulting tree (BFS or DFS, states scored by a classifier or majority vote). LLM+P outsources planning entirely to a classical PDDL planner, translating in and out of natural language.
Memory has two forms: short-term memory is in-context learning, bounded by the context window; long-term memory is an external vector store queried at retrieval time, which is Retrieval-Augmented-Generation under another name. Weng maps these onto human memory (sensory / short-term / long-term) and calls the mapping a rough analogy.
Tool use calls external APIs for what is not in the weights. MRKL routes queries to expert modules, neural or symbolic. TALM and Toolformer finetune the model to call APIs. HuggingGPT uses the LLM as a task planner selecting HuggingFace models across four stages. tool-interface-design separates access from reliability: schemas, validation, bounded permissions, useful errors, and result formatting determine whether the agent can understand and recover from a failed call.


                  
                  What distinguishes an agent's short-term memory from its long-term memory? 
                  
                

Short-term is in-context learning, bounded by the context window. Long-term is an external vector store queried at retrieval time — which is retrieval-augmented generation under another name.


MRKL found that knowing when and how to use a tool is harder than operating the tool. Their 7B model could not extract arguments for basic arithmetic from a verbal problem with consistency, though it had access to a calculator that worked without error.


                  
                  What did MRKL's arithmetic failure show about tool use? 
                  
                

That the hard part is knowing when and how to call a tool, not the tool itself. Their 7B model could not reliably extract the arguments from a verbal problem even though the calculator it needed was available and perfectly reliable.


Self-reflection is what makes trial and error possible
ReAct interleaves Thought / Action / Observation and beats an act-only baseline on both knowledge-intensive and decision-making tasks, showing the value of the reasoning trace. Reflexion adds a heuristic that detects inefficient trajectories and hallucination, using a run of identical actions that produce identical observations as its operational definition, and can reset the environment to start a fresh attempt. reflection-evaluator-loop generalises the pattern to generate, critique, externally test, and revise; an executable check or separate evaluator can catch what self-critique misses.


                  
                  How does Reflexion detect hallucination operationally? 
                  
                

As a run of identical actions producing identical observations. The agent is repeating itself and learning nothing, which is a signal available without knowing what the right answer was. Chain of Hindsight conditions on a sequence of past outputs annotated with feedback and ranked by reward.


Four design patterns
The workflow patterns are Reflection (the agent evaluates and revises its own output; the simplest pattern and consistently effective), Tool Use, Planning, and Multi-agent Collaboration (distinct roles contributing specialised work)1. single-vs-multi-agent-economics supplies a selection rule: add agent boundaries only when parallelism, specialization, or independent verification repays their latency, serialization, information loss, and governance cost.
The protocol layer
An agent has two connection boundaries (agent-protocol-layer): MCP standardises how a model application reaches tools and data, while A2A describes discovery, tasks, messages, and artifacts between agents. Neither protocol supplies correctness, permissions, or competent tool choice by itself.
Three limits Weng names

Finite context length: vector stores extend reach, but their representational power is weaker than full attention.
Brittle long-horizon planning: LLMs struggle to revise a plan after an unexpected error, where humans learn from trial and error.
Natural language is an unreliable interface: the model may produce malformed output or decline to follow an instruction, which is why so much agent code is output parsing.



                  
                  Why doesn't a vector store simply solve the finite-context limit? 
                  
                

Its representational power is weaker than full attention. Retrieval extends reach but does not give the model the same access to the retrieved material that having it in context would.




                  
                  What does long-horizon planning break on? 
                  
                

Revising a plan after an unexpected error. Trial and error is where humans learn most, and it is the case LLM planners handle worst.


Multi-agent failure is structural
The 2025 MAST study2 examined ~150 execution traces across MetaGPT, ChatDev, AG2 and Magentic-One, human-annotated at κ = 0.88. It found 14 failure modes in three groups: system design flaws, inter-agent alignment failures, and missing task verification. Simple fixes gained ChatDev only 15.6%, leading the authors to classify the failures as design flaws rather than bugs.
This evidence qualifies the multi-agent collaboration pattern in Primers • Agents1: current implementations fail for reasons that patches do not resolve.


                  
                  What made MAST conclude multi-agent failures are design flaws rather than bugs? 
                  
                

Simple fixes bought ChatDev only 15.6%. The 14 failure modes cluster into system design, inter-agent alignment and missing verification — categories patching does not reach.

sections/machine-learning/entities/lstm.title: LSTM
sections/machine-learning/entities/lstm.content:
LSTM
Long Short-Term Memory is a recurrent architecture whose repeating module uses a cell state and learned gates. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber introduced it (1997). Designed to reduce the long-term-dependency difficulty of plain recurrent networks, it became a widely used sequence model before attention-based architectures.
flowchart LR
  C1[Cell state arriving from the previous step] --> FG[Forget gate — what to drop]
  FG --> AD[Input gate, with a tanh proposing candidates — what to add]
  AD --> C2[Cell state — a belt of minor linear interactions only]
  C2 --> OG[Output gate — how much of the state to expose]
  OG --> H[Hidden output for this step]
  C2 --> C3[Carried forward, persisting unless actively forgotten]
  S[Step t must finish before step t+1] --> P[Training time scales with sequence length]
  P --> T[Displaced by the Transformer — on parallelism, not accuracy]

In short

The cell state is a conveyor belt of minor linear interactions, so information persists along it unless a gate changes it.
Forget, input, and output gates are sigmoid-scaled multiplies that decide what to drop, what to add, and what to expose.
Large comparisons found the popular variants about the same, pointing to cell state plus gating as the source of performance.
Trained on raw characters, LSTMs produced plausible text and code, with roughly 5% of cells learning legible features.
Sequential steps limit parallelism, a central reason the Transformer displaced it in many large models, though LSTMs remain useful.

The cell state is the idea
The cell state is a conveyor belt running the length of the chain, subject only to minor linear interactions1. Information flows along it unchanged unless a gate changes it. Everything else in the LSTM is machinery for deciding what changes.
This inverts the vanilla RNN’s practical tendency: the cell state supplies a path along which information can persist unless a gate changes it. Gate values, training, finite precision, and recurrent depth still prevent a guarantee of perfect memory, but this path makes long retention easier to learn.


                  
                  What default does the cell state invert, relative to a vanilla RNN? 
                  
                

In a plain RNN information decays unless actively preserved; along the cell state it persists unless actively forgotten. Remembering becomes the default rather than the thing the network has to learn.




                  
                  Why does the cell state only take linear interactions?
                  
                

Because repeated non-linear transformation is what destroys information across many steps. Keeping the belt to minor linear operations is what lets a signal travel the length of the chain intact.


Three gates
A gate is a sigmoid layer followed by a pointwise multiply. The sigmoid emits a value in [0, 1] per component: 0 lets nothing through, while 1 lets everything through.

Forget gate — what to drop from the cell state.
Input gate (with a tanh layer proposing candidate values) — what to add.
Output gate — what portion of the cell state to expose as this step’s output.

One running example carries all three: a language model holding the grammatical gender of the current subject so it can pick the right pronoun, dropping it when a new subject appears, and outputting singular/plural in case a verb comes next.


                  
                  Why is a gate a sigmoid followed by a pointwise multiply? 
                  
                

The sigmoid emits a value in [0, 1] per component, and multiplying by it scales that component between “let nothing through” and “let everything through” — so the gate is a learned, per-component, continuous filter rather than a switch.




                  
                  What distinguishes the output gate's job from the forget and input gates'? 
                  
                

Forget and input edit the cell state itself; the output gate decides only how much of that state is exposed as this step’s output. The network can hold something it is not currently using.


The one-line version
VIP Cheatsheet: Deep Learning2 compresses all of the above into one sentence, that an LSTM is an RNN that avoids the vanishing gradient problem by adding “forget” gates, plus a table naming each gate by the question it answers: input (“write to cell or not?”), forget (“erase a cell or not?”), output (“reveal a cell or not?”), and the gate proper (“how much writing?”). Beside Olah’s essay, it shows how pacing can serve different purposes while teaching the same content.
The variants are a footnote
Peephole connections let the gates see the cell state. Coupled forget/input gates decide together. The GRU merges forget and input into one update gate and merges cell state with hidden state, making the result simpler. Greff et al. (2015) compared the popular variants and found them about the same; Jozefowicz et al. (2015) searched over ten thousand architectures. These comparisons point to the cell-state-plus-gating idea, rather than any particular arrangement, as the source of their performance.


                  
                  What do the LSTM variant comparisons establish? 
                  
                

That no particular gate arrangement matters much — the popular variants perform about the same across large comparisons and searches. The work is being done by the cell-state-plus-gating idea itself.


What it could do
The empirical half comes from experiments that all use an LSTM3. Trained on raw characters, it produces plausible Shakespeare, valid markdown, syntactically coherent C, and LaTeX. Visualising individual cells reveals one that switches on inside a URL, one that tracks position within a [[ ]] scope, and one that counts through “www”. Roughly 5% of cells learn something legible without anyone specifying those features.


                  
                  What is the significance of a single cell that switches on inside a URL? 
                  
                

The structure was never specified — the model was trained on raw characters. It shows that interpretable, discrete features emerge from character prediction alone, in roughly 5% of cells.


Why it stopped being the default for many large models
Parallelism was a central reason. An LSTM must process step t before step t+1, which limits parallel execution across sequence positions; the Transformer removed that recurrent dependency during training. Accuracy, scaling behaviour, and task fit also influenced the shift, and LSTMs remain useful where their recurrence and state fit the task. Olah’s 2015 conclusion identified attention as the next architectural step.


                  
                  What ended the LSTM's dominance, and what did not?
                  
                

A central factor was parallelism: recurrent step t precedes t+1, while transformer training can process positions in parallel. Accuracy, scaling, and task fit also contributed, and LSTMs were not eliminated.

sections/machine-learning/entities/llama.title: Llama 3
sections/machine-learning/entities/llama.content:
Llama 3
Llama 3 is Meta’s family of open-weight language models with 8, 70, and 405 billion parameters. The Llama 3 Herd of Models1 presents the Llama 3.1 releases under the shorter family name and documents pre-trained and instruction-tuned variants.
In short

A dense decoder-only Transformer, chosen for training stability and kept close to Llama 2, underlies all three sizes.
The 405B flagship trains on 15.6 trillion tokens with 3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs, while the 8B and 70B models train past compute-optimal.
Six post-training rounds combine supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling, direct preference optimisation, and a reward model.
The 405B chat model nears leading closed models on many tasks, while adversarial math, prompt injection, and some safety tests expose weaker cases.

Architecture and scale
The family uses a dense decoder-only Transformer, chosen for training stability, kept close to Llama 2, and extended with grouped-query attention, a 128,000-token vocabulary, document-aware attention masks, and rotary position embeddings configured for longer contexts. The 405B model has 126 layers, a model dimension of 16,384, and 128 attention heads.
The team pre-trains the flagship on 15.6 trillion tokens with 3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs. scaling-laws experiments project about 402 billion parameters and 16.55 trillion tokens for that budget; a broad loss minimum supports the final 405B choice. The 8B and 70B models receive more training than their compute-optimal points because the team values quality under a smaller inference budget.
Training path
training-data-engineering produces a multilingual corpus with dedicated general-knowledge, reasoning, code, and multilingual portions. Initial pre-training uses contexts up to 8K tokens. Six continued-training stages raise the window to 128K, and a final annealing stage lowers the learning rate while raising the share of selected high-quality data.
The 405B run uses four-dimensional distributed-llm-training across as many as 16,384 H100 GPUs. Tensor, pipeline, context, and sharded data parallelism split the work. The training system also handles checkpoints, network topology, device failures, and numerical agreement between parallel configurations.
Instruction-tuned models pass through six post-training rounds. The team combines supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling, direct preference optimisation, and a Reward-Model. Human and synthetic data target code, mathematical reasoning, multilingual use, factuality, long context, and response steering.
Capabilities and evaluation
The instruction-tuned family supports eight named languages, a 128K context window, coding, reasoning, and tool calls. It can call search, Python, and a mathematical engine, or produce calls for functions described in its prompt. The chat protocol uses message headers and termination tokens to route tool and user messages. tool-interface-design explains why function descriptions, schemas, results, and errors remain system concerns outside model weights.
pretraining-evaluation separates base-checkpoint tests from chat-model tests. The paper reports benchmark suites, adversarial sets, prompt-format robustness, contamination estimates, and pairwise human evaluation. Its 405B chat model performs near leading closed models on many reported tasks, while adversarial math, file-upload tools, prompt injection, and some safety tests expose weaker cases.
Safety and release boundary
The team applies corpus filters, safety fine-tuning, red teaming, and tests that balance violation rate against false refusal. It also releases Llama Guard 3 for prompt and response classification, Prompt Guard for jailbreak and prompt-injection detection, and Code Shield for insecure generated code. The paper reports residual jailbreak, prompt-injection, and code-interpreter risks. Application builders still need permissions, isolation, and output checks through harness-engineering.
The paper also reports image, video, and speech adapters that compose frozen or separate encoders with the language model. Those experiments remained under development at publication and did not form part of the broad Llama 3 language-model release described in the paper.
