sections/machine-learning/entities/lora.title: LoRA
sections/machine-learning/entities/lora.content:
LoRA
Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, adapts a pretrained model through small factorised weight updates. Hu and coauthors’ method freezes each selected base matrix W₀ and represents its task-specific change as BA, using B ∈ Rd×r and A ∈ Rr×k with rank r far below the original dimensions.
In short

The layer computes W₀x + BAx; only A and B train, and B starts at zero so the initial update is zero.
On GPT-3 175B, rank-4 adaptation cut a task checkpoint from about 350 GB to 35 MB.
Merging BA into W₀ adds no inference latency, but makes same-batch serving of several tasks awkward.
Results matched or exceeded full fine-tuning, though low rank may not fit every downstream task.

How the update works
For input x, the modified layer computes W₀x + BAx. A is initialised with Gaussian values and B with zeros, which makes the initial update zero, and the LoRA branch is scaled by α/r. gradient-descent updates A and B while W₀ receives no gradient update.
The method can target any dense layer. The paper studies attention projections in the Transformer, with most experiments adapting the query and value matrices across all layers while freezing feed-forward modules. Under an equal parameter budget on GPT-3, applying a smaller rank to both query and value projections outperformed concentrating a larger rank in one projection.
Why the factors save resources
A full fine-tune stores one model-sized parameter change and optimiser state for each task. LoRA stores only A and B for each selected matrix. Rank-4 query-and-value adaptation on GPT-3 175B reduced a task checkpoint from about 350 GB to 35 MB. Freezing the base parameters also cut the reported training-memory requirement from 1.2 TB to 350 GB and raised training throughput by 25% in that setup.
An operator can merge BA into W₀ before inference. The resulting layer performs the original dense matrix multiplication, so LoRA adds no inference path or sequence positions. Adapters add extra sequential layers, which increased latency in the paper’s small-batch measurements, and prefix methods consume part of the input length.
Evidence for low intrinsic rank
LoRA matched or exceeded full fine-tuning performance across RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, and GPT-3 tasks. On GPT-3, 4.7 million LoRA parameters reached 73.4% WikiSQL accuracy and 91.7% matched MultiNLI accuracy. Full fine-tuning of 175 billion parameters reached 73.8% and 89.5% on those tasks.
Ranks of one or two remained competitive in several GPT-3 experiments. Singular-vector subspaces compared across ranks and random seeds share leading directions. Hu and coauthors’ analysis suggests that LoRA amplifies task-relevant directions that pretraining encoded weakly. A cross-language thought experiment in the paper warns that low rank may not fit every downstream task.
Operational limit
Merging task factors into the base matrix makes same-batch inference across several tasks awkward because each sample would require a different merged weight. A service can leave the factors separate and route samples through different modules, but it then gives up the merged path’s latency property. The paper also leaves principled selection of target matrices and ranks as open questions.
Related Entities & Topics

Transformer: the architecture used for the paper’s language-model experiments
gradient-descent: optimises the low-rank factors while the base weights stay fixed
machine-learning: parent section



Works cited

Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang and Weizhu Chen, LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models — method, resource measurements, benchmark comparisons, and rank analysis

sections/machine-learning/entities/marko.title: Markov Decision Process
sections/machine-learning/entities/marko.content:
Markov Decision Process
A Markov decision process (MDP) formalizes sequential choice under partly stochastic outcomes. It is defined by states (S), actions (A), transition probabilities (P(s’\mid s,a)), rewards (R(s,a,s’)), and a discount factor (\gamma)1. A policy (\pi(a\mid s)) selects actions, and its objective is to maximize expected discounted return.
flowchart LR
  S[Current state] --> P[Policy selects an action]
  P --> A[Action]
  A --> R[Reward]
  A --> N[Stochastic next state]
  N --> S
  R --> O[Expected discounted return guides the objective]

In short

A policy picks an action per state, and its objective is expected discounted return.
An action shifts the distribution over next states without guaranteeing one outcome.
A state that omits relevant history is not Markov, even if the algorithm treats it as one.

In detail


                  
                  What does a policy specify in a Markov decision process? 
                  
                

An action distribution for each state.




                  
                  What objective does an MDP policy optimize? 
                  
                

Expected discounted return.


The transition distribution separates what the agent controls from what the environment determines. Choosing an action changes the distribution over possible next states; it does not guarantee one outcome. The discount factor controls how future reward contributes to the present objective, with smaller values emphasizing near outcomes and values closer to one extending the horizon.
The Markov assumption says the represented state contains the information needed to model the next transition. A representation that omits relevant history is not Markov, even if the algorithm treats it as one. Some applications may require memory or belief state rather than a raw observation.
Why it matters
The MDP makes policy, value, and learning targets refer to the same object. value-return-advantage evaluates outcomes under a policy; temporal-difference-bootstrap uses successor estimates implied by the process; exploration-exploitation concerns which transitions to sample. Deep networks expand representation capacity but do not remove these structural assumptions.
Related

on-vs-off-policy-learning — relation between sampling and target policies
offline-policy-evaluation — estimating a target policy from logged transitions
machine-learning — parent section



Works cited

Aman Chadha, Primers • Reinforcement Learning

sections/machine-learning/entities/mixtu.title: Mixture of Experts
sections/machine-learning/entities/mixtu.content:
Mixture of Experts
A sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts layer is a set of feed-forward expert networks plus a trainable gate, as Shazeer and coauthors define it. For each input x, the gate assigns nonzero weights to a small subset of experts, and the layer sums their weighted outputs. Sparse selection lets a model hold far more parameters than it evaluates for one input.
In short

A noisy top-k gate selects a few experts per input, and unselected experts perform no computation.
Importance and load losses counter the feedback loop in which favoured experts train faster and attract more traffic.
On a 100-billion-word corpus, 65,536 experts cut perplexity by 39%, but 131,072 experts performed worse.
MoE learns routing and experts together, unlike independently trained specialists in knowledge distillation.

Noisy top-k routing
The paper’s gate projects the input into one score per expert, adds Gaussian noise with a learned scale, retains the k highest scores, and applies softmax. Unselected experts receive weight zero and perform no computation for that input. With more than one selected expert, gradient-descent can update the gate through the selected softmax values while backpropagation trains the experts and surrounding network in the same pass.
The noise serves exploration and load estimation. A gate without controls tends to favour a few experts. Those experts then receive more training, improve faster, and attract more traffic. The paper counters this feedback loop with an importance loss over gate weights and a load loss over estimated example counts. It also initialises gate parameters at zero to distribute early traffic.
Distributed execution
Sparse routing shrinks each expert’s batch, which wastes accelerator capacity. Ordinary layers run with data parallelism and one shared set of experts is distributed across devices. Each expert then receives all relevant examples from the combined device batches. In the paper’s language systems, the same expert layer applies to every sequence position and those positions are batched together.
Network traffic sets another constraint because devices must send expert inputs and outputs across the cluster. Experts with large hidden layers are chosen, increasing arithmetic per transferred value. For thousands of experts, a two-level hierarchy lets one gate select groups and secondary gates select experts within those groups.
Results and specialisation
On the One Billion Word benchmark, a 4,096-expert model used about the same operations per timestep as smaller comparisons and cut test perplexity by 24% against a four-expert version. On a 100-billion-word corpus, 65,536 experts and 68 billion parameters reduced perplexity by 39% against the matched recurrent baseline. The next scale, 131,072 experts and 137 billion parameters, performed worse and ran at lower hardware efficiency.
The paper inserts expert layers between stacked LSTM layers for translation. Its 2,048-expert English-to-French model reached 40.56 BLEU against 39.22 for the cited GNMT baseline while using fewer operations per timestep. Inspection of routed text showed experts concentrating on recurring syntactic and semantic contexts, such as phrases about leadership or rapid change.
Distinction from independent specialists
A sparse MoE learns routing and expert parameters together. In knowledge-distillation, Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean describe specialist models whose class subsets come from a generalist’s confusion patterns and whose training proceeds independently after assignment. Their design simplifies parallel training; the MoE gate instead changes assignments as the experts learn.
Related Entities & Topics

LSTM: the recurrent backbone used in the paper’s language models
knowledge-distillation: compresses model behaviour into one student rather than routing through selected experts
gradient-descent: jointly trains the gate, experts, and balancing objectives
machine-learning: parent section



Works cited

Noam Shazeer, Azalia Mirhoseini, Krzysztof Maziarz, Andy Davis, Quoc V. Le, Geoffrey Hinton and Jeff Dean, Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer — sparse gating, balancing losses, distributed execution, and language experiments
Geoffrey Hinton, Oriol Vinyals and Jeff Dean, Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network — independently trained specialists and their contrast with learned MoE routing

sections/machine-learning/entities/multi.title: Multilayer Perceptron
sections/machine-learning/entities/multi.content:
Multilayer Perceptron
A multilayer perceptron is the simplest neural network architecture: it stacks alternating matrix multiplications (plus biases) and term-wise non-linear functions. It does not connect the computations at different positions.
In short

A single perceptron learns one straight boundary, so XOR needs combined neurons, and hidden layers generalize that composition.
Weights choose the pattern, the bias sets how much is enough, and the non-linearity keeps the stack from collapsing into one linear function.
In a transformer the up-projection’s rows ask questions and the down-projection’s columns are the edits added back.
The MLP processes each position without sharing information across positions, which attention supplies.
It ignores pixel adjacency, and its neurons rarely represent one clean feature.

Why the second layer matters
The architecture starts from its smallest case1. A single perceptron multiplies inputs by weights, adds a bias, and thresholds the sum; geometrically, it can learn only one straight decision boundary. That is enough for AND or OR but not XOR, whose true and false cases are not linearly separable. Combining neurons makes the missing composition possible: one can represent OR, another NOT-AND, and their outputs together represent XOR. Hidden layers generalize this move from one boundary to learned combinations of boundaries.
The same construction also explains the bias. Without it, the decision boundary is forced through the origin because zero inputs always yield zero weighted input. A constant input of one with its own learned weight lets the boundary shift. In this geometric reading, weights determine the boundary’s orientation and the bias determines its offset.
flowchart LR
  A[Attention moves information between positions] --> X[Input vector]
  X --> U[Up-projection — rows are directions that ask a question]
  W[Weights say which pattern] --> U
  B[Bias says how much is enough] --> U
  U --> R[ReLU — a neuron is the value leaving it]
  N[Without the non-linearity the stack collapses to one linear function] --> R
  R --> D[Down-projection — columns are edits in embedding space]
  D --> O[Added back to what flowed in]
  O --> S[Neurons rarely carry one clean feature — see superposition]


a⁽¹⁾ = σ(W a⁽⁰⁾ + b)

But what is a Neural Network?2 builds one to classify handwritten digits, with 784 input neurons, two hidden layers of 16, 10 outputs, and 13,002 weights and biases. How might LLMs store facts — Deep Learning Chapter 73 finds the same structure inside GPT-3, where it holds about two-thirds of the 175 billion parameters. The examples show the same object at two different scales.
What the parts are for
Each component answers a requirement:

Weights say which pattern a neuron responds to. Drawn as a 28×28 grid, a band of positive weights sums brightness in a region. Because that also fires on blobs, negative weights above and below restrict the response to a narrow edge.
The bias says how much is enough. A bias of −10 means the neuron becomes meaningfully active only once the weighted sum exceeds 10.
The non-linearity is structurally required. Without it every layer is matrix-multiply-plus-offset, the whole network collapses into one linear function, and expressiveness drops dramatically.



                  
                  Why do the weights of an edge-detecting neuron carry negatives above and below the band? 
                  
                

A band of positive weights alone sums brightness in a region, which also fires on a solid blob. The negative weights either side make the neuron fire only when the bright region is narrow — an edge.




                  
                  What does the bias contribute that the weights cannot? 
                  
                

A threshold. Weights say which pattern the neuron responds to; the bias says how strong that match has to be before the neuron becomes meaningfully active.




                  
                  What happens to a deep network with the non-linearities removed? 
                  
                

Every layer becomes matrix-multiply-plus-offset, so the whole stack collapses into a single linear function. Depth buys nothing without it.


Why ReLU helped deep optimisation
Sigmoid saturates at both extremes, so its derivative can become very small and weaken a gradient propagated through many layers. ReLU retains a constant positive-side derivative, which often makes deep optimisation easier. It is still flat for negative inputs and can produce inactive or “dead” units, so the source’s claim that it “never flattens” is useful shorthand only on the positive side. Transformer MLPs often use smoother alternatives such as GELU3.


                  
                  Why did ReLU displace sigmoid, and why did depth make that decisive? 
                  
                

Sigmoid’s derivative becomes small at both extremes. ReLU keeps a nonzero derivative on its positive side, which often preserves stronger gradients through deep stacks—but it is flat on the negative side and can create dead units.


Two readings of the two matrices
The two matrix multiplications read in different orientations3:




















MatrixRead asMeaningW↑ (up-projection)rowseach row is a direction; the dot product asks a question about the input vectorW↓ (down-projection)columnseach column is a direction in embedding space; it is the edit added when its neuron is active
Rows ask, columns answer. In GPT-3, W↑ has just under 50,000 rows, exactly four times the 12,288 embedding dimensions. The designers chose this ratio for hardware friendliness, without a deeper theoretical reason.


                  
                  Why are the two MLP matrices read in different orientations? 
                  
                

The up-projection’s rows are directions the input is dot-producted against — each row asks a question. The down-projection’s columns are directions in embedding space — each column is the edit added when its neuron fires. Rows ask, columns answer.


”Neurons” means the post-ReLU values
The word “neuron” is overloaded. In a transformer, it refers to a value leaving the ReLU: active when positive and inactive at zero. The familiar dots-and-lines diagram depicts a matrix multiplication followed by a term-wise non-linearity.
Inside a transformer it is the block that does not communicate
It alternates with attention4: attention lets vectors pass information between positions, then the MLP processes each vector in parallel without sharing information across positions, and its output is added back to what flowed in. Attention moves information among positions; the MLP applies learned feature transformations at each position. The source uses “storage” as an interpretive model rather than a literal separation between memory and computation.


                  
                  What is the division of labour between attention and the MLP block? 
                  
                

Attention moves information between positions; the MLP processes each position independently and adds its result back. One supplies context, the other supplies the stored capacity.


What it does not do, in either era

The digit network’s learned first-layer weights look almost random rather than edge-like, and it declares random noise to be a 5 with full confidence5. The architecture neither uses the adjacency of pixels nor transfers a pattern learned in one region to another, a gap that motivates convolution.



                  
                  What does an MLP fail to exploit about image data? 
                  
                

That pixels are adjacent. Nothing in the architecture knows about spatial locality, and a pattern learned in one region cannot transfer to another — which is the gap convolution was invented to fill.



The same disappointment holds at scale3: an MLP neuron rarely represents one clean feature. See superposition.

sections/machine-learning/entities/rlhf.title: RLHF
sections/machine-learning/entities/rlhf.content:
RLHF
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback is the third phase of the pipeline that turns a pretrained language model into a chat assistant. Researchers have taught machines from human preferences for over a decade. OpenAI began exploring the method as a safety technique because writing an explicit goal function for a complex objective is dangerous. Its product improvements later brought wider attention.
flowchart LR
  P[Pretraining — capability, about 98 percent of the compute] --> S[Supervised finetuning — format, answering not continuing]
  S --> C[Comparison data — which of two responses is better]
  C --> R[Reward model trained on the pairwise loss]
  R --> O[PPO optimises the SFT policy against the reward model]
  K[KL penalty against the SFT policy] --> O
  O --> A[Preference — the better of several valid answers]
  S -->|cloning answers past the model's knowledge| H[Hallucination, which RLHF made worse]

In short

Pretraining supplies capability, SFT supplies format, and RLHF supplies preference among valid answers, on thousands of examples rather than trillions of tokens.
The reward model trains on pairwise comparisons because labelers rank consistently but score inconsistently, and about 73% agreement caps it.
The KL penalty keeps PPO from drifting into regions where the reward model’s scores are wrong.
RLHF made hallucination worse, and why it beats SFT rests on three hypotheses with no proof.
Agents reopen credit assignment, because their reward arrives after a long trajectory of tool calls.

Three phases, three different problems

























PhaseSolvesScalePretrainingCapability — statistical knowledge of language~98% of total compute; trillions of tokensSupervised finetuningFormat — answering rather than continuing~14.5K (prompt, response) pairs for InstructGPTRLHFPreference — which of several valid answers is better50K prompts → 300K–1.8M comparisons
RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback1 uses the ratio to argue that SFT and RLHF are best understood as unlocking capability the pretrained model already has but prompting cannot reach.


                  
                  Why are SFT and RLHF described as unlocking capability rather than adding it?
                  
                

Pretraining takes ~98% of the compute and all the trillions of tokens. The later phases run on thousands of examples — far too little to install knowledge, but enough to reach knowledge prompting cannot.


Why SFT alone is insufficient: demonstration data shows the model which responses are plausible without indicating their quality. A pretrained model asked “How to make pizza” may validly add context, ask follow-ups, or answer; SFT picks the third. It cannot rank two answers that are both in the right shape.


                  
                  What can demonstration data never tell a model? 
                  
                

How good a response is. Demonstrations show which responses are plausible, so SFT can fix the shape of an answer but cannot rank two answers that are both in the right shape.


The comparison trick
Labelers give inconsistent absolute scores but can say which of two responses is better with consistency. The Reward-Model therefore trains on (prompt, winning_response, losing_response) with loss −log σ(sw − sl), which pushes the winner above the loser. Absolute scores emerge from relative judgements.


                  
                  Why does the reward model train on comparisons rather than scores? 
                  
                

Labelers cannot give consistent absolute scores but can reliably say which of two responses is better. The loss only pushes the winner above the loser, and absolute scores emerge from those relative judgements.


Inter-labeler agreement is about 73%, placing a measurable ceiling on the method. In a group of ten people ranking two responses, seven agree.


                  
                  What does ~73% inter-labeler agreement bound? 
                  
                

The reward model’s achievable accuracy. Its training signal is only as consistent as the humans producing it, so roughly a quarter of the comparisons it learns from disagree with each other.


The KL term is load-bearing
PPO optimises the SFT model against the reward model, while the objective includes a KL-divergence penalty against the SFT policy. Without it, the policy drifts toward regions the reward model never saw, where the model assigns scores that are far too high and optimisation chases them. A second term keeps performance on plain text completion from degrading.


                  
                  What breaks if the KL penalty is removed from PPO? 
                  
                

The policy drifts into regions the reward model never saw, where it scores things extremely highly by mistake, and optimisation chases those errors instead of the preference they were meant to stand in for.


This produces reward-proxy-failure: policy optimisation targets a learned proxy for human preference and searches for gaps between the two.
It made hallucination worse
RLHF made hallucination worse1. Schulman’s hypothesis is that behavior cloning causes hallucination: SFT trains the model to imitate answers a human wrote using knowledge the human had and the model lacks, teaching it to produce confident text beyond its knowledge. Although researchers expected RLHF to help, the InstructGPT paper shows that it worsened hallucination while improving enough else that labelers still preferred the result.


                  
                  By what mechanism would behaviour cloning cause hallucination?
                  
                

The model imitates answers a human wrote using knowledge the human had and it does not. What it learns from those examples is the habit of producing confident text past the edge of what it knows.


Why it works: three hypotheses, no proof
Via Yoav Goldberg, Huyen presents the diversity hypothesis (SFT penalises valid-but-different answers), the negative feedback hypothesis (demonstrations only ever show good responses; RL can show bad ones), and the hallucination hypothesis. She has not seen a foolproof argument for why RLHF beats SFT.
The agent-era update
AI Agents in Depth: Design Principles and Engineering Practice2 places RLHF inside a wider post-training landscape (Ch. 7) and adds two things Huyen’s 2023 account predates. First, an explicit account of when to choose SFT and when to choose RL, rather than treating the three phases as a fixed pipeline everyone runs. Second, multi-turn credit assignment: RLHF as described scores a single response, but an agent’s reward arrives after a long trajectory of tool calls, which is the credit-assignment problem from classical RL returning at the application layer.
The classical vocabulary sharpens the mapping. A sampled generation has a realised return; a critic estimates expected return; advantage measures whether a chosen token or action did better than the policy’s baseline. PPO is an on-policy method in the sense captured by on-vs-off-policy-learning, so new policy updates depend on trajectories close to the current policy rather than unrestricted reuse of old generations.


                  
                  Why does the agent setting reopen credit assignment for RLHF? 
                  
                

RLHF as described scores one response. An agent’s reward arrives only after a long trajectory of tool calls, so something must decide which of those steps earned it.


Li’s stated priority that data and environment matter more than algorithms echoes the reward-model problem: the algorithm is not usually the limiting factor.
Related Entities & Topics

reward-proxy-failure — why optimizing the learned scorer can miss the intended preference

exploration-exploitation — the RL inheritance

Works cited

Chip Huyen, RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — primary
Bojie Li, AI Agents in Depth: Design Principles and Engineering Practice — post-training in the agent era; multi-turn credit assignment
Aman Chadha, Primers • Reinforcement Learning — the RL machinery — policy, reward, PPO — that RLHF borrows

sections/machine-learning/entities/retri.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
sections/machine-learning/entities/retri.content:
Retrieval Augmented Generation
Retrieval augmented generation gives a language model access to an external knowledge source at query time, extending its knowledge beyond what its weights contain. Weights are an expensive and uncorrectable place to store facts, while a database is cheap and correctable.
flowchart LR
  I[Ingest — chunk, embed, store the corpus] --> Q[Embed the query in the same space]
  Q --> R[Retrieve semantically similar segments]
  V[Vector store — flexible, returns confident irrelevance] --> R
  GR[Graph store — precise, needs near-exact matching] --> R
  SQ[Relational SQL — reliable, semantically rigid] --> R
  R --> K[Re-rank — the stage most implementations skip]
  K --> G[Generate — retrieved context plus the query]



                  
                  What is the argument for keeping facts out of the weights? 
                  
                

Weights are an expensive and uncorrectable place to store a fact; a database is cheap and correctable. Knowledge held outside the model can be audited, updated and cited.


In short

The pipeline ingests, embeds the query, retrieves, re-ranks and generates, and almost all the difficulty sits in retrieval.
Vector stores are flexible but confidently irrelevant, graph stores precise but schema-bound, and SQL reliable but semantically rigid.
Agent literature calls the same vector store long-term memory, weaker in representational power than full attention.
Retrieval keeps evidence outside the weights, where it can be audited, updated, access-controlled and cited.
Retrieval and generation must be scored separately, because their failures look identical end to end.

The pipeline

Ingest: choose a retrieval-chunking-boundary, represent the units, and store them.
Embed the query in the same embedding space.
Retrieve semantically similar segments.
Re-rank with the retrieval-reranking-funnel for precision, business rules, personalisation, context, and response budget.
Generate: concatenate retrieved context with the query and hand the whole thing to the model.

Step 4 is the stage people skip but should include1. The LLM is the last and least interesting stage, with almost all the engineering difficulty in retrieval.


                  
                  Which stage of a RAG pipeline carries most of the engineering difficulty? 
                  
                

Retrieval — and re-ranking in particular, the stage most implementations skip. The LLM is the last and least interesting step.


Three retriever families

Vector database: dense embeddings (BERT-style) or sparse (TF-IDF). It offers semantic flexibility but can return irrelevant neighbours with high confidence.
Graph or structured retrieval: traverses explicit entities and relations. It can answer relational queries directly, but depends on schema quality, extraction, and translating the question into the right path.
Relational SQL: structured and reliable, but semantically rigid.



                  
                  What is the trade between a vector store and a graph store as retrievers? 
                  
                

Dense retrieval is flexible enough to recover paraphrases but can return irrelevant neighbours. Graph retrieval exploits explicit relations, but only relations the system represented and queried correctly. The trade is learned semantic similarity against structured relational coverage.


hybrid-retrieval combines lexical exact-term matching, dense semantic retrieval, metadata filters, and structured paths to improve candidate recall; its practical problem is score normalization or fusion before unlike candidates can be compared.
Retrieval or memory, depending who is asking
The agent literature in LLM Powered Autonomous Agents2 uses the same machinery under a different name. It calls RAG’s vector store long-term memory: an external store the agent attends to at query time, contrasted with the short-term memory of the context window. The engineering is identical: both use approximate nearest neighbour search via LSH, ANNOY, HNSW, FAISS or ScaNN. Weng’s caveat applies to either framing: a vector store extends reach, but its representational power is weaker than full attention.
Where it goes
Multi-hop RAG chains retrievals when one lookup cannot answer the question, preserving each intermediate dependency and its provenance. Hierarchical and multimodal RAG extend the index. Agentic RAG lets the model decide which store to use, how many hops to make, and whether to retrieve at all. Moving retrieval from a fixed pipeline stage into model control connects it to the LLM-Agent.


                  
                  What changes when RAG becomes agentic? 
                  
                

Retrieval stops being a fixed pipeline stage and becomes a decision the model takes — which store to hit, how many hops, whether to retrieve at all.


RAG vs. long context is a design trade. Retrieval reduces tokens and isolates evidence; long context preserves material a retriever might omit. Longer windows change what needs retrieving and move the cost around.
RAG 2.0 means optimising retriever and generator end to end instead of bolting a frozen retriever onto a frozen model.


                  
                  Why doesn't a longer context window simply retire retrieval? 
                  
                

It changes what needs retrieving and moves the cost around rather than removing it. The question is treated as open, not settled by window size.


The alternative it competes with
When a model lacks knowledge, developers can have it look up the missing information or change its weights. Domain pretraining or supervised finetuning can internalise patterns, while RLHF primarily tunes preferences and behaviour rather than installing general knowledge. Retrieval keeps evidence outside the weights, where people can audit it, update it, control access to it, and cite it.
Evaluate the halves separately
component-wise-rag-evaluation separates retrieval precision, recall, and relevance from groundedness and answer quality. A bad answer may follow either perfect retrieval that the generator used poorly or bad retrieval that it used faithfully. An aggregate score cannot distinguish these cases, which require opposite fixes.


                  
                  Why can't one aggregate score diagnose a RAG system? 
                  
                

A bad answer can come from perfect retrieval badly used, or from garbage retrieval faithfully used. The two look identical end-to-end and need opposite fixes.

sections/machine-learning/entities/rewar.title: Reward Model
sections/machine-learning/entities/rewar.content:
Reward Model
A reward model is a learned scoring function that takes a (prompt, response) pair and returns a scalar. RLHF needs it because people can recognise “a good answer” but cannot specify one as a function.
flowchart LR
  R[A good answer cannot be written as a function] --> C[But people can recognise one]
  C --> P[Pairwise comparisons — the winner pushed above the loser]
  P --> M[A learned scorer, initialised from the SFT model]
  M --> S[Absolute scores emerge from ordering consistently]
  M --> L1[Preferences are not one function — it averages a disagreement]
  M --> L2[About 73 percent labeler agreement caps its accuracy]
  M --> L3[Off its training distribution the scores go wildly wrong]
  L3 --> H[A policy hunting maxima is hunting those errors specifically]
  H --> K[The KL penalty pins the policy where the scorer is valid]



                  
                  Why does a reward model have to be learned rather than written? 
                  
                

Nobody can specify “a good answer” as a function, but people can recognise one. Fitting a scorer to recognition is the only route from the judgement that exists to the scalar the optimiser needs.


In short

The reward model trains on pairwise comparisons, and absolute scores emerge as a side effect of consistent pair ordering.
Initialising it from the SFT model works better than training from scratch.
It averages diverse human preferences, and about 73% inter-labeler agreement caps its accuracy.
Off its training distribution its scores go wrong, so a KL penalty pins the policy where the scorer is more trustworthy.
It is classical reward design past the point where anyone can specify the reward by hand.

Trained on comparisons, not scores
Absolute quality scores from labelers produce data too inconsistent to learn from. Pairwise comparisons produce data consistent enough to learn from. The training data is therefore (prompt, winning_response, losing_response) and the loss is

−log σ(sw − sl)

The loss is large when the winner scores below the loser and small otherwise. The model never sees an example of a 7/10; absolute scores emerge as a side effect of consistent pair ordering.


                  
                  Where do a reward model's absolute scores come from, if it is never shown one? 
                  
                

They are a side effect of consistently ordering pairs. The loss only ever pushes a winner above a loser; a usable scale falls out of doing that consistently across the data.


Ranking four responses A > B > C > D yields six pairs, multiplying the required annotator time1. Initialising the reward model from the SFT model also works better than training from scratch. The intuition is that a scorer must be at least as capable as the thing it scores.


                  
                  Why initialise the reward model from the SFT model rather than from scratch? 
                  
                

A scorer has to be at least as capable as the thing it scores. Starting from the policy’s own weights gives it the understanding of the responses it is being asked to rank.


Three limits, all structural
1. Preferences are not one function. Huyen prefers the losing response in an example from Anthropic’s HH-RLHF dataset and says so in the post. Human preferences are diverse, and no single mathematical formulation can capture them. The reward model averages this disagreement instead of approximating a fact.


                  
                  What is a reward model actually approximating, if not a fact? 
                  
                

A disagreement. Human preferences are diverse and do not reduce to one function, so fitting a single scorer to them averages people who genuinely want different answers.


2. Agreement caps accuracy. Inter-labeler agreement runs around 73%. The reward model cannot be more reliable than the signal it was fit to.
3. It is only valid where it has seen data. Outside its training distribution, the reward model can assign scores far from the correct values. The policy searches for high scores and will find those errors. This is reward-proxy-failure under optimisation pressure. The RLHF objective therefore carries a KL penalty that pins the policy near the SFT model, keeping it inside the region where the reward model is more trustworthy.


                  
                  Why is a policy searching for high reward guaranteed to find a reward model's errors? 
                  
                

Because the errors are high scores. Off-distribution mistakes look exactly like the objective, so an optimiser hunting maxima is hunting them specifically — the KL penalty exists to keep it where the scorer is valid.


The same problem, older name
Reward design is a first-class challenge in classical RL2: sparse and delayed rewards break credit assignment, while reward shaping adds intermediate rewards to guide the agent. Reward design has no general solution. When no one can specify the reward by hand, practitioners fit a reward model instead of shaping a written function. Its scalar then supplies the trajectory signal from which they estimate return, value, and advantage.


                  
                  How does a reward model relate to classical reward design? 
                  
                

It is the same problem past the point where hand-specification is possible. Classical RL shapes a reward function you can write; when you cannot write one at all, you fit one from data instead.


Schulman’s proposed fix for hallucination changes the reward model to punish the model more for making things up, which is reward shaping under a different name.
Related Entities & Topics

RLHF — the pipeline it sits inside
reward-proxy-failure — the gap between a measurable scorer and the intended objective
evaluation-metrics — a learned metric is still a metric, with all a metric’s assumptions
exploration-exploitation — the RL context
machine-learning — parent section



Works cited

Chip Huyen, RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — primary — comparison data, loss, KL constraint
Aman Chadha, Primers • Reinforcement Learning — reward design and shaping in classical RL

sections/machine-learning/entities/trans.title: Transformer
sections/machine-learning/entities/trans.content:
Transformer
The Transformer is a stack of encoders and decoders, introduced in Attention is All You Need (2017). Only self-attention connects positions to one another; the feed-forward network, residual connections and layer normalisation each act on positions independently.
Because positions interact only in the attention layer, the network runs every other operation in parallel across the sequence. This removed the sequential training bottleneck that limited LSTM models.
flowchart TD
  S[Positions interact only inside the attention layer] --> P[Everything else runs in parallel across the sequence]
  P --> T[The sequential training bottleneck is removed]
  S --> Q[Cost becomes quadratic in sequence length]
  Q --> LC[Long-context research exists because of this cell]
  S --> O[Order is no longer implicit in a recurrence]
  O --> PE[Positional encoding added back into the embeddings]
  S --> M[Masking — future positions to minus infinity, so generation stays causal]
  S --> MO[Indifferent to modality — patches can play the role tokens play]
  MO --> B[Encodes how to spend compute, not what is true about language]



                  
                  Why can a Transformer train in parallel across a sequence when an RNN cannot? 
                  
                

Positions interact only inside the attention layer. Everything else — feed-forward, residuals, layer norm — acts on each position independently, so there is no step-by-step dependency to serialise on.


In short

Positions interact only in attention, so everything else runs in parallel, removing the sequential bottleneck of recurrent models.
The price is cost quadratic in sequence length, which drives long-context research.
Removing recurrence removed order, so positional encoding is added back and decoder masking keeps generation causal.
Indifference to modality let the Vision Transformer reuse the architecture almost unchanged, with 16×16 patches as tokens.
It encodes almost no knowledge about language, which reconciles it with the Bitter Lesson.

What replaced what

























Recurrent modelsTransformerState carried step by stepEvery position attends to every other from layer oneO(n·d²) — linear in sequence length, quadratic in hidden dimensionO(n²·d) — quadratic in sequence length, linear in model dimensionOrder is implicit in the recurrenceOrder must be added back as positional encodingLong-range dependency degrades with distanceDistance costs nothing; sequence length costs quadratically
The complexity row holds the trade1: Transformers gain parallelism at the cost of quadratic scaling with sequence length. That quadratic cost drives long-context research.


                  
                  What does the Transformer pay for removing the recurrence? 
                  
                

Cost quadratic in sequence length (O(n²·d)) instead of linear. Distance between two positions becomes free, but total length becomes expensive — which is why long-context research exists.




                  
                  Why does a Transformer need positional encoding at all? 
                  
                

Order was implicit in the recurrence it removed. With every position attending to every other from layer one, nothing in the architecture distinguishes sequence order, so it has to be added back into the embeddings.


The pieces

Query / key / value: three learned projections per position. Attention scores each query against every key by dot product, scales by √dk, applies softmax, weights the values and sums them.
Multi-head attention: eight independently initialised Q/K/V sets provide eight “representation subspaces.” The layer concatenates them and projects them by WO. In Alammar’s example one head binds “it” to “the animal” while another binds it to “tired.”
Positional encoding: sinusoidal vectors added to the input embeddings, because removing recurrence removed all notion of order.
Masking: decoder self-attention sets future positions to −inf before the softmax, so generation stays causal.
Cross-attention: queries from one source, keys and values from another. This mechanism makes the architecture multimodal.



                  
                  What does multi-head attention buy over a single attention head? 
                  
                

Several independently initialised Q/K/V sets give several representation subspaces, so different heads can bind the same word to different antecedents — one head tying “it” to “the animal” while another ties it to “tired.”




                  
                  What does decoder masking do, and why is it necessary? 
                  
                

It sets future positions to −inf before the softmax. Without it, attention over the whole sequence would let a position see the tokens it is supposed to be predicting, so generation would not be causal.


Why it generalised beyond language
The Transformer’s indifference to modality is a more durable contribution than its performance on text1. The Vision Transformer’s architecture is nearly identical to the 2017 original; the only real adaptation is cutting the image into 16×16 patches so that patches can play the role tokens play. Earlier architectures used a separate specialised model per data type, making them one-trick ponies.


                  
                  What is the single adaptation that turns a Transformer into a Vision Transformer? 
                  
                

Cutting the image into 16×16 patches so patches can play the role tokens play. The architecture is otherwise nearly identical to the 2017 original — which is the evidence that it is indifferent to modality.


The prediction that landed
Understanding LSTM Networks2 closes, in August 2015, by naming attention as the next big step after LSTMs. The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks3, three months earlier, calls attention “the most interesting recent architectural innovation in neural networks.” Both were written two years before the Transformer paper.
The Transformer complicates The Bitter Lesson4: humans designed its architecture, while Sutton argues that such design plateaus. The two positions fit together because the Transformer encodes almost no knowledge about language. It provides a general method for converting compute into performance, the kind Sutton says survives.


                  
                  How does the Transformer escape the Bitter Lesson's verdict on human architectural design? 
                  
                

It encodes almost no knowledge about language. What Sutton says plateaus is built-in domain knowledge; a general method for turning compute into performance is the category he says survives.


Related Entities & Topics

self-attention: the mechanism the architecture is built around
LSTM: what it replaced
Diffusion-Models: increasingly built on transformer backbones
LLM-Agent: what gets built on top of it
machine-learning: parent section



Works cited

Christopher Olah, Understanding LSTM Networks — the predecessor, and the prediction
Andrej Karpathy, The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks
Richard S. Sutton, The Bitter Lesson — what an architecture is worth if only compute scales
Jay Alammar, The Illustrated Transformer — primary: the mechanism, illustrated

sections/machine-learning/entities/tulu-.title: Tulu 3
sections/machine-learning/entities/tulu-.content:
Tulu 3
Tulu 3 is a family of post-trained language models built from Llama 3.1 base checkpoints at 8B, 70B, and 405B parameters. Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training1 releases model weights, intermediate checkpoints, training datasets, code, evaluation tools, and the recipe used to connect them.
In short

Training runs through prompt curation, supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
Binary verifiers replace a learned reward model for checkable tasks, but weak KL constraints let models game format checks.
Tulu 3 70B averaged 76.2 on its development suite, with English focus, short conversations and little long-context data as limits.

Training path
The family follows four stages. The team first curates licensed public and synthetic prompts around knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, coding, instruction following, chat, and safety, then removes prompts that overlap its evaluations. supervised-fine-tuning trains the first behavioral checkpoint. Length-normalized preference-optimization trains on chosen and rejected responses, including generations from the SFT model. A final reinforcement-learning stage uses deterministic answer and constraint checks for mathematics and precise instruction following.
The final stage, called reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, replaces a learned Reward-Model with a binary verifier for tasks that have checkable outcomes. The 8B run improved MATH, GSM8K, and IFEval over its DPO checkpoint. Verifiers can also be overoptimized: under weak KL constraints, models sometimes satisfied count or formatting requirements while failing to answer the prompt.
Open artifacts and evaluation
The release includes Open Instruct training code, OLMES evaluation code, decontamination tools, SFT and preference mixtures, and checkpoints for each model size. The evaluation suite separates development tasks from unseen tasks selected for the same core skills. This design exposed weak transfer from IFEval’s known constraint types to a new out-of-distribution constraint set.
On the authors’ development suite, Tulu 3 70B averaged 76.2, compared with 74.1 for Llama 3.1 70B Instruct and 75.3 for the reported Claude 3.5 Haiku results. The paper’s 405B tables place its final checkpoint near the compared GPT-4o and DeepSeek V3 results. These comparisons depend on the suite’s prompts, extraction rules, and unknown contamination in closed training sets.
Boundaries
The released mixture focuses on English, averages 2.4 conversation turns, and contains little long-context data. The team leaves multilingual depth, long conversations, and tool-use-tuning for future work. Safety also regressed after its SFT peak, which makes Tulu 3 a documented recipe with visible tradeoffs. No one checkpoint dominates every stage.

Does long context obviate retrieval, or relocate it? Primers • Retrieval Augmented Generation treats this as unresolved: longer windows change what needs retrieving and move the cost without removing it.
Why does RLHF beat SFT? RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback offers three hypotheses (diversity, negative feedback, hallucination) and, in its own words, no foolproof argument for any of them.
Does architectural design contradict the bitter lesson? sections/machine-learning/pages-index.title: Outline: Machine Learning
sections/machine-learning/pages-index.content:
Outline: Machine Learning

90 pages in 11 domains, in reading order. Each domain opens with its overview page.

Machine Learning · Works
1. Foundations of Machine Learning
Overview — Loss, gradients, backpropagation, generalisation

Gradient Descent — Gradient descent moves the parameters against the gradient of the cost at a pace set by the learning rate α.
Backpropagation — Backpropagation applies the chain rule efficiently to compute gradients through a composed computational graph.
Variance Tradeoff — The bias/variance tradeoff is the pull between two errors: the simpler the model the higher the bias, the more complex the model the higher the variance (VIP Cheatsheet…
Estimation and Uncertainty — A sample statistic estimates an unknown population quantity: the sample mean targets expectation, and sample variance targets dispersion.
Regression Loss Geometry — Regression loss geometry describes how a metric transforms residuals before aggregation.
Classification Error Trade-offs — Classification error trade-offs begin with four counts rather than one score: true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives.
Multilayer Perceptron — A multilayer perceptron is the simplest neural network architecture: it stacks alternating matrix multiplications (plus biases) and term-wise non-linear functions.
Regularization — Regularization is any device that controls a network’s capacity to prevent it from fitting noise.
Batch Normalization — Batch normalization (Ioffe & Szegedy) forces the activations throughout a network toward a unit gaussian at the start of training.
Generative Learning — Generative learning algorithms model what the data itself looks like — p(x|y), the features of each class — and classify by turning that around with Bayes rule.
Matrix Calculus for Learning — Matrix calculus expresses how scalar objectives change with vector or matrix parameters.
Optimizers — An optimizer is the update rule that turns gradients into parameter steps.
Convolutional Networks — A convolutional network is an ordinary neural network with two extra assumptions about images, and those two assumptions are the entire invention (CS231n: Convolutional…
Learning Theory — Learning theory turns the practice of fitting training data into guarantees about unseen data.
Support Vector Machines — The support vector machine chooses the decision boundary that separates classes with the largest possible gap, and ranks among the best off-the-shelf supervised…
Transfer Learning — Transfer learning reuses a network trained on one task as the starting point for another.

2. Language-Model Architecture
Overview — A token’s route from input representation to prediction

Tokenization — Tokenization converts text into vocabulary IDs before a model maps those IDs to an Embedding.
Embedding — An embedding is a token’s vector and the space it inhabits, where directions carry meaning.
Positional Encoding — Positional encoding gives a Transformer the sequence order it would otherwise lack, because Self-Attention treats its inputs as a set.
Self-Attention — Self-attention lets every position in a sequence look at every other position and use learned similarity to decide how much of each to absorb.
Layer-Wise Representations — A layer-wise representation is the vector at one sequence position after a particular block has modified it.
Next-Token Prediction — Next-token prediction trains a model to assign a probability to each token given the tokens before it.
LSTM — Long Short-Term Memory is a recurrent architecture whose repeating module uses a cell state and learned gates.
Transformer — The Transformer is a stack of encoders and decoders, introduced in Attention is All You Need (2017).
GPT-2 — GPT-2 is a 1.542-billion-parameter, decoder-only Transformer trained for Next-Token Prediction rather than for any one downstream benchmark.
Long-Term Dependency — A long-term dependency occurs when a prediction needs information from far back in a sequence.
Superposition — Superposition is a layer carrying far more features than it has neurons, each feature a specific combination of neurons along nearly perpendicular directions.
Variational Autoencoders — A variational auto-encoder is what EM becomes when the latent-variable model is parameterized by neural networks.
Unsupervised Learning — Unsupervised learning finds structure in data with no labels at all.

3. Language-Model Pretraining
Overview — The decisions that turn raw corpora and compute into a base model

Pretraining — Pretraining updates a model on a large, data-rich objective before anyone adapts it to a narrower task.
Pretraining Objectives — A pretraining objective determines which prediction error supplies the updates during Pretraining.
Scaling Laws — Scaling laws estimate how model loss changes as researchers add parameters, training data, or compute.
Distributed LLM Training — Distributed LLM training partitions model state, activations, sequences, and examples across devices while keeping one optimization run coherent.
Training Data Engineering — Training data engineering turns raw corpora into the token mixtures used for pre-training and post-training.
Pre-training Evaluation — Pre-training evaluation measures the base checkpoint before Instruction Tuning changes its behavior.
Llama 3 — Llama 3 is Meta’s family of open-weight language models with 8, 70, and 405 billion parameters.

4. Language-Model Post-Training
Overview — The training signals that change a pretrained model

Instruction Tuning — Instruction tuning uses supervised examples from many tasks to update a pretrained language model, with each input phrased as a natural-language request.
Supervised Fine-Tuning — Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) updates a pretrained model on prompt-response demonstrations.
Preference Optimization — Preference optimization trains a language model from comparisons between responses to the same prompt.
RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback is the third phase of the pipeline that turns a pretrained language model into a chat assistant.
Reward Model — A reward model is a learned scoring function that takes a (prompt, response) pair and returns a scalar.
Safety Tuning — Safety tuning uses targeted post-training data to teach a model when to refuse, when to comply, and how to handle requests that lack enough information or fall outside…
Tool-Use Tuning — Tool-use tuning trains a language model to emit calls to external systems at useful points in its generation.
Tulu 3 — Tulu 3 is a family of post-trained language models built from Llama 3.1 base checkpoints at 8B, 70B, and 405B parameters.
Post-Training — Post-training changes a pretrained language model’s behavior or skills with smaller, targeted datasets and objectives.

5. Efficient and Sparse Adaptation
Overview — Three ways to cut the cost of deploying or changing a model

Knowledge Distillation — Knowledge distillation trains a deployable student model to reproduce the output distribution of a cumbersome teacher, which may be an ensemble or a large regularised…
LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, adapts a pretrained model through small factorised weight updates.
Mixture of Experts — A sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts layer is a set of feed-forward expert networks plus a trainable gate, as Shazeer and coauthors define it.

6. Model Evaluation
Overview — Metrics for ranked, generated, and retrieved output

Rank-Aware Evaluation — Rank-aware evaluation treats relevance and position as separate inputs.
Reference-Based Text Evaluation — Reference-based text evaluation compares generated text with one or more accepted answers.
Component-Wise RAG Evaluation — Component-wise RAG evaluation measures retrieval evidence separately from generation behaviour, because an end-to-end answer score cannot locate a RAG failure.
Evaluation Metrics — An evaluation metric encodes a decision about which errors matter, so choosing one is part of modelling and is no reporting formality.

7. Grounding and Retrieval
Overview — The retrieval-and-generation pipeline and its parts

Retrieval Augmented Generation — Retrieval augmented generation gives a language model access to an external knowledge source at query time, extending its knowledge beyond what its weights contain.
Retrieval Chunking Boundary — The chunking boundary determines what unit a retriever can return.
Hybrid Retrieval — Hybrid retrieval combines signals with different failure modes: lexical methods such as TF-IDF or BM25, dense Embedding similarity, graph relationships, structured SQL…
Retrieval-Reranking Funnel — A retrieval-reranking funnel separates broad candidate discovery from precise evidence selection.
Multi-Hop Retrieval Planning — A multi-hop question contains evidence dependencies: the first result identifies an entity, relation, or constraint needed to formulate the next query.
Agentic Retrieval Routing — Agentic retrieval routing moves retrieval decisions into the control loop: a model decides whether to retrieve, which source or specialist to call, how to reformulate a…
RAG vs Long Context — Long context and retrieval allocate evidence differently: long context sends more of the corpus into the model, while RAG searches first and sends a selected subset…

8. Language-Model Agents
Overview — Models that plan, call tools, and act in a loop

LLM Agent — A system in which a language model controls the process: it decides what to do next, calls tools, and carries state across steps.
Context Engineering — Context engineering decides what a model sees on each call.
Tool Interface Design — A tool’s interface is part of the agent system: names and descriptions guide tool selection, schemas constrain arguments, middleware formats results, and validation and…
Harness Engineering — The harness is everything built around the model, and it separates an agent demo from an agent product.
Agent Control Boundary — At the agent control boundary, a human fixes some transitions in code while a model chooses others at run time.
Agent Protocol Layer — The agent protocol layer covers two interoperability boundaries (Primers • Agents).
Reflection-Evaluator Loop — A reflection-evaluator loop replaces one-pass generation with four stages: produce a draft, evaluate it against a goal, convert the evaluation into actionable feedback…
Single- vs Multi-Agent Economics — Architecture choice trades unified reasoning against structured coordination.

9. Reinforcement Learning
Overview — The formal model, value estimates, and how experience is collected

Markov Decision Process — A Markov decision process (MDP) formalizes sequential choice under partly stochastic outcomes.
Exploration vs. Exploitation — An agent must balance finding better actions against using what it has found: pure exploitation blocks the first, and pure exploration blocks the second.
On- vs Off-Policy Learning — On- and off-policy learning differ in whether experience comes from the policy being learned about.
Value, Return, and Advantage — Return is an observed outcome, while value and advantage are expectations built around it (Primers • Reinforcement Learning).
Temporal-Difference Bootstrapping — Temporal-difference (TD) learning updates a value estimate before a trajectory ends.
Reward Proxy Failure — A reinforcement-learning agent optimizes the reward it receives, not the intention the designer had.
Offline Policy Evaluation — Offline policy evaluation (OPE) estimates how a target policy would perform without deploying it.
Policy Gradients — Policy-gradient methods learn a randomized policy πθ(a|s) directly by gradient ascent on expected total payoff — no model of transitions or rewards required, only the…

10. Generative Modelling
Overview — Diffusion, from forward corruption to learned denoising

Diffusion Models — Diffusion models form a family of generative models that destroys data with noise in a fixed forward process and learns only the reverse.
Diffusion Noise Prediction — A diffusion model can train without simulating every forward step, by predicting the noise added at one sampled timestep (What are Diffusion Models?).
Diffusion Guidance — Diffusion guidance steers the reverse process toward a condition such as a class label or text representation.

11. Machine-Learning Research Strategy
Overview — Search and learning against hand-built knowledge

Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering — General methods that convert computation into performance eventually beat methods that encode human understanding of a domain.

sections/mathematics/concepts/bayes-theo.title: Bayes' Theorem
sections/mathematics/concepts/bayes-theo.content:
Bayes’ Theorem
Bayes’ theorem gives the probability of a hypothesis given data from the probability of the data given the hypothesis: P(H | E) = P(H) · P(E | H) / P(E).
In short

It turns an “inverse” probability, the likelihood P(E | H), into the “direct” one we want, P(H | E).
Likelihoods are usually easier to know and less disputed than direct probabilities, which is why the theorem earns its keep.
Every form of it says the same thing: conditional probability = unconditional probability × predictive power.
Data confirm a hypothesis exactly when the hypothesis predicts them better than its negation does.

How it works
Conditional probability is a ratio, P(H | E) = P(H & E) / P(E). Writing P(H & E) as P(H) · P(E | H) gives the theorem. Here P(H) is the prior, P(E | H) the likelihood of H on E, and P(E) the overall probability of the data.
When P(E) is not known directly, expand it over the two cases:
P(H | E) = P(H)P(E | H) / [P(H)P(E | H) + P(~H)P(E | ~H)]
In odds the theorem is a single multiplication. The posterior odds equal the prior odds times the likelihood ratio P(E | H) / P(E | ~H). For a diagnostic test that ratio is sensitivity / (1 − specificity).
Worked example
Of the 275 million Americans alive on 1 January 2000, about 2.4 million died that year, so P(died) = 0.00873. About 16.6 million were seniors (75 or older), and 57% of the deaths were among them, so P(senior | died) = 0.57. Then
P(died | senior) = 0.57 × (2.4M / 16.6M) = 0.57 × 0.144 ≈ 0.082,
which matches the direct count of 1.36 million senior deaths out of 16.6 million. Knowing someone died makes them 0.57 / 0.056 ≈ 10 times likelier to be a senior than knowing they lived: that is the likelihood ratio.
What follows for evidence

Confirmation is mutual: if E supports H, H supports E.
Data a hypothesis entails confirm it, for anyone not already certain, which is the Bayesian reading of hypothetico-deductive testing.
With the likelihood held fixed, rarer evidence confirms more. Severe chest pain is better evidence of a heart attack than shortness of breath because it is less common.
On learning E for certain, update by conditioning on E. When experience only shifts P(E) to q, Jeffrey conditioning mixes the two cases: Q(H) = q·P(H | E) + (1 − q)·P(H | ~E).

Where people disagree
The ratio and difference measures of support agree on whether E supports H but can disagree on how much, across two hypotheses. Likelihoodists drop priors and keep only the likelihood ratio, on the grounds that priors are personal.

sections/mathematics/concepts/epsilon-de.title: Epsilon-Delta Limit
sections/mathematics/concepts/epsilon-de.content:
Epsilon-Delta Limit
The epsilon-delta definition makes “f(x) gets close to L as x gets close to a” precise: for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that 0 < |x − a| < δ implies |f(x) − L| < ε.
In short

It is a statement with a universal quantifier, an existential quantifier and a conditional, and each can be read as distance.
|f(x) − L| < ε means L − ε < f(x) < L + ε; 0 < |x − a| < δ means x is within δ of a but not equal to it.
Every proof follows one five-line template, and the only real work is finding δ beforehand.
δ may depend only on ε, which is why nonlinear cases need a cap on δ.

The proof template

Let ε > 0.
Choose δ (found in advance, by working backwards from |f(x) − L| < ε, or from the graph).
Assume 0 < |x − a| < δ.
Show |f(x) − L| < ε.
Conclude that the limit is L.

“There exists” is a signal to go looking for δ; “for every” means the argument must work for an arbitrary ε. These are the same quantifier rules a formal proof uses (see natural-deduction).
Worked example
Prove lim (2x + 1) = 3 as x → 1. Working backwards, |(2x + 1) − 3| = |2x − 2| = 2|x − 1|, which is less than ε when |x − 1| < ε/2. So choose δ = ε/2. Then 0 < |x − 1| < δ gives 2|x − 1| < 2(ε/2) = ε. The same reasoning gives δ = ε/4 for lim (4x + 1) = −3 at x = −1: the slope sets the factor.
When the function is not linear
For x² − 2x + 3 near −1, the algebra leaves |x + 1|·|x − 3|, and the stray |x − 3| has to be bounded by something that does not involve x. Restrict δ ≤ 1 first; then x lies in (−2, 0), so |x − 3| < 5, and δ = min{1, ε/5} works. Assuming an upper bound on ε (ε ≤ 4, say) is always allowed in these arguments; a lower bound never is, because the claim has to hold for every small ε.
Variants and negation

Right-hand limit: replace 0 < |x − a| < δ with 0 < x − a < δ; left-hand, with −δ < x − a < 0.
Infinite limit: replace |f(x) − L| < ε with f(x) > M, for every M > 0.
No limit: flip each clause. There is some ε such that for every δ some x within δ of a escapes. |x|/x has no limit at 0: with ε = 1/2, points on either side give values 1 and −1.

The sum law follows from the definition: choose δ₁ and δ₂ that each deliver ε/2, take the smaller, and apply the triangle inequality |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.

sections/mathematics/concepts/four-funda.title: Four Fundamental Subspaces
sections/mathematics/concepts/four-funda.content:
Four Fundamental Subspaces
The four fundamental subspaces of an m × n matrix A are its column space and nullspace and those of its transpose; the fundamental theorem of linear algebra gives their dimensions, their orthogonality, and the bases that make A diagonal.
In short

Ax = b is solvable exactly when b is in the column space C(A).
Row space and column space both have dimension r, the rank; the nullspaces have dimensions n − r and m − r.
The row space is orthogonal to the nullspace in Rⁿ, and the column space to the left nullspace N(Aᵀ) in Rᵐ.
Orthonormal bases for these spaces diagonalise A: that is the singular value decomposition A = UΣVᵀ.

The theorem in three parts

Counting. Elimination is reversible step by step, so it preserves independence and dimension; the counts r, r, n − r, m − r follow.
Orthogonality. Ax = 0 says x has zero dot product with every row, so the nullspace is perpendicular to the row space. The same argument on Aᵀ gives the other pair.
Bases. Choose orthonormal vᵢ in the row space (eigenvectors of AᵀA) and uᵢ in the column space with Avᵢ = σᵢuᵢ. In those bases A is the diagonal Σ.

The pseudoinverse A⁺ reverses step 3, sending each uᵢ to vᵢ/σᵢ. A⁺b is the shortest solution of Ax = b, and A⁺A is the projection onto the row space.
Worked example: a rank-one 2 × 2
Take A = xyᵀ with unit vectors x and y. Then:

the column space is the line through x;
the row space is the line through y;
the nullspace is the line along y⊥;
the left nullspace is the line along x⊥.

The trace is xᵀy = cos θ, where θ is the angle between row space and column space. The SVD is clean: Σ = diag(1, 0), with two orthonormal bases. The eigenvectors are x and y⊥, one from the column space and one from the nullspace, which need not be perpendicular. When x = y⊥ the trace is zero, both eigenvalues are 0, the two eigenvectors merge, and A cannot be diagonalised at all.
What it is confused with
Eigenvalues are not part of the theorem. Eigenvectors pair spaces that have no natural relation, so they can be skew or missing, while the singular vectors are always orthogonal. Schur’s form QᵀAQ = T, with one orthonormal basis, is the stable middle ground: it survives cos θ = 0 by becoming the Jordan form.
Related

sections/mathematics/concepts/fundamenta.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
sections/mathematics/concepts/fundamenta.content:
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
The fundamental theorem of calculus says that differentiation and integration are inverse operations: the derivative of the accumulated area under a continuous f is f, and so a definite integral equals any antiderivative’s change between the endpoints.
In short

Part 1: if f is continuous on [a, b] and F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt, then F′(x) = f(x).
Part 2: if F is any antiderivative of a continuous f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).
Part 1 guarantees that every continuous function has an antiderivative; Part 2 turns integration from a limit of Riemann sums into evaluation at two points.
Both proofs rest on a mean value theorem.

How it works
The mean value theorem for integrals. A continuous f on [a, b] takes on its average value somewhere: there is a c in [a, b] with f(c) = (1/(b − a)) ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. The integral is trapped between m(b − a) and M(b − a), where m and M are f’s minimum and maximum, and the intermediate value theorem supplies c.
Part 1. The difference quotient of F is (1/h) ∫ₓ^{x+h} f(t) dt, the average of f over [x, x + h]. By the mean value theorem that average is f(c) for some c between x and x + h. As h → 0, c is squeezed to x, and continuity gives f(c) → f(x).
Part 2. Split [a, b] into n equal pieces and write F(b) − F(a) as a telescoping sum of F(xᵢ) − F(xᵢ₋₁). The derivative mean value theorem turns each term into f(cᵢ)Δx, so F(b) − F(a) is a Riemann sum for every n, and its limit is the integral.
With a variable upper limit u(x), Part 1 combines with the chain rule: d/dx ∫ₐ^{u(x)} f(t) dt = f(u(x))·u′(x).
Worked example
Two skaters race for 5 seconds. James’s velocity is 5 + 2t ft/s, so his distance is ∫₀⁵ (5 + 2t) dt = [5t + t²]₀⁵ = 50 ft. Kathy’s is 10 + cos(πt/2), with antiderivative 10t + (2/π) sin(πt/2), so she covers 50 + 2/π ≈ 50.6 ft. Kathy wins, by about half a foot. Any antiderivative would have done: the + C cancels in the subtraction.
What it is confused with
A definite integral is net signed area, not area. ∫₋₂² (t² − 4) dt = −32/3, because the curve lies below the axis on the whole interval; area itself is never negative.

sections/mathematics/concepts/natural-de.title: Natural Deduction
sections/mathematics/concepts/natural-de.content:
Natural Deduction
Natural deduction is a way of defining proof by giving, for each logical symbol, one rule to introduce it and one to eliminate it, so that a derivation mirrors the steps of ordinary mathematical reasoning.
In short

Γ ⊢ φ means φ can be derived from the premises Γ; every derivation is finite.
Each connective and quantifier gets an introduction rule and an elimination rule; a rule of assumptions lets each premise follow from itself.
The quantifier rules carry provisos about fresh terms, which is the formal version of “let n be arbitrary”.
Classical logic adds double-negation elimination, which is what makes excluded middle provable, and what intuitionists reject.

The rules

& — from θ and ψ, infer (θ & ψ); from (θ & ψ), infer either.
∨ — from θ, infer (θ ∨ ψ). To use (θ ∨ ψ), show φ follows from θ and also from ψ; then φ.
→ — if ψ follows from the assumption θ, infer (θ → ψ). From (θ → ψ) and θ, infer ψ (modus ponens).
¬ — if an assumption θ yields both ψ and ¬ψ, infer ¬θ. Classically, from ¬¬θ infer θ.
∀ — from ∀vθ, infer θ for any term. To infer ∀vθ, derive θ for a term t that appears in no premise: t was arbitrary.
∃ — from θ(t), infer ∃vθ. To use ∃vθ, reason from θ(t) for a fresh t to a conclusion φ that does not mention t.
= — t = t always; from t₁ = t₂, substitute one for the other.

Worked example: excluded middle
Show ⊢ (A ∨ ¬A) with no premises.

Assume ¬(A ∨ ¬A) and A. From A, (A ∨ ¬A) by ∨-introduction. That contradicts the first assumption, so ¬A, discharging A.
Now assume ¬A as well. From ¬A, (A ∨ ¬A) by ∨-introduction: the same contradiction, so ¬¬A.
Under ¬(A ∨ ¬A) we have derived both ¬A and ¬¬A, so ¬¬(A ∨ ¬A), discharging the last assumption.
Double-negation elimination gives (A ∨ ¬A).

The last step is the only one an intuitionist refuses.
Derived rules
The system proves, without adding them as rules: weakening (extra premises never hurt), cut (proved lemmas can be chained), and ex falso quodlibet (from θ and ¬θ, anything follows). Relevance and paraconsistent logics reject the last, because the conclusion may have nothing to do with the premises.
Related

epsilon-delta-limit: the ∀ and ∃ rules at work in a calculus proof

sections/mathematics/concepts/soundness-.title: Soundness and Completeness
sections/mathematics/concepts/soundness-.content:
Soundness and Completeness
Soundness and completeness are the two theorems that make classical first-order logic’s rules of proof and its definition of truth agree: every derivable argument is valid, and every valid argument is derivable.
In short

Soundness: if Γ ⊢ φ, then Γ ⊨ φ. The rules never lead from truths to a falsehood.
Completeness (Gödel, 1930): if Γ ⊨ φ, then Γ ⊢ φ. Equivalently, every consistent set of sentences has a model.
Together they give compactness: a set has a model if every finite subset does.
Compactness and the Löwenheim–Skolem theorems then show what first-order languages cannot say.

Two definitions of consequence
Deductive: Γ ⊢ φ when φ can be derived from Γ by the rules of natural-deduction. Semantic: Γ ⊨ φ when every interpretation (a non-empty domain plus extensions for the non-logical symbols) that makes all of Γ true makes φ true. Nothing guarantees in advance that these coincide. The rules might be too strong (soundness fails) or too few (completeness fails).
How the proofs go
Soundness is an induction on the length of the derivation: check that each rule preserves truth in every interpretation.
Completeness builds a model out of language itself. Start with a consistent Γ. Add a new constant for each existential sentence, to act as its witness, keeping the set consistent. Extend to a maximally consistent set, one where adding any sentence not already in it makes it inconsistent (the Lindenbaum lemma; its proof uses excluded middle, so intuitionists do not accept it). Take the constants as the domain, read the extensions off the sentences in the set, and show by induction that the model makes true exactly the sentences in the set.
Worked example: what follows
Derivations are finite, so a contradiction can only ever use finitely many premises. That gives compactness. Since the model built in the completeness proof is made of countably many constants, any consistent countable set has a countable model (downward Löwenheim–Skolem). And if a set has arbitrarily large finite models, it has infinite models of every size (upward).
Apply this to arithmetic. Take every first-order sentence true of the natural numbers. That set still has uncountable models. So no first-order theory can pin down “the natural numbers”, or “countable”, or “finite”.
The trade
Second-order logic with standard semantics can characterise the natural numbers, but it loses completeness and compactness. That trade is a large part of the case for and against classical first-order logic as the “one true logic”.

sections/mathematics/topics/calculus-and.content:
Calculus and Linear Algebra
Calculus and linear algebra are the two working languages of the quantitative sciences: one for quantities that change continuously, the other for many quantities that change together.
In short

A limit is made precise by quantifying closeness with ε and δ, and every limit proof follows one template.
Integration and differentiation undo each other, so an area can be computed from an antiderivative at two points.
A matrix acts between four subspaces whose dimensions and orthogonality are fixed by its rank.
The singular value decomposition picks orthonormal bases in which any matrix is diagonal.

Choose a route
