sections/physics/concepts/conservation-o.title: Conservation of Energy
sections/physics/concepts/conservation-o.content:
Conservation of Energy
Conservation of energy is the statement that, for a system acted on only by conservative forces, the sum of kinetic and potential energy, E = T + V, does not change in time.
In short

The work done by a force equals the change in the kinetic energy T = ½mṙ².
A force is conservative when it depends only on position and does the same work along every path between two points; then it can be written F = −∇V.
For conservative forces E = T + V is constant. Written in position and momentum, E is the Hamiltonian.
Friction is not conservative, and mechanical energy is then lost. Thermodynamics restores conservation by counting heat: ΔE = Q + W.

How it works
Start from the second law, F = mr̈. Dot both sides with ṙ: the left side is the power F·ṙ, the right is the time derivative of ½mṙ². Integrate along the path, and the work ∫F·dr equals the change in T.
If the work is path-independent and the force depends only on r, define V(r) as minus the work done in getting from a reference point to r. Then F = −∇V, the work from A to B is V(A) − V(B), and T + V takes the same value at both ends.
Worked examples

Harmonic oscillator. F = −kx comes from V = ½kx². Energy ½mẋ² + ½kx² is conserved, but momentum is not: the object keeps reversing.
With friction. Add a term −γẋ to the force. It depends on velocity, so it is not conservative, and the energy decreases.
Gravity of a large mass. V = −GMm/r is conservative and central, so both energy and angular momentum of the smaller body are conserved.

Beyond mechanics
Many particles. Energy is conserved if the external forces are conservative and each pair of particles interacts through a potential that depends only on their separation. Kinetic energy then splits into the motion of the centre of mass plus motion about it.
Thermodynamics. The first law says the work needed to take an isolated system between two states does not depend on how it is done, which defines E as a function of state. When energy can also enter as heat Q, E = Q + W.
Quantum mechanics. Only theories that conserve energy can be written with a Hamiltonian, so there is no Schrödinger equation for a system with friction.
Related

newtons-laws-of-motion: the second law this is derived from
second-law-of-thermodynamics: what conservation does not forbid

sections/physics/concepts/gauss-law.title: Gauss' Law
sections/physics/concepts/gauss-law.content:
Gauss’ Law
Gauss’ law says that the electric flux through any closed surface equals the total charge inside it divided by ε₀: ∮ E·dS = Q/ε₀.
In short

It is the integral form of the Maxwell equation ∇·E = ρ/ε₀, obtained with the divergence theorem.
The shape of the surface does not matter, only what it encloses: the result depends on topology, not geometry.
Charges outside the surface contribute zero net flux; their field goes in on one side and out the other.
With enough symmetry, it alone gives the field; without symmetry it must be combined with ∇×E = 0.

How it works
Integrate ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ over a region V with boundary S. The divergence theorem turns the left side into the flux through S, ∮ E·dS, and the right side is the enclosed charge Q over ε₀. The surface S is called the Gaussian surface, and the skill is choosing one on which E is constant or zero.
Worked example: Coulomb’s law
Take any spherically symmetric charge Q inside radius R and ask for the field at r > R. Choose a sphere of radius r as the Gaussian surface. By symmetry E points radially and has the same size E(r) everywhere on it, so the flux is E(r)·4πr². Setting that equal to Q/ε₀ gives
E = Q / (4πε₀r²),
pointing outwards. A test charge q there feels F = qQ/(4πε₀r²): repulsive for like charges, attractive for opposite ones. Nothing about the inside of the distribution mattered except its total and its symmetry.
Other shapes

An infinite line charge gives a field falling as 1/r.
An infinite plane gives a field that does not fall off at all, because the farther you move, the more of the plane is in view.
Crossing a surface charge, the perpendicular field jumps; inside a uniform charged shell the field is zero, so there is a discontinuity at the shell.

Where it is not enough
Without symmetry, E cannot be pulled out of the integral and Gauss’ law no longer fixes it. Then the electrostatic potential, E = −∇φ, is the general method. Gauss’ law also proves there is no point of stable electrostatic equilibrium in empty space.
Related

Maxwell-Equations: the four equations, of which this is the first
Electromagnetism
Physics

David Tong, Electromagnetism, Chapter 1: Introduction

sections/physics/concepts/measurement-pr.title: Measurement Problem
sections/physics/concepts/measurement-pr.content:
Measurement Problem
The measurement problem is the conflict between quantum mechanics’ two rules for how a state changes: smooth, linear Schrödinger evolution predicts that a measurement leaves the apparatus in a superposition of results, while the collapse postulate says it shows exactly one.
In short

Ordinarily a quantum state evolves by the Schrödinger equation, which is deterministic, unitary and linear.
On measurement, it is said to collapse into one eigenstate of the measured quantity, chosen with Born-rule probabilities.
Applied to a measuring device, the first rule contradicts the second.
Nobody has said, in the theory’s own terms, which interactions count as measurements.

How the contradiction arises
A device S* measures observable A on system S if its pointer B ends up correlated with A’s value. If S starts in the state A = a₁, the pair goes from (a₁, ready) to (a₁, pointer b₁); likewise for a₂.
Now start S in the superposition (1/√2)|a₁⟩ + (1/√2)|a₂⟩. Because Schrödinger evolution is linear, the pair must end in
(1/√2)|a₁, b₁⟩ + (1/√2)|a₂, b₂⟩,
a superposition in which the pointer has no definite reading. The collapse rule says instead that the pair ends in either |a₁, b₁⟩ or |a₂, b₂⟩, each with probability ½. Both cannot be right.
The ways out, and their cost

Drop collapse. Then the theory is consistent, but it conflicts with experience: we know what an apparatus in an eigenstate of its pointer looks like, and after a measurement that is what we see.
Keep collapse. Then the theory needs a principled line between ordinary interactions and measurements, which it does not supply.

Every interpretation of quantum mechanics is in large part a proposal about this problem. Ismael’s point is that it lies in the dynamics, not in the Hilbert-space mathematics, which by itself makes good sense.
Related

wavefunction: the state, and the two-slit case where measurement destroys interference
Quantum-Mechanics
Physics

David Tong, Quantum Mechanics, Chapter 1: Introduction

sections/physics/concepts/newtons-laws-o.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
sections/physics/concepts/newtons-laws-o.content:
Newton’s Laws of Motion
Newton’s laws say that free particles move uniformly in inertial frames, that force is the rate of change of momentum, and that internal forces come in equal and opposite pairs; together they already contain the conservation of momentum and angular momentum.
In short

First law: there exist inertial frames, in which a particle with no force on it moves at constant velocity.
Second law: F = ṗ, with momentum p = mṙ. F = ma is the special case of constant mass.
Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction; the strong form adds that the forces point along the line joining the particles.
Position and velocity at one instant fix the whole future trajectory.

How the laws build up
Frames. Ten independent transformations take one inertial frame to another: three rotations, three translations, three boosts and a shift of time. Together they form the Galilean group, under which Newton’s laws are unchanged. It is what the Poincaré group of special relativity becomes when the speed of light is taken to infinity.
Rotation. Angular momentum L = r × p and torque τ = r × F obey τ = L̇. Both depend on the choice of origin. A central force, one parallel to r, exerts no torque, so the Earth’s angular momentum about the Sun is constant.
Many particles. Add up the second law over all particles. By the third law, internal forces cancel in pairs, leaving F_ext = MR̈ for the centre of mass R. Total angular momentum is conserved only if the strong form of the third law holds.
Worked example: the cat and the tennis ball
Throw a tennis ball and a very lively cat along the same initial path. The cat twists and flails, but every one of those forces is internal and cancels by the third law. Only gravity is external, so the cat’s centre of mass follows the same parabola as the ball’s.
Where it breaks
The magnetic forces between two moving charges are not equal and opposite, so the third law fails. Momentum is still conserved, because the electromagnetic field carries the difference. Tong compares it to an underwater swimmer who seems to push off nothing. The cure is to count the field as part of the system (see Maxwell-Equations).
Tong’s complaint about the Newtonian framework as a whole is that it is awkward for extended bodies and hides the symmetries underneath. The Lagrangian and Hamiltonian reformulations trace each conservation law to a symmetry of space and time.

sections/physics/concepts/second-law-of-.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics
sections/physics/concepts/second-law-of-.content:
Second Law of Thermodynamics
The second law says that no process can have, as its only effect, the complete conversion of heat into work (Kelvin), or equivalently the flow of heat from a colder body to a hotter one (Clausius); its consequence is that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
In short

Its content is that time has a preferred direction.
Kelvin’s and Clausius’s statements imply each other.
From it: no engine beats a reversible one, an absolute temperature exists, and entropy is a function of state.
“Entropy increases” is a theorem derived from the law, not the axiom.

How it works
Carnot’s theorem. A Carnot engine runs a reversible cycle between a hot reservoir T_H and a cold one T_C: isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression. Its efficiency is η = W/Q_H. Suppose some engine did better. Run a Carnot engine backwards as a heat pump, driven by the better engine’s output, and the pair would move heat from cold to hot with no other effect, violating Clausius. So no engine beats a reversible one, and all reversible engines between the same two temperatures have the same efficiency.
Temperature. That common efficiency depends only on the two temperatures, which lets it define an absolute temperature, with η = 1 − T_C/T_H. Working through the cycle for an ideal gas gives the same formula, so the thermodynamic and ideal-gas temperatures agree.
Entropy. Around any reversible cycle ∮ dQ/T = 0, so dS = dQ/T defines a state function S. For any cycle at all, Clausius’s inequality gives ∮ dQ/T ≤ 0, and from that ΔS ≥ 0 for an isolated system. Combined with the first law, dE = T dS − p dV.
Worked example
An engine runs between a boiler at 500 K and surroundings at 300 K. Carnot’s bound is η = 1 − 300/500 = 0.4. At most 40% of the heat taken from the boiler can become work, whatever the engine is made of, and at least 60% must be dumped into the cold side. An engine with η = 1 would be exactly what Kelvin forbids.
What it is not
A refrigerator moving heat from cold to hot does not break Clausius’s statement, because heat transfer is not its sole effect: it consumes work.
Free energy
For a system held at fixed temperature by a reservoir, the total entropy of system plus reservoir cannot decrease, which means the system’s Helmholtz free energy F = E − TS cannot increase. At fixed temperature and pressure, the Gibbs free energy plays the same role.
Related

conservation-of-energy: the first law, which the second constrains
shannon-entropy: the information-theoretic entropy

sections/physics/concepts/wavefunction.title: Wavefunction
sections/physics/concepts/wavefunction.content:
Wavefunction
The wavefunction ψ(x, t) is the complete state of a quantum particle: a complex function over space whose squared modulus |ψ|² is the probability density of finding the particle at x.
In short

Classically the state is a position and a velocity; quantum mechanically it is a whole function.
Born rule: P(x, t) = |ψ(x, t)|². The particle is always found in one place; ψ is a wave of probability, not a spread-out substance.
This probability is not ignorance. There is no hidden information that would remove it.
Wavefunctions can be added: the sum of two states is a state, and that superposition produces interference.

How it works
Normalisation. The particle has to be somewhere, so ∫|ψ|² dx = 1. Only functions with a finite integral, which fall off fast enough at infinity, are physical states.
Phase. Multiplying ψ by a constant e^{iα} changes nothing measurable. A phase that varies with position leaves |ψ|² unchanged but alters other observables, so it is a different state.
Evolution. The Schrödinger equation iħ ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ is first order in time, so ψ at one moment fixes it at every other, and it keeps a normalised ψ normalised. Ĥ, the Hamiltonian, is the energy.
Vectors. The allowed wavefunctions form a vector space. In Hilbert-space language, ψ is the list of a state vector’s expansion coefficients in the position basis, written as a function because there are infinitely many of them.
Worked example: two slits
Fire electrons one at a time at a wall with two slits. With only slit 1 open, the screen pattern is P₁ = |ψ₁|²; with only slit 2, P₂ = |ψ₂|². With both open, superposition says the state is ψ₁ + ψ₂, so the pattern is
|ψ₁ + ψ₂|² = |ψ₁|² + |ψ₂|² + (cross terms),
not P₁ + P₂. The cross terms can be negative, so some places on the screen get fewer electrons with both slits open than with either alone. Each dot lands in one place, and the interference pattern builds up over thousands of electrons. Any device that records which slit an electron passed destroys the pattern.
What it is confused with
A field, like the electric field, is a real quantity spread through space. The wavefunction is not: no detector ever finds a fragment of a particle. Tong’s phrase is that it is a wave only of probability.
Related

measurement-problem: what happens to ψ when it is measured
conservation-of-energy: why there is no Schrödinger equation with friction

sections/physics/entities/maxwell-equati.title: Maxwell Equations
sections/physics/entities/maxwell-equati.content:
Maxwell Equations
The Maxwell equations are the four equations that say how charges and currents create electric and magnetic fields; with the Lorentz force law, which says how fields move charges, they are the whole of classical electromagnetism.
In short

Charged particles make the fields E and B; the fields push the particles; the motion changes the fields.
Influence travels through the fields and takes time, which is what makes electromagnetism local and compatible with relativity.
The equations look like four arbitrary lines of vector calculus but are, seen properly, essentially the unique ones that can describe the force.
Two constants set the strengths: ε₀ ≈ 8.85 × 10⁻¹² for electric interactions and μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ for magnetic ones (SI units).

The equations

∇·E = ρ/ε₀ — charge is the source of the electric field (Gauss’ law).
∇·B = 0 — the magnetic field has no sources.
∇×E + ∂B/∂t = 0 — a changing magnetic field makes a circulating electric field.
∇×B − μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t = μ₀J — currents, and changing electric fields, make a circulating magnetic field.

Here ρ is the charge density and J the current density. The force on a charge q moving with velocity ṙ is F = q(E + ṙ × B), or, per unit volume, f = ρE + J × B.
What they encode
Charge is conserved locally: ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J = 0. It can leave a region only by flowing through its boundary.
With nothing moving, J = 0 and B = 0, and the equations reduce to electrostatics: ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ and ∇×E = 0, which have a unique solution for a fixed charge distribution. A sphere of charge Q then gives Coulomb’s field, Q/(4πε₀r²).
Worked example: rescuing momentum
The magnetic forces between two moving charges are not equal and opposite, so Newton’s third law fails for them. Momentum is still conserved, because the electromagnetic field itself carries momentum. The field is a physical system with its own energy and momentum, not bookkeeping.
Related

gauss-law: the first equation in integral form, and how it gives Coulomb’s law
newtons-laws-of-motion: the third law the field rescues

sections/physics/topics/classical-mechan.title: Classical Mechanics
sections/physics/topics/classical-mechan.content:
Classical Mechanics
Classical mechanics is the physics of particles and bodies moving under forces, from Newton’s three laws to the conservation laws they contain.
In short

Force is the rate of change of momentum, and position plus velocity at one instant fix the future.
The third law makes internal forces cancel, so a body’s centre of mass moves as if all external force acted there.
For conservative forces, E = T + V is conserved; with friction it is not.
The Lagrangian and Hamiltonian reformulations trace each conservation law to a symmetry.

Choose a route

newtons-laws-of-motion: the laws, inertial frames, angular momentum and many-particle systems.
conservation-of-energy: work, potentials and when E = T + V holds.

sections/physics/topics/electromagnetism.title: Electromagnetism
sections/physics/topics/electromagnetism.content:
Electromagnetism
Electromagnetism is the theory of electric and magnetic fields: how charges and currents make them, and how they push charges in turn.
In short

Charge is conserved locally, which is the continuity equation.
Four Maxwell equations say how fields are made; the Lorentz force says how they act.
Fields make the force local, so influence takes time to travel.
In electrostatics, Gauss’ law plus symmetry gives fields directly, including Coulomb’s law.

Choose a route

sections/physics/topics/quantum-mechanic.title: Quantum Mechanics
sections/physics/topics/quantum-mechanic.content:
Quantum Mechanics
Quantum mechanics describes a system’s state as a vector in Hilbert space, a wavefunction for a single particle, whose squared magnitude gives the probabilities of what measurement will find.
In short

The state is a whole function, and |ψ|² is the probability of finding the particle at each place.
That probability is fundamental, not a lack of information.
States add, and their superposition produces interference that no trajectory can explain.
The rule for measurement contradicts the rule for evolution, which is the measurement problem.

Choose a route

wavefunction: the state, the Born rule, the Schrödinger equation and the double slit.

For the linear algebra behind Hilbert space, see four-fundamental-subspaces. Return to the physics domain map.

sections/physics/topics/thermodynamics.title: Thermodynamics
sections/physics/topics/thermodynamics.content:
Thermodynamics
Thermodynamics is the theory of heat, work and equilibrium, built from a few axioms that make no mention of atoms.
In short

The zeroth law makes temperature well defined; the first law is conservation of energy, with heat counted.
The second law forbids turning heat wholly into work, and so gives time a direction.
From it follow Carnot’s bound on engines, an absolute temperature, and entropy.
At fixed temperature, systems minimise free energy.

Choose a route

second-law-of-thermodynamics: Kelvin, Clausius, Carnot and entropy.

For entropy as a measure of information, see shannon-entropy. Return to the physics domain map.

sections/psychology/concepts/active-read.title: Active Reading
sections/psychology/concepts/active-read.content:
Active Reading
Active reading aims for comprehension and unaided reconstruction. The method has three gates1: build a rough schema before details arrive, summarize each section before advancing, and retrieve the ideas from memory before checking the text.
flowchart LR
  B[Before: scan structure and activate prior knowledge] --> D[During: read one section]
  D --> S{Can you summarize it?}
  S -->|no| D
  S -->|yes| R[After: close text and reconstruct]
  R --> C[Compare with source]
  C --> G[Target gaps on the next pass]

In short

A brief scan of structure gives working memory a schema to attach new material to, without replacing the reading.
A reader who cannot summarize a section and continues anyway carries the comprehension gap forward.
Retrieval from memory with the source closed, then comparison, reveals omissions; the difficulty is diagnostic, not failure.

Before: make somewhere for the ideas to go
A brief scan of headings, opening and closing sentences, emphasized terms, and summaries gives working memory a map for attaching new material to a section and question instead of receiving it as unrelated detail. This scan activates a schema but does not replace reading the argument.
During: summary is the gate
After each section, the reader pauses and states its function in one sentence. If the reader cannot produce a summary, continuing would optimize completion while carrying the comprehension gap forward. Slowing down, asking a question, predicting the next move, or connecting the claim to prior knowledge can repair the gap.
After: generation before recognition
Closing the source removes recognition cues. Writing or speaking from memory requires reconstruction, and a later comparison reveals omissions and distortions. The difficulty helps diagnose gaps and strengthen learning; it does not mean the method has failed.


                  
                  What are the three gates in the active-reading protocol? 
                  
                

Before: scan and activate a schema. During: do not advance without a section summary. After: retrieve without looking, then compare and target the gaps.


The metric changes the behavior
Page counts reward motion through a book. Active reading measures concepts that the reader can explain, connect, and later use. It takes longer per page because the reader moves effort from exposure to encoding. The screen-versus-paper question is secondary: reader mode, larger text, linear navigation, and removed notifications can protect the same architecture on a screen.
Crosslinks

Knowledge-Architecture: retained ideas become inputs to an external system
Deliberate-Practice: feedback targets the part that failed reconstruction
Working memory: overload explains why fluent eye movement can outlast comprehension


Built from sources written by ixcarus.



Works cited

sections/psychology/concepts/anxious-att.title: Anxious Attachment
sections/psychology/concepts/anxious-att.content:
Anxious Attachment

A relational pattern formed by an inconsistent childhood caregiver who might withdraw attachment at any moment, producing a nervous system that perpetually scans for signs of abandonment.

flowchart LR
  C[Inconsistent caregiver — the attachment might go at any moment] --> H[Hypervigilance — monitor tone, timing, energy]
  H --> A[Ambiguity read as an abandonment signal]
  A --> R[Reassurance seeking, then protest behaviours]
  R --> H
  I[An inconsistent partner keeps prediction error running] --> AC[High activation]
  AC -->|read as depth of feeling| B[Bonded hardest to the least reliable partner]
  S[A consistently available partner] --> L[Low activation]
  L -->|read as absence of love| B
  T[Tolerating distance, with a non-retaliatory figure] --> U[The working model slowly updates]

In short

An inconsistently available caregiver trains a child to watch for withdrawal. A consistently cold one produces avoidant-attachment instead.
In adults the same vigilance reads ambiguity as abandonment, then seeks reassurance, then escalates.
Activation gets read as depth of feeling, so the least reliable partner produces the strongest bond.
It is a default strategy and it updates: tolerate distance, self-soothe, and stay with someone consistent.

The Developmental Origin
A child develops anxious attachment when the primary caregiver is inconsistently available: sometimes warm and attuned, sometimes emotionally absent or withdrawn, with no reliable pattern the child can internalize and depend on.
Inconsistency drives this pattern. A consistently cold or unavailable caregiver teaches the child to stop expecting an emotional response, producing avoidant-attachment. An inconsistently available caregiver trains the child’s nervous system to stay alert to the caregiver’s emotional state because that unpredictable state mattered enormously.
The child develops hypervigilance as a survival strategy. Predicting when the attachment was safe and when it might be withdrawn helped the child secure it. The child therefore learned to monitor tone of voice, facial expression, energy level, and small behavioral shifts as early warning signals of potential withdrawal.


                  
                  Why is anxious hypervigilance a rational strategy rather than a distortion? 
                  
                

The threat-detection system is pattern-matching accurately against its own history. In that history, those small signals genuinely did precede withdrawal — the system is doing exactly the job it was trained for.


The Adult Pattern
In adulthood, any attachment figure who matters can activate this childhood working model, including a romantic partner and, at times, a close friendship or professional relationship. The nervous system repeats its childhood task: scanning for withdrawal signals and trying to prevent abandonment.
The characteristic features:
Hypervigilance to ambiguity: A delayed text message, a shorter response than usual, or a change in tone can register as an abandonment signal that requires evaluation. The person’s threat-detection system is matching these cues against a history in which they did precede withdrawal.
Reassurance seeking: Confirmation that the attachment remains secure eases the hypervigilance. Frequent check-ins, questions such as “are you okay?” or “are we okay?”, and a need for explicit statements of care all express the nervous system’s attempt to resolve uncertainty about the attachment’s stability.
The need feels real and urgent, while asking for it feels risky because the request could trigger the withdrawal they fear.


                  
                  What is the bind inside anxious reassurance-seeking? 
                  
                

The need is real and urgent, and asking for it is itself an exposure that could trigger the withdrawal being feared. The only direct route to relief runs through the risk it is trying to avoid.


Protest behaviors: When the attachment figure withdraws, either in fact or ambiguously, the anxiously attached person often escalates by calling or texting more, pushing for conversation, or becoming accusatory or emotionally intense. These protest behaviors attempt to re-establish the connection by making its absence more costly to maintain.
In an argument the anxious person is almost always the pursuer: they escalate, need resolution, and cannot tolerate unresolved tension, because disconnection feels like a limbic survival threat.


                  
                  What are protest behaviours? 
                  
                

Escalations — calling more, pushing for the conversation, becoming accusatory — that attempt to re-establish a connection by making its absence more costly to maintain. The intensity is a reconnection strategy, not an attack.


The Intermittent Reinforcement Trap
Anxiously attached people often feel the strongest attraction and form the tightest bonds with partners who trigger their attachment system most intensely. Avoidant or unpredictable partners often produce this intensity, while reliably loving partners do not.
The mechanism overlaps with variable-reward-mechanisms. A consistently warm, reliable partner produces little prediction error and therefore little phasic dopamine response around the attachment. An inconsistent partner produces continuous prediction error because the question of security remains unresolved, keeping the anticipatory dopamine system running.
An anxiously attached person can therefore experience stronger feelings of love, passion, and connection with an inconsistent partner than with a secure one. The inconsistent relationship is not better; the anxious nervous system interprets activation as depth of feeling. A nervous system trained to experience closeness as uncertain and urgent equates high anxiety with strong attachment.


                  
                  Why can a secure partner feel like less love than an inconsistent one? 
                  
                

Because activation is being read as depth of feeling. A reliable partner produces little prediction error and so little activation, and a nervous system trained on uncertain closeness interprets that calm as the absence of love.


Panic when a reply takes two hours is this loop running. The anxiety is dopamine withdrawal more than it is about the person.
Reading Anxious Attachment in Conversation
Four tells show up in conversation:

Reaction-checking: pausing mid-story to gauge your response, then adjusting to how you seem to receive it
Validation fishing: framing statements to invite reassurance (“you probably think I’m being ridiculous, but…”)
Who-personalizes-criticism: hearing feedback about a specific action as a comment on fundamental worth (“you’re saying I’m a bad person”)
Escalation velocity: reaching emotional intensity three levels above the current conversation by responding to tension with the weight of every previous time this kind of tension preceded abandonment

They are responding to every previous version of this moment. The amygdala matches the current situation to historical precedents, so the reaction carries the weight of those earlier moments.


                  
                  Why does a small tension trigger a response three levels above it? 
                  
                

The reaction is not to the current moment. The amygdala has matched it against every previous occasion that this kind of tension preceded abandonment, and fired at the weight of the whole set.


Heartbreak as Reset Point
Heartbreak can force recalibration. It hits anxiously attached people hardest because their attachment fear has always felt real, and it shows them who they were being for someone else: the parts they suppressed, the boundaries they ignored, the standards they lowered.
For an anxiously attached person, heartbreak may be the first time the abandonment threat materializes without proving fatal. Surviving it provides evidence against the nervous system’s core prediction.


                  
                  What can heartbreak specifically disprove for an anxiously attached person? 
                  
                

The nervous system’s core prediction. The abandonment it has spent a lifetime preventing actually happens and is survived, which is direct evidence against the belief that made the vigilance necessary.


After heartbreak, the anxiously attached person can use the clarity of loss to find where they abandoned their standards and lost themselves while pursuing attachment security, rather than focusing first on the next relationship.
Movement Toward Security
Anxious attachment is a default strategy rather than a permanent state. The path toward earned security involves:

Building the capacity to self-soothe without external reassurance (internal validation capacity, per validation-seeking)
Tolerating ambiguity in relationships without reaching at once for reassurance-seeking behavior
Sustaining a relationship with a consistently available, non-retaliatory attachment figure, which provides the corrective experience that slowly updates the internal working model

Tolerating distance without panic runs counter to everything the anxiously attached person’s nervous system has learned, which makes it the behavior they most need to practice.
Related

attachment-theory: the full framework and the caregiver patterns
avoidant-attachment: the complementary insecure pattern, and the one anxious attachment most often attracts
validation-seeking: the same drive expressed through social media
modern-dating-psychology: how these patterns meet contemporary dating infrastructure



Works cited

ixcarus, How To Read Someone’s Childhood From How They Talk To You
ixcarus, Why Modern Relationships Collapse After 6 Months
ixcarus, Why You Need to Get Your Heart Broken at Least Once
ixcarus, A Lack Of Purpose Leads To Romantic Obsessions

sections/psychology/concepts/attachment-.title: Attachment Theory
sections/psychology/concepts/attachment-.content:
Attachment Theory

The relationship with your first caregiver becomes the internal template for every significant relationship that follows, which is why the seven-year-old who learned to survive their family still runs your adult responses under pressure. The framework is John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth’s.

flowchart TD
  L[Limbic circuitry fires before the prefrontal cortex] --> T[Under real stakes the childhood pattern runs first]
  C1[Consistently responsive caregiver] --> S[Secure — conflict without catastrophe, closeness without suspicion]
  C2[Inconsistent caregiver] --> A[Anxious — continuous monitoring for withdrawal]
  C3[Consistently emotionally unavailable] --> V[Avoidant — the need shut down, distance under intensity]
  C4[Caregiver is both comfort and threat] --> DG[Disorganized — the impossible bind, closeness and flight at once]
  A --> T
  V --> T
  DG --> T
  R[Awareness, a sustained secure relationship, work on the wound] --> U[The internal working model updates]

In short

The child-caregiver pattern of the first years becomes the internal working model for later close relationships.
Limbic attachment circuitry fires before the prefrontal cortex, so under real stakes the childhood pattern runs first.
Responsive, inconsistent, unavailable, and frightening caregivers produce secure, anxious, avoidant, and disorganized patterns respectively.
Conflict is the most reliable place to read a style, because learned composure falls away fastest there.
Styles are default strategies that awareness, sustained secure relationships, and work on the wound can update.

The Core Claim
Psychiatrist John Bowlby developed attachment theory, and Mary Ainsworth expanded it through her Strange Situation experiments in the 1960s-70s. The theory makes an empirically robust claim: the relationship pattern formed between a child and their primary caregiver in the first years of life becomes the internal working model for all subsequent close relationships.
The theory describes a template, rather than a guide or tendency: a pre-conscious, neurologically encoded schema that determines default responses to closeness, vulnerability, conflict, and potential abandonment before the rational mind can evaluate the situation.
What comes through underneath is not the adult. It is the seven-year-old who learned how to survive the particular emotional environment they grew up in.
The Neurological Installation
Attachment patterns persist and resist conscious override partly because of anatomy. Early childhood encodes emotional responses and relational patterns in the limbic system, particularly the amygdala for threat responses and the broader attachment circuitry that governs how safe or dangerous other people feel.
This circuitry operates below conscious awareness and activates faster than the prefrontal cortex, the rational, deliberate, self-aware part of the brain. Under emotional pressure, the limbic attachment response fires before the adult self can evaluate the situation.
The consequence is that intelligent, self-aware, accomplished adults still collapse in conflict into patterns that look nothing like their normal selves. The child is always in there, and comes out when the stakes feel real.
The brain’s timing, rather than a failure of self-knowledge or intelligence, drives this response: the limbic system acts first, and the prefrontal cortex evaluates second. Under enough emotional pressure, the prefrontal cortex has little influence.


                  
                  Why can a self-aware adult still collapse into a childhood pattern under pressure? 
                  
                

Timing. The limbic attachment circuitry fires faster than the prefrontal cortex, so under real emotional stakes the response is already running by the time the deliberate mind gets to evaluate it.


The Four Attachment Styles
In her Strange Situation experiments, Ainsworth placed toddlers under mild stress and observed their responses when the caregiver left and returned. She first identified three attachment patterns; researchers later recognized a fourth:
Secure Attachment
Caregiver pattern: Consistently responsive. Present when needed, appropriately attuned, and reliably available without being intrusive.
Adult signature: Can tolerate conflict without catastrophizing. Receives care and vulnerability without suspicion. Maintains stable, trusting relationships. Can be close and separate at different times without reading either as rejection or entrapment.
Securely attached people seem to navigate relationships with a baseline of ease that others find almost confusing. ixcarus describes this as the rarest clinical pattern and says that most people carry some degree of insecure attachment.
What it protects: These individuals see others as basically trustworthy and themselves as basically worthy of care. They do not need to perform for love or brace against withdrawal.


                  
                  What internal model does secure attachment install? 
                  
                

That others are basically trustworthy and the self is basically worthy of care. Nothing has to be performed to earn love and nothing has to be braced against, which is what produces the ease others find confusing.


Anxious (Preoccupied) Attachment
Caregiver pattern: Inconsistent. Sometimes warm and attuned, sometimes withdrawn or emotionally unavailable, with no reliable pattern the child could learn. The child never knew which caregiver version was walking through the door.
Adult signature: Hypervigilance for abandonment signals. Reading into response times, tone, and ambiguity. Need for reassurance that feels uncomfortable to ask for directly. Escalation in relationships as the nervous system detects the withdrawal it was trained to expect.
Inconsistency taught the child’s nervous system that the attachment might be lost at any moment. The child responded by monitoring the attachment figure’s emotional state, and that monitoring transfers to new attachment figures in adulthood.


                  
                  Why does inconsistent caregiving produce a different pattern than consistently cold caregiving?
                  
                

Consistent unavailability teaches the child to stop expecting a response at all. Inconsistency teaches that the attachment is winnable but unpredictable, so the child develops continuous monitoring instead of shutdown.


See anxious-attachment for the full pattern.
Avoidant (Dismissive) Attachment
Caregiver pattern: Consistently emotionally unavailable. The caregiver may be physically present but unresponsive to emotional needs, dismissive of distress, uncomfortable with emotional expression, and inclined to reward independence and stoicism.
Adult signature: Emotional self-sufficiency to the point of distance. Withdrawal under emotional intensity. Genuine discomfort with high emotional demand. The person may appear indifferent to intimacy after learning to shut down a need that caregivers would not meet.
In conversation the avoidant is the one who disappears when things get real. The conversation gets vulnerable or difficult and they go flat, though not obviously: they are still talking and still physically present, but something has withdrawn.
See avoidant-attachment for the full pattern.
Disorganized (Fearful-Avoidant) Attachment
Caregiver pattern: The caregiver was both the source of comfort and the source of fear, often because of abuse, severe inconsistency, or the caregiver’s own overwhelming fear or grief.
Adult signature: This pattern creates what Bowlby called an “impossible bind.” The biological attachment system drives the child toward the caregiver for safety while the threat system drives the child away. No coherent strategy can manage this contradiction. As an adult, the person may swing between intense closeness and withdrawal, wanting and fearing connection at the same time.
The pattern is most commonly associated with trauma in the early environment. Adults with disorganized attachment often have the most chaotic relationship histories because their internal model of attachment contradicts itself, not because they want chaos.


                  
                  What is the "impossible bind" behind disorganized attachment? 
                  
                

The caregiver was both the source of comfort and the source of fear. The attachment system drives toward them for safety while the threat system drives away, and no coherent strategy can satisfy both.


Reading Attachment Styles in Real Time
Conflict and emotional activation are the most reliable diagnostic context. In these situations, adult scaffolding such as social skill and learned composure falls away fastest, allowing the childhood response pattern to take over.
Key observational dimensions:

Who pursues vs. who withdraws: In nearly every conflict, one person escalates and seeks resolution (anxious pattern), while the other withdraws and goes quiet (avoidant pattern). Both are scared but learned different ways to manage fear.
Who personalizes feedback: Hearing criticism of behavior as a verdict on personal worth signals a childhood history of conditional love, where what you did was who you were and mistakes were evidence of being a mistake.
Who needs to win: An inability to let conflict resolve through mutual agreement usually points to a childhood where being wrong had consequences and admitting fault felt unsafe.
Validation-checking frequency: The frequency with which someone references others’ opinions or checks your reaction while telling a story directly measures the internal validation available in childhood.



                  
                  In the pursue-withdraw conflict pattern, what do the two roles have in common? 
                  
                

Both are frightened. The escalation and the withdrawal are two different fear-management strategies learned in two different childhood environments, not a difference in how much either person cares.




                  
                  What does it indicate when someone hears criticism of an action as a verdict on their worth? 
                  
                

A history of conditional love, where what you did was who you were. The behaviour and the person were never separated, so a comment on one still lands as a judgement on the other.


The Malleability Question
Some accounts present attachment theory as deterministic, making a person no more than their childhood pattern. Bowlby did not take that position, and research does not support it. Attachment styles are default relational strategies, not fixed personality traits, and people can modify them through:

Awareness (seeing the pattern as a pattern rather than as reality)
Sustained secure relationships (a consistently responsive partner or therapist provides corrective experiences over time that gradually update the internal working model)
Explicit psychological work around the childhood wound itself

The work starts with learning to see the childhood pattern running in yourself and others. Understanding someone’s patterns is information about where they are: what they are managing and have not yet healed. It is not a tool for advantage.
Related

anxious-attachment: one of the two most common insecure patterns
avoidant-attachment: the other of the two most common insecure patterns

sections/psychology/concepts/attention-r.title: Attention–Retention Gap
sections/psychology/concepts/attention-r.content:
Attention–Retention Gap
The attention–retention gap measures how much content passes through awareness against how much remains as memory, judgment, action, or a chosen restorative experience. The illustrative case is 47 videos watched and perhaps three remembered.
flowchart LR
  F[Feed items consumed] --> A[Attention spent]
  A --> R[Retrievable memory]
  A --> D[Decision or action]
  A --> X[Chosen restoration]
  A --> N[Nothing retained]
  C[Continuation design] --> F



                  
                  What does the attention–retention gap measure that screen time alone misses? 
                  
                

Whether spent attention left anything retrievable, actionable, deliberately restorative, or chosen. Equal minutes can produce very different retained value.


The ratio is an anecdote, not a diagnostic threshold. Entertainment may have value without producing an artifact, though a continuation loop can keep the session running after its chosen purpose ends. A stopping condition and brief recall test expose the difference.

Attention-Economy: platforms optimise continuation, not retained value

sections/psychology/concepts/attribute-s.title: Attribute Substitution
sections/psychology/concepts/attribute-s.content:
Attribute Substitution
Attribute substitution is answering a hard question by silently answering an easier, related one: a judgment is heuristic when a target attribute is assessed through a heuristic attribute that comes more readily to mind.
In short

It is the common mechanism behind judgment heuristics such as representativeness and availability.
The substitute must be related to the target and highly accessible.
People are not confused about the question; they fail to notice they answered a different one.
Each heuristic is identified by the characteristic errors it produces.

How it works
The 1974 review by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman named three heuristics of judgment under uncertainty (representativeness, availability, anchoring) and a dozen biases, among them base-rate neglect, non-regressive prediction, overconfidence, and overestimating how often easily recalled events happen. Kahneman and Shane Frederick later gave them a single definition: substitution. Asked what proportion of long-distance relationships end within a year, someone answers whether examples of quick break-ups come easily to mind (availability). Asked the probability that one team beats another, they map relative strength onto a probability scale.
The definition excludes anchoring, which works by making one value of the target attribute more accessible, not by swapping attributes. It includes far more than probability: there is no finite list of heuristic attributes. Affect is a general-purpose one (Slovic and colleagues): an emotional valuation stands in for judgments of risk, benefit, donation size or punitive damages.
Worked example
Linda is 31, single, outspoken, very bright, a philosophy major once active on discrimination and anti-nuclear causes. Respondents ranked eight possible current descriptions, one group by how much Linda resembles each, another by how probable each is. The two rankings correlated .99. About 89% of the probability group ranked “bank teller and active in the feminist movement” above “bank teller”, which no conjunction can be (the conjunction fallacy). Their probability judgment was a resemblance judgment. The same design with Tom W., written to resemble students in small fields, gave a .97 correlation between probability and similarity, with base rates ignored.
A family: prototype heuristics
Some targets are sums over a set (how much a category contains, how bad a whole experience was), but what comes to mind is the prototype, an average. Substituting the average produces extension neglect. Households would pay $80, $78 and $88 to save 2,000, 20,000 and 200,000 migratory birds. Colonoscopy patients’ overall ratings correlated .03 with the procedure’s length and .67 with the average of the worst moment and the last (peak/end).
Related

dual-process-theory — why the substitution goes unchecked
Halo-Effect — the self-mastery section’s page on one impression standing in for unrelated traits
Judgment-and-Decision-Making — the domain this belongs to



Works cited

Daniel Kahneman, Maps of Bounded Rationality: A Perspective on Intuitive Judgment and Choice

sections/psychology/concepts/avoidance-r.title: Avoidance–Relief Loop
sections/psychology/concepts/avoidance-r.content:
Avoidance–Relief Loop
The avoidance–relief loop is a negative-reinforcement cycle: escaping an anticipated rejection, failure, confrontation, or aversive task removes distress at once, making escape more likely next time. The Neuroscience of Rejection: Why It Feels Like Pain (And How to Override It)1 applies the cycle to social pain; The Psychology Behind Procrastination2 applies it to task emotion. Both identify relief, rather than a lack of ambition, as the reward that maintains the pattern.
flowchart LR
  C[Anticipated rejection or confrontation] --> A[Threat arousal and narrowed thinking]
  A --> V[Avoid, delay, or stay silent]
  V --> R[Immediate relief]
  R --> L[System learns: avoidance produced safety]
  L --> H[Next cue carries greater threat and lower expected capacity]
  H --> A
  A -->|bounded exposure| E[Act while discomfort is manageable]
  E --> S[Survive outcome and collect corrective evidence]
  S --> H

In short

Escaping an anticipated rejection, failure, or aversive task removes distress at once, which makes escape more likely next time.
Relief, not a lack of ambition, is the reward that maintains the pattern.
Small, tolerable exposures give the system a learning event beyond relief, without guaranteeing acceptance.

Why avoidance feels like a solution
The feared event has not happened, arousal falls, and the open decision disappears. In the short term, withdrawal worked. The learning system cannot observe that the person might also have survived asking, failing, or setting the boundary, so it credits escape with producing safety.


                  
                  What reward keeps avoidance repeating? 
                  
                

Immediate relief. When withdrawal makes arousal stop, the system learns that escape produced safety and approaches the next similar cue with still less evidence of its own capacity.


Exposure changes the evidence, not the past
Small, intentional exposures need outcomes tolerable enough to process. Each attempt can show that rejection is a mismatch rather than bodily damage or a total identity verdict. The aim is to give the system a learning event beyond relief without seeking harm or causing overwhelm.
Slow exhalation can lower arousal enough to preserve a choice point. It supports the attempt without making rejection pleasant or guaranteeing acceptance.
Crosslinks

Insecurity: concealment similarly prevents corrective social evidence
Amygdala: anticipated threat can precede deliberate evaluation
Self-Sabotage: retreat restores a familiar baseline and is reinforced by relief
task-emotion-mapping: the task version asks which feeling is being escaped


Built from sources written by ixcarus.



Works cited

ixcarus, The Neuroscience of Rejection: Why It Feels Like Pain (And How to Override It)
ixcarus, The Psychology Behind Procrastination

sections/psychology/concepts/avoidant-at.title: Avoidant Attachment
sections/psychology/concepts/avoidant-at.content:
Avoidant Attachment

The avoidant craves connection as deeply as anyone, then dismantles it the moment it becomes real. This nervous-system solution to a childhood problem that no longer exists is not pathology.

flowchart TD
  C[Needs ignored, ridiculed, or made conditional] --> L[Learned — needing someone leads to pain]
  L --> S[Stop needing, build self-sufficiency, hold a distance]
  S --> A[Attractive early — independence reads as confidence]
  A --> I[Intimacy deepens]
  I --> T[Closeness registers as threat rather than safety]
  T --> D[Deactivating strategies — withdrawal, flaw-finding, distance-fights]
  D --> S
  P[Partner pushes for more closeness] -->|read as threat| T
  R[Predictable low-pressure presence] --> E[Evidence that vulnerability does not end as it did]
  E --> L

In short

Avoidant attachment rests on a learned association between closeness and danger, installed when early needs were ignored, ridiculed, or made conditional.
As intimacy deepens, closeness registers as threat and deactivating strategies such as withdrawal, flaw-finding, and distance-creating fights fire.
Under stress the avoidant seeks distance from the relationship and must self-regulate alone, which looks like coldness.
Fearful avoidants want connection intensely while fearing it, and oscillate between anxious and avoidant behaviors.
Pushing for closeness accelerates deactivation; consistent, predictable, low-pressure presence calms the system.

The Pattern
Avoidant attachment rests on a learned association between closeness and danger. Early caregivers consistently ignored the child’s emotional needs (dismissive parenting), met them with ridicule or punishment (shaming parenting), or offered care only when the child suppressed those needs.
The child’s developing nervous system learned that needing someone leads to pain. To avoid that pain, the child stopped showing vulnerability, built a self-sufficient internal world, and kept people at a functional distance.


                  
                  What lesson installs avoidant attachment? 
                  
                

That needing someone leads to pain. The nervous system’s solution is to stop needing — suppress the vulnerability, build a self-sufficient internal world, and hold people at a functional distance.


In adulthood, this manifests as:

Strong independence and self-sufficiency (often a genuine strength)
Discomfort when relationships become too close or demanding
Pulling back precisely when intimacy deepens
Emotional shutdown under relational stress through stonewalling, withdrawal, or silence
A pattern of ending relationships “just when they were getting serious”
Genuine enjoyment of connection from a distance but claustrophobia up close

The Intimacy Paradox
Avoidant people often make attractive partners early in relationships. Their independence, self-containment, and competence can make emotional unavailability look like confidence or mystery.
As intimacy deepens and the relationship begins to require genuine emotional presence, the avoidant nervous system detects a threat. Closeness registers as dangerous, prompting deactivating strategies such as emotional withdrawal, sudden attention to the partner’s flaws, idealization of single life, and fights that create distance.
The nervous system runs this survival program outside conscious choice: closeness brought danger in the past, so distance restores safety. The partner experiences the distance as rejection, while the avoidant experiences it as self-preservation.


                  
                  What are deactivating strategies, and when do they fire? 
                  
                

Withdrawal, suddenly noticing the partner’s flaws, idealising singlehood, picking distance-creating fights — and they fire precisely as intimacy deepens, because that is when the nervous system registers threat.


Neurological Roots
For an avoidant person, the attachment system seeks proximity to an attachment figure under stress while the threat-detection system pulls away from threatening stimuli.
In secure attachment, the nervous system registers close relationships as safe and uses them to reduce stress.
In avoidant attachment, the nervous system registers close relationships as threatening and responds to stress by seeking distance from the relationship instead of turning toward the relationship. Avoidant people must then self-regulate without relational support, an exhausting and demanding internal process that can look like coldness or emotional unavailability.


                  
                  Why is avoidant self-sufficiency expensive rather than easy? 
                  
                

Because the relationship cannot be used as a regulation resource. Where secure attachment turns toward the partner under stress, the avoidant must self-regulate alone — which looks like coldness and is actually a high-maintenance internal process.


The Dismissive vs. Fearful Avoidant Distinction
Two sub-types have different underlying drivers:
Dismissive avoidant: High self-view, low other-view. “I don’t need anyone.” This person deactivates attachment needs through genuine self-sufficiency and tends to minimize emotion: “It’s not a big deal.” They are rarely conscious of distress.
Fearful avoidant (also called disorganized): This person wants connection intensely while fearing it at the same time. The pattern often comes from severe early experiences such as abuse, neglect, or a parent who provided both comfort and fear. The person oscillates between anxious and avoidant behaviors; this is the most dysregulated attachment style.


                  
                  What separates the dismissive avoidant from the fearful avoidant? 
                  
                

The dismissive holds a high self-view and low other-view and genuinely deactivates the need — rarely in conscious distress. The fearful wants connection intensely and fears it simultaneously, oscillating between both patterns.


What Avoidants Actually Need
Pushing an avoidant person for more closeness when they pull back accelerates deactivation.


                  
                  Why does pushing an avoidant for closeness make the distance worse? 
                  
                

Pressure is read as threat, and threat is what triggered the deactivation in the first place. What calms the system is predictable low-pressure presence — safety without urgency.


The following practices help both avoidant people and secure partners who relate to them:

Consistent low-pressure presence: safety without urgency
Respecting the regulatory need for space without turning it into a rejection narrative
Predictability: avoidant nervous systems calm when they can predict relational outcomes; unpredictability, which anxious partners often create through protest behavior, increases the threat response
Healing for the avoidant themselves: recognizing the deactivating pattern in real time, tolerating the discomfort of closeness in increments, and building evidence that vulnerability does not produce the same outcome it produced in childhood

Reading Avoidance in Communication
Several markers reveal avoidant attachment in ordinary communication:

Late or inconsistent text responses as a regulation tool (maintaining distance)
Deflection through humor when conversations become emotional
Changing the topic when the conversation turns to needs, feelings, or future commitment
Focusing on problems in the partner or relationship when intimacy deepens (the critical eye appears at the point of closeness)
“I just need space” appearing at relationship milestones rather than in general

Related Concepts

sections/psychology/concepts/byproduct-s.title: Byproduct Signaling
sections/psychology/concepts/byproduct-s.content:
Byproduct Signaling
Byproduct signaling is the reading of a visible trait as an output of broader capability, as distinct from the same trait read as the optimized goal. Physique is the example: an observer may read muscle as evidence of health or practical capacity, or as evidence that appearance dominates the project.
flowchart LR
  P[Underlying practice] --> T[Visible trait]
  T --> O[Observer]
  C[Disclosure and context] --> O
  O --> B[Byproduct interpretation: trait points beyond itself]
  O --> G[Goal interpretation: trait is the project]
  U[Unknown history] --> O

In short

Interpretation determines the signal, and appearance alone cannot reveal the history, motives, health or competence behind a trait.
Disclosure changes the narrative around a trait without changing the body or proving the narrative correct.
Hiding effort to preserve an illusion is less defensible than building the substrate and communicating with restraint.

In detail
Interpretation determines the signal. An observer cannot reliably infer the history, motives, health, or competence behind a trait from appearance alone. Disclosure changes the narrative around the signal without changing the body or proving that narrative correct.


                  
                  What changes when a trait moves from a byproduct signal to a goal signal? 
                  
                

The observer’s account of what the trait points to changes. The trait itself does not reveal whether the account, the motive, or the claimed capability is true.


Ethical application
The essay recommends hiding effort to preserve an illusion. A more defensible approach develops the substrate and communicates with restraint: build health, competence, or craft; answer the question asked; do not invent effortless genetics or fictional labour. Honest effort can signal commitment and skill.
This distinction also limits Attraction-as-Health-Signaling. Visible features are proxies, not medical tests. Culture, individual preference, presentation, and context shape what an observer thinks a proxy means.
Crosslinks

body-composition: the physical trait used in the source’s example
health-signaling-theory: underlying state and visible proxy can diverge
strategic-adaptation: legibility of real work differs from fabrication
Relationships-and-Attraction: no universal gender preference follows from one anecdote



Works cited

ixcarus, The Gym Bro Paradox: Great Body, Zero Game
ixcarus, Why Attraction Is Health Signaling (And How to Optimize It)

sections/psychology/concepts/calibrated-.title: Calibrated Self-Interest
sections/psychology/concepts/calibrated-.content:
Calibrated Self-Interest
Calibrated self-interest combines self-protection, pride, ambition, and recognition-seeking with empathy and reciprocity. This middle range distinguishes ordinary self-focus from self-erasure and exploitative narcissism1.
flowchart LR
  Z[Too little self-protection] --> B[Weak boundaries, resentment, burnout]
  C[Calibrated self-interest] --> H[Self-respect, pride, ambition, contribution]
  H --> E[Empathy and reciprocity keep costs represented]
  P[Fragile grandiosity] --> V[Constant validation requirement]
  V --> X[Entitlement, devaluation, exploitation]

In short

Self-interest is healthy when worth stays stable without applause and another’s perspective survives a conflict of interests.
Too little represents none of one’s own needs and too much represents only one’s own; calibration keeps both parties in the model.
Grandiosity depends on external confirmation, so criticism or another’s success can provoke devaluation; stable pride needs no such defense.

Self-prioritization is not sufficient evidence of pathology
Sharing an achievement, setting a boundary, and wanting recognition can all be ordinary. What distinguishes them is their organization and cost: does worth remain stable without applause, and can the person retain another’s perspective when interests conflict?


                  
                  What calibrates healthy self-interest? 
                  
                

Empathy and reciprocity. Self-respect, pride, and ambition remain healthy when they do not require another person to be diminished, exploited, or made responsible for stabilizing one’s worth.


Too little and too much can share one missing boundary
At one end, the person cannot represent their own needs and calls every boundary selfish. At the other, the person represents only their own needs. Calibration keeps both parties in the model instead of seeking a morally pure absence of self-interest.
Fragility is more diagnostic than confidence
Grandiosity may look like excess confidence while depending on external confirmation. Criticism, divided attention, or another person’s success can then threaten it and provoke devaluation. Stable pride does not require that defense.
Crosslinks

Ego: self-reference and identity protection
Universal-Selfishness: self-interest as a general behavioral input
Dark-Triad: the exploitative end of the source’s continuum
self-respect-through-kept-promises: internally generated evidence of worth


Built from sources written by ixcarus.



Works cited

ixcarus, Why We’re All Narcissistic (And Why That’s Okay)

sections/psychology/concepts/childhood-w.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
sections/psychology/concepts/childhood-w.content:
Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
Early relationships can supply templates for later expectations about safety, need, conflict, and care. Adult behaviour may carry traces of those templates, but it does not reveal a childhood with diagnostic certainty; the same conversational pattern can arise from many histories and contexts.
flowchart TD
  W[Birth to seven — high plasticity, minimal critical filtering] --> E[Emotional unavailability]
  W --> C[Conditional love]
  W --> P[Emotional punishment]
  W --> I[Inconsistency]
  W --> PA[Parentification]
  E --> D[A body-level operating system for every later relationship]
  C --> D
  P --> D
  I --> D
  PA --> D
  D -->|left uninterrupted| G[Transmitted to the next generation]
  R[Somatic awareness, corrective relationship, exposure, naming] --> D

In short

In early childhood a dependent child learns relational expectations before it can contextualise them, though no hard neurological cutoff fixes them.
Emotional unavailability, conditional love, emotional punishment, inconsistency and parentification each install a recognisable adult pattern.
Communication patterns can prompt a curious question about someone’s history, never a diagnosis from a single behaviour.
Without deliberate interruption, parents transmit what they received, so the wound is generational and not a personal fault.
Awareness alone does not change a body-level pattern; somatic awareness, corrective relationships, exposure and naming do.

The Installation Window
Early childhood is a high-plasticity period in which a dependent child learns relational expectations before having an adult’s capacity to contextualise them. The “birth to seven / theta / no critical filter” formula is an author-level simplification, not a hard neurological boundary after which these patterns become fixed.
During this window, the child builds a basic self-concept around four questions: Am I lovable? Am I safe? Are other people reliable? Is the world threatening or benign? The answers are body-level encodings rather than intellectual conclusions, myelinated into the nervous system through thousands of repetitions of early relational experience.


                  
                  Why does the birth-to-seven window carry disproportionate weight? 
                  
                

Plasticity is unusually high, theta activity dominates, and critical filtering is minimal. The environment is absorbed without the capacity to evaluate or reject it, and the encodings are body-level rather than intellectual.


These encodings become the default operating system for later relationships.
How Wounds Are Installed
Emotional unavailability: A parent may be physically present but emotionally absent, distracted, depressed, anxious, or uninvested. The child learns: emotional needs are not worth expressing; connection is unreliable; I should not expect to matter to others. In adulthood: difficulty with intimacy, emotional self-sufficiency that feels like coldness, chronic low-grade loneliness.
Conditional love: “I love you when you’re good/successful/quiet/grateful.” The child learns: I am only worthy of love when I perform well. Love is earned, not given. Self-assessment remains contingent on external validation. In adulthood: achievement-seeking as a bid for love, perfectionism, vulnerability avoidance, compulsive people-pleasing.
Emotional punishment: A caregiver met anger, sadness, or fear with punishment, rejection, or ridicule. The child learns: my emotions are dangerous; showing them leads to worse outcomes. The child suppresses those emotions. In adulthood: emotional numbness, inability to identify feelings, explosive eruptions when suppression fails, attraction to emotionally suppressive environments because they feel normal.
Inconsistency: A caregiver may alternate between warmth and cold or frightening behaviour without warning. The child cannot model when connection is safe. In adulthood: hypervigilance for emotional tone shifts; attachment anxiety; compulsive attempts to stabilize others’ emotional states.
Parentification: The child has to take care of the parent’s emotional needs by managing depression, mediating between parents, or serving as a confidant. This inverts boundaries. In adulthood: compulsive caretaking, inability to receive care without guilt, relationships where the person is always the helper.


                  
                  What does parentification produce in adulthood? 
                  
                

Inverted boundaries that never righted — compulsive caretaking, an inability to receive care without guilt, and relationships in which the person is permanently the helper.


Reading Someone’s Childhood From How They Talk to You
Communication patterns can serve as hypotheses about relational learning. The observations below can guide a curious question; they should not be used to infer another person’s trauma, attachment, or caregivers from a single behaviour:
How they handle conflict: A person who goes cold and silent may have learned that direct conflict was unsafe. Someone who escalates at once may have learned that only intensity gets a response. Someone who apologizes regardless of fault may have learned that appeasing was safest.
Their relationship with needs: Does someone ask for things directly or hope you’ll notice? Someone who cannot state needs directly may have learned that doing so led to rejection or punishment.
How they receive compliments: A person who dismisses or deflects compliments may not have received warm mirroring. Someone who returns a compliment at once may have learned that receiving without reciprocating felt unsafe.
Disproportionate reactions: A tone shift or request for space may activate an older expectation. The trigger identifies a present sensitivity; it does not by itself reveal the original event.
How they show love: People often love others the way they were loved or the way they wished they had been loved. This can offer a window into history and create relational mismatch. Two people whose love languages were shaped by different wounds may both offer real love while missing each other again and again.


                  
                  How can two people both love genuinely and consistently miss each other? 
                  
                

Because each loves the way they were loved, or the way they wished they had been. Two histories produce two grammars, and neither is failing to give — they are giving in a form the other was not taught to receive.


The Inheritance Pattern
Without deliberate interruption, parents can transmit wounds:

The anxiously-attached parent raises anxiously-attached children (hyper-monitoring of emotional cues, conditional availability)
The emotionally unavailable parent raises children who either replicate unavailability or develop anxious hypervigilance in response to it
The family’s relationship to money, conflict, closeness, success, and emotion becomes the child’s default model

The framework describes a mechanism rather than assigning blame. Most parents pass on what they received without examining its origins. The wound is therefore generational and is not treated as a personal fault.


                  
                  Why is the inheritance framing offered as mechanism rather than blame? 
                  
                

Because most parents are transmitting what they themselves received, without having examined its origin. The wound is generational, so locating it is a description of the transfer rather than an accusation.


Interrupting the Pattern
Awareness alone cannot change patterns encoded in the nervous system as well as the intellect. Interruption requires:
Somatic awareness: Learning to notice an old wound in the body before it shapes behavior, such as the contraction in the chest before defensive speech or the shutdown before stonewalling. Change becomes possible in the interval between trigger and response.
Therapeutic relationship: A consistent, regulated, reliable relational presence can provide a corrective experience at the nervous system level. Experiencing safety in a relationship updates the body’s prediction model more effectively than intellectual understanding alone.
Intentional exposure: Practicing new responses to old triggers in low-stakes contexts. This might mean asking for something when the impulse is to wait and hope someone notices, or staying emotionally present when the old pattern would be to shut down. Small-scale repetitions myelinate new response pathways.
Pattern recognition: Naming the pattern, such as “I’m doing the thing where I go quiet when I feel criticized”, makes it less automatic. A visible pattern is easier to interrupt.


                  
                  Why is awareness necessary but not sufficient here? 
                  
                

The patterns are encoded in the nervous system rather than the intellect. Naming one removes its automatic quality, but changing it needs somatic awareness and corrective relational experience, not insight alone.


Related Concepts

sections/psychology/concepts/chunking.title: Chunking
sections/psychology/concepts/chunking.content:
Chunking
Chunking is grouping input into larger familiar units, so that a memory span fixed in the number of units can hold more information.
In short

Immediate memory holds a roughly constant number of items, about seven, whatever each item carries.
Absolute judgment is different: it is capped by the amount of information, about 2.6 bits on one dimension.
So the way to remember more is to pack more bits into each chunk, by recoding.
Recoding only pays once the translation is close to automatic.

Two limits that look alike
George Miller noticed seven turning up in two places and argued they are different limits. In absolute judgment (name which of N tones you just heard) people top out at a fixed amount of transmitted information: about 2.5 bits for pitch, 2.3 for loudness, 1.9 for salt concentration, 3.25 to 3.9 for a pointer’s position on a line. Across such dimensions the mean is 2.6 bits, about 6.5 categories, and adding dimensions raises the total while making each judgment cruder.
If memory worked the same way, the span would shrink as items got richer. A decimal digit carries 3.3 bits and a word drawn from 1,000 monosyllables about 10, so a fixed 23-bit store would hold seven digits but only two or three words. Hayes and Pollack found otherwise: the span is about nine binary digits and still about five words. Memory is limited in chunks, not bits.
How recoding works
Group the input events, give the group a new name, and remember the name instead of the events. A learner of radiotelegraphic code first hears every dit and dah as a separate chunk, then letters, then words, then phrases; the amount he can hold grows as the chunks grow.
Worked example
Eighteen binary digits, 101000100111001110, are well past the binary span of about nine. Read them in threes, 101 000 100 111 001 110, and rename each triple as an octal digit: 5 0 4 7 1 6. Six chunks fit easily. Sidney Smith drilled himself on this kind of recoding at ratios up to 5:1. His octal span was 12, and with practised recoding he could repeat about 40 binary digits without error. Subjects given only 5 to 10 minutes with the scheme gained less, because converting one group cost them the next.
Beyond digits
Miller thought the commonest recoding is verbal: we remember an event by remembering our own description of it and rebuild the details on recall, which is why eyewitness errors follow the witness’s wording rather than falling at random. Memorising may simply be forming chunks until there are few enough to recall.
Related

forgetting-curve — what happens to material once it is past the span
Psychology-of-Memory — the domain this belongs to
Psychology — the field hub



Works cited

George A. Miller, The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on our Capacity for Processing Information

sections/psychology/concepts/cognitive-d.title: Cognitive Decentering
sections/psychology/concepts/cognitive-d.content:
Cognitive Decentering
Cognitive decentering is the stance that a thought can be observed without being treated as the observer’s identity, a fact, or an instruction. It starts from noticing both the act of reading and awareness of reading1, then applies the same distance to self-statements such as “I cannot change.”
flowchart LR
  T[Thought appears] --> N[Notice it]
  N --> L[Label it as a mental event]
  L --> Q[Question evidence and context]
  Q --> C[Choose an action]
  C --> B[Thought no longer defines the available behaviour]



                  
                  What is the practical sequence of cognitive decentering? 
                  
                

Notice the thought, label it as a mental event, question it, then choose an action.




                  
                  What does decentering change without removing resistance? 
                  
                

It stops a momentary thought from automatically defining identity or available behaviour.


In short

Notice, label, question, and choose: the thought becomes a mental event examined before action.
Joined to experiments, it supports Identity-Shift by supplying disconfirming experience.
The exercise does not establish that awareness is the true self.

In detail
The practical sequence is notice, label, question, and choose. “I am lazy” becomes “a thought that I am lazy is present”; its evidence and context can then be examined before action. The extra distance does not remove resistance, but it prevents a momentary mental event from automatically defining the available behaviour.
Decentering can support Identity-Shift when it is joined to experiments. Seeking a different conversation, environment, or activity supplies disconfirming experience; repeated action can show that an inherited self-story is incomplete. Observation and behaviour therefore update one another.
Metaphysical boundary
The source moves from the experience of observing thoughts to claims that awareness is the true self, limitless, unconditioned, and able to make transformation inevitable. The exercise does not establish those claims. Decentering can be used as a psychological technique while remaining neutral about the ontology of consciousness and the Phenomenal-Self.
Related

Subconscious-Programming: stories and conditioned responses
